- **Scenarios run: all six, none dropped — plus a seventh set of entries from the infrastructure build-out that had to precede them.** W3-1 (cache object deleted / torn mid-restore — Parts A1 / A' / B1 / B2 / C1 / C2 / C3 plus the cleanup-interval read: **5 entries**), W3-2 (S3 outage during archival and artifact upload — Parts A / A2 / B arms 1-2 / C / D across two stack phases: **4 entries**), W3-3 (mixed-KEK replicas — Parts A / B / B5 / C / D / D3: **4 entries**), W3-4 (bulk log-append duplication — Parts A / B / C / D / D2 / D3 / D4, plus a Part E archive limb re-run added after Task 3 gave the rig an object store: **2 entries**), W3-5 (archive seal racing the final log flush — Parts A / B / C / E: **2 entries**), W3-6 (run retention racing an in-flight artifact upload — Parts A / B / C, with Part D skipped and the skip argued in the entry: **3 entries**), and **W3-infra** — Task 3's rig build-out, which is not a scenario and produced **3 entries** of its own plus the object store every later scenario depended on. **23 entries total = 9 violation entries (9 new violations) + 13 observations + 1 resolved branch-internal asset bug.** *(Tallied mechanically from the title markers and Severity lines, then reconciled by hand. Several classifications and attributions were corrected during this wave's reviews and the corrections are load-bearing — the numbers below are as the entries now state them and must not be re-merged.)* **The 9/13 split supersedes an 8/14 one that stood until the branch review: W3-2's archiver-backoff entry (`:1736`) was filed as an observation ruling "the docs are silent" on `docs/operations.md:53`, a published paragraph that names the log archiver and whose two clauses that entry's own measurements falsify. It is now a documented-contract violation. The entry count is unchanged — one entry moved buckets, nothing was added or split.**
- **Classification rule:** unchanged from W0, W1 and W2 and applied to every entry above — **violation** = observed behaviour contradicts an invariant (I1-I7) **or a documented contract**; **observation** = behaviour matched expectations but reveals a risk; **third bucket** = a defect in the campaign's own assets, fixed inside this branch, reported outside both tallies. The W1/W2 clarifications carry unchanged: the "documented contract" limb requires a *published* promise (an exported API field, a schema column, or a statement in `docs/`) and **not** an unexported helper's own doc comment. **W3 extended that limb once, and the extension is deliberate: an inline comment inside the body of an *exported, routed* handler is also not a contract.** W3-6 (`:1838`) met the letter of the W2 rule — `handleArtifactUpload` is exported and routed, so the rule as written did not disqualify its comment — and declined to use it anyway, on the ground that a comment inside a function body is not *published* to anyone. The same call is made at W3-1 (`:1996`) for `Save`'s comment and at W3-2 (`:1790`) for the archiver's. **In all three the comment is cited as evidence of intent, which is worth more than a contract would be, because in two of the three the comment's own second sentence is false in exactly the case its first sentence warns about.** W2's *procedural* amendment (an entry may be a violation entry without being an additive violation) had no occasion to fire this wave: all nine violation entries are additive, so **violation entries 9 = new violations 9**. **One number replaces it and W4 must carry it forward: of those 9, exactly one — W3-6 (`:1864`) — was NEVER EXECUTED.** It is a code read filed as a violation because leaving it unfiled would have made a sibling entry's completeness claim false, and it says so in its own Repro line ("**NONE. This entry was not executed**"). It is counted in the tally, and any triage that acts on it must measure it first; the entry itself specifies the measurement and says it takes minutes.
- **Violations: 9 new — 4 major, 5 minor.** Per scenario: W3-1 **1** (0 major / 1 minor), W3-2 **2** (0/2), W3-3 **2** (1/1), W3-4 **1** (1/0), W3-5 **1** (1/0), W3-6 **2** (1/1), W3-infra **0**. By primary limb: **documented contract 5, I4 2, I5 1, I7 1** — which is the same 9, and is the first wave in the campaign where the *contract* limb outnumbers every invariant — and, after the branch review moved `:1736`, outnumbers **all four invariant limbs combined** (5 versus 4) and is the outright majority of the wave's violations.
  - **major, I4 — W3-4** (`:1521`): a bulk log append is a bare per-line loop with no transaction and no idempotency, so any failure the agent sees for a request the controller already committed is answered by re-sending it. A `Succeeded` run whose workload emitted **2002** lines was stored, and served, with **8493** — **4.24x** — with 2000 duplicate groups and 8490 of 8491 burst lines out of position; the cheaper arm turned one 200 ms proxy-timeout **arm** into three separately timed-out requests each leaving a committed prefix (**173/193/190**, surplus 556 = 2558 rows against 2002 emitted). Postgres confirms there was never a transaction to roll back: **2558** `INSERT INTO logs`, **0** `rollback`. - **THE WAVE FOUND TWO HOLES IN THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN INVARIANT SET, AND THIS IS THE CHECKPOINT'S MOST IMPORTANT CARRY-FORWARD. They are coverage gaps, not absences of defect.** Both were found the same way — an entry with a real, permanent, silent data defect looking for the invariant that covers it and finding none — and both are flagged at the entries themselves (`:1621`, `:1947`) with an explicit instruction to raise them here.
  1. **No secret-store integrity clause (W3-3).** I4's subject is "Log/**artifact** integrity" by its own text (`…design.md:51`) and nothing covers secrets. I7 (`:54`) enumerates "run status, approval status, and audit rows", so the secrets list API reporting a **permanently undecryptable** secret as present is adjacent to that and outside its stated scope, and stretching it would repeat the mis-attribution W2-9 had withdrawn in review. **W3-3 escaped the gap only because it found a published-contract limb** (`docs/secrets.md:420`), and that limb is an accident of the docs, not of the invariant set.
  2. **No cache-integrity clause (W3-1).** Same reason, same text. The other six invariants are about run terminality (I1), at-most-once execution (I2), lock leaks (I3), bounded recovery (I5), zombie windows (I6) and status/audit consistency (I7). **W3-1 had no contract limb** — its Expected rules the docs silent on a survey re-derived independently in review — so here the gap is **load-bearing**: it is the sole reason the wave's most damaging cache finding is filed as an observation rather than a violation.
  - **What should be done about it, stated as a recommendation rather than an action, because amending the spec is out of this wave's scope.** The cheapest correct fix is a **single generalised clause**, not two: I4's subject should read *stored-state integrity* and enumerate the object classes the system persists on a run's behalf — logs, artifacts, log archives, **cache entries** and **secrets** — with the existing predicate ("matches what was written; no duplicates, no reordering; stays readable and decryptable") applied to each. Two narrow clauses would leave the next class (`run_outputs`? `step_outputs`? the git-template cache?) uncovered by the identical argument. **Whoever takes it must re-run the classification of exactly two entries and no others** — W3-1 (`:1938`) becomes a violation with no new evidence, and W3-3 (`:1620`) gains a second limb without changing its disposition — and must **not** disturb W3-1 (`:1986`), which already stands on a contract. **Until that happens, W4-W6 must not read "no invariant contradicted" as "nothing is wrong": check whether the invariant's *subject* reaches the object before concluding anything from its silence.** This is the third consecutive wave in which the campaign's own definitions, rather than the product, were the thing that needed correcting — W1 refined I1-vs-I7, W2 amended it again and added the non-additive-violation rule, and W3 found two holes in the coverage itself.

### Cross-wave carry-forward

- **1. The two invariant-coverage gaps above are the wave's highest-value follow-up, and they are cheap.** See the bullet immediately above for the recommended amendment and for the exactly-two entries that must be re-classified with it. Nothing else in the W3 batch changes as much for as little.
- **2. `RunGitResolver` is STILL OPEN, and W3 did not take it. It should go to W4 or W5, and it needs the fixture W2 specified.** The W2 checkpoint's item 3 recommended "one W3 task builds the git-over-HTTP fixture (dumb protocol: bare repo + `git update-server-info` + static file server) and four scenarios consume it". **That did not happen.** W3's infrastructure task added *object storage* (Garage + an `mc` client + an S3 interposer), which is a different dependency entirely and does nothing for a git-backed job. Nothing in W3 touched `resolveGitPendingRuns`, `ResolveSpec`, or a `git://` `uses:`. **So every W2 finding queued behind that fixture is untouched and carries forward unchanged:** the resolver's per-candidate `ResolveSpec` (a git fetch plus, for private repos, a secret decrypt) running on **every** replica with no lock; the per-replica `failureBackoff` that `docs/operations.md:53` — a *published* paragraph, which is the strongest available limb and better than the unexported comment — says "is held by the current leader only and resets on failover"; the resolve-deadline `AppendLog` that N replicas can each write to one run's log with no lock and no CAS; **W1-7** (AppSource reconciler); **W2-4's** un-run git variant; and **W2-9's** git amplifier and its second, independent hardcoded 50. **Recommendation: W4 takes it if W4 has a task to spare, and W5 otherwise — but it must be the same task that builds the fixture, and it must not be split across waves again.** W3 is the second wave to defer it; a third deferral should be read as a decision to drop it rather than as scheduling. **One thing W3 does contribute:** the object store now exists on `test/ha`, so a git fixture no longer has to bring its own storage, and the `s3proxy` interposer pattern (an nginx sitting between the product and a dependency, stamping `arm=` on every request) is directly reusable as a **git-over-HTTP** interposer — which would give the resolver scenario per-request brackets for free. **CORRECTED AT BRANCH REVIEW — this item forwarded the wrong scope for `docs/operations.md:53` and W4 must read the narrowed version.** That paragraph covers three sweeps, and W3 **did** measure one of them: **W3-2 (`:1736`) falsified both of its clauses live on the log archiver and is filed as a documented-contract violation**, so the archiver's instance is no longer unfiled and must not be re-filed by whoever takes the fixture. What carries forward here is the **git resolver's** instance only — same sentence, different sweep, still unmeasured for want of the fixture — alongside the run-retention sweeper's, which is likewise still code-read. **The measured archiver result strengthens the resolver item rather than replacing it:** the resolver's backoff is per-replica by an *even weaker* mechanism (no lock at all, versus a lock that is merely not sticky), so a scenario that reaches it can now cite a live falsification of the same sentence on a sibling sweep instead of arguing from code alone — see the ledger at `:1758`.
- **3. The `LogPusher` quadratic request amplification remains a W6-S2 input, unchanged by W3, and W3 sharpened the caution attached to it.** W1-6 measured `flushLocked` re-issuing a full `AppendLogBulk` for **every** batch still pending on each 2 s tick, so cumulative volume is triangular — **O(t²) in outage duration, not O(t)**. W3 exercised nothing that bears on the amplification itself, and **W3-5's Part B is not a counter-measurement**: its nine bulk requests over 3 s are a heal-burst, not a sustained outage. It stays owned by **W6-S2**, which must measure request-count *shape* alongside drop-marker frequency and lost-line counts, and the disk-spill decision stays gated on that measurement and must be taken together with the coalesce-the-backlog fix. **W3-5 added the caution that now sits at both ends** (`:474`, `:496`, `:1491`, `:1934`): before any coalescing change is generalised beyond one per-`(run, step)` pusher into an **agent-level** batcher, fix `handleAgentLogBulk`'s scalar `droppedRun` — and note the refinement W3-5 made in its own note, that W1-6's fix **as written** ("coalesce all pending batches", batches not runs) cannot produce a mixed batch and the conflict is with the agent-level generalisation only. **Keep the five `LogPusher`/`AppendLog` shapes distinct when triaging, because W3 added a fourth and a fifth and none overlaps the others:** **F9** is loss at the 1 MiB `p.pending` byte cap (never approached in any W3 arm — `grep -c` over both agents for W3-4's whole session: **0**); the **W1-2 major** is loss at the bounded 5 s step-end `Flush` budget; **W1-6** is pure wasted request volume with no loss; **W3-4** is no loss at all and a permanent *surplus* instead, and is the only one where the **controller**, not the agent, is the party that gets it wrong; and **W3-5** is bytes that arrive, are accepted with a `204`, and are discarded server-side.
- **4. Four escalation calls are left explicitly to the operator, and they are left open on purpose rather than by omission.** Each entry argues its own severity against this file's bands (`:6-8`) and each says where the boundary is. **W3-3** (`:1640`): permanent, silent destruction of secrets written during a mixed window, with no marker on the row, no way to enumerate affected rows and no health surface that goes red — held below critical only because it requires an operator to have already violated a boldfaced, thrice-repeated checklist item. **W3-4** (`:1562`): permanently duplicated *and reordered* stored content served by every read surface, which meets the "silent corruption" disjunct on its text, filed major purely for **calibration** — this file holds zero criticals across 72 entries at the time of filing and the W1-2 major is the mirror-image defect in the same machinery. **W3-1** (`:1950`): the same calibration argument, made explicitly against W1-2, W3-4 and W3-5, with the note that a reader who weighs the docs' own canonical `if [ ! -d vendor ]` cache example may reasonably read it as critical. **W3-6** (`:1866`): `jobs delete` leaks both key spaces for every run of the job on 100 % of invocations, with an automated caller. **The pattern is now stable enough to name: this campaign's `major` band is load-bearing and its `critical` band is empty, and that is a calibration decision, not a measurement.** If the operator escalates any one of these, all four should be re-read together, because each of the four cites the others as its calibration anchor — moving one alone breaks the argument the other three rest on.
- **5. THE AGENT DESTROYS EVERY CONTROLLER ERROR BODY, and this is the single most operationally important fact W3 established for every later wave's *instrumentation*, not just for the product.** `Client.do` replaces the body of every response `>= 400` with the literal `"response omitted"` (`internal/agent/client.go:107-108`), so **no agent-side failure is diagnosable from a run's own logs.** W3-3 measured it at full strength: all 23 secret-fetch failures wrote one identical, content-free line — a `SELECT DISTINCT` over all 23 returns exactly **one** value — while the controller had built a precise message at `api_secrets.go:142` that never crossed the socket. **The consequence for W4-W6 is procedural: capture the controller's `slog` container-side, and do it BEFORE any `force-recreate`, because a recreate erases it** (W3-3 lost controller3's mixed-window WARNs to exactly that and had to note that they were captured beforehand). **Two refinements W3 added and W4 must keep straight, because a fix for one does not fix the other:** `Client.UploadArtifact` does **not** go through `Client.do` — it hand-builds its request and returns a bare `fmt.Errorf("upload artifact http %d", …)` at `client.go:369`, so the body is **never read at all** rather than redacted (W3-2 `:1806`, W3-infra `:1681`); and that is also why the 413 is one of the few agent-side errors that is legible — an operator does get the number. **Two independent mechanisms, same content-free result, two different fixes.**
- **6. W3-6's job-delete entry (`:1864`) needs a measurement before it needs a fix, and it is the only unexecuted item in any wave's violation tally.** The entry specifies it: trigger a job, let a run archive its logs and upload an artifact, `DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{name}`, then `mc ls --recursive` both prefixes. Any rig with an object store does it in minutes, and after W3 every rig has one. **W4 should run it as a warm-up on its first stack rather than filing it forward again** — it costs less than reading this paragraph, and until it is run the wave's second-highest-severity violation rests on a code read.
- **7. W3-6's PRODUCTION window was never attempted — untested, not unreachable — and it is a cheap, high-value W4 arm.** W3-6 produced its orphan with a synthetic agent because that gives a window as wide as the payload and repeatable on demand. The entry then established, as a **code fact** and against its own earlier draft, that an ordinary agent-driven run reaches the same state through documented operator routes with no instrument at all: `handleCancelRun` marks the row terminal **synchronously** (`api_runs.go:374`) while the executing agent learns only by polling at `CancelPollInterval = 5 s`, and the same branch fires for a stuck-run reap and for a failover-driven terminalisation. **So an ordinary run is terminal-while-still-uploading for up to 5 s, and `DELETE /api/v1/runs/{id}` is legal for all of it.** What is genuinely unknown is whether the in-flight `Put` completes before the poller's `cancelRun()` tears down `runCtx` — **nobody tried.** This is the same discriminator W2 carry-forward item 2 asks for on the approval fence (does `cancelRun()` actually kill a long in-flight operation, or does it run to completion?), reached from a second direction, and **the two should be scheduled together on the same arm** because one long-running post-terminal operation answers both.

### Forward questions answered

- **(a) Was I4 actually exercised, and is W2's coverage gap closed? Yes, on both sides, and the per-scenario breakdown is above.** Short form for anyone triaging: **breached** by W3-4 (literal text, three of four clauses) and W3-5 (restated scope); **confirmed to hold, by measurement**, by W3-2 three times over; **not exercised** by W3-3, which says so; **ruled not contradicted, clause by clause**, by W3-1 and W3-6 — and in both of those the reason is that I4's *subject* does not reach the object that was corrupted, which is the coverage gap above and not a pass.
- **(b) Is `RunGitResolver` still open? Yes — see carry-forward item 2.** W3 added object storage, not a git server. Recommend W4, or W5 if W4 has no slot, as one task that builds the fixture and consumes it.
- **(c) What the Garage addition to `test/ha/` means for later waves — three things, and one of them is a constraint rather than a capability.** Task 3 added a Garage service, an idling `mc` client and the `UNIFIED_S3_*` / `UNIFIED_CACHE_*` wiring to `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml` (+108 lines, `0b51fa3`). **(i) Four subsystems that were silently off are now on** — the log archiver, cache cleanup, artifact upload and the agent cache. W2-1's null-result instruction (`:577`) is retired for three of them: a key with zero holders on `test/ha` is no longer "not wired". **The exception is cache cleanup, which is still unobservable** — its ticker's first fire is at t+24 h and no scenario in this campaign lives that long (W3-1 `:2015`); a wave that needs `DeleteExpired` to execute must drive `cache.DeleteExpired` directly from an `edgeprobe` build-tagged test, which is the same recommendation the W2 checkpoint already made for audit retention (`:1503`). **(ii) `docker compose down -v` between scenarios is now MANDATORY, not hygiene** — cache entries, artifacts and log archives live in a dedicated `ha-garagedata` volume and survive a plain `down`, and one leftover `caches/<jobhash>/<keyhash>` object turns a cache-miss expectation into a hit. Every W3 scenario tore down with `-v` and said so in its own entry. **(iii) The constraint: a controller that starts while Garage is unreachable now CRASHLOOPS** (W3-2's own violation, `:1710`), so any scenario that both faults the store and restarts a replica must order the two deliberately. **For W4 specifically (kind):** the compose Garage does **not** transfer — a kind rig needs its own object store or it is back to the pre-W3 state with the same four subsystems off, and W4 should decide that explicitly rather than discover it. **For W6:** the log/NOTIFY hotspot work now has a real archiver and a real seal to race against, which is what made W3-5's finding reachable at all; W6-S2's spill measurement should be taken on a rig with the object store wired, because an unwired archiver means the seal never fires and the drop path W3-5 measured does not exist.
- **(d) The methodological record — this plan's facts block was corrected before the wave began, and then by seven of eight tasks during it.** See the Methodological findings below; the answer to "is the claims-to-check discipline still earning its keep in a third consecutive wave" is **yes, and W3 sharpened it into something more useful than a yes.**

### Methodological findings — four, and all four are wave-level

- **1. The plan's "Verified code facts (do not re-derive)" block was corrected by SEVEN of eight tasks, the third consecutive wave this has happened — but W3-1 offered a refinement that makes the rule actionable rather than merely repeated.** The corrections: **W3-3** overturned "the reason is visible in the run's own logs" (`plan:85`), which was not merely wrong but the opposite of what the path delivers, and overturned "not a contradicted contract" (`plan:88`) by finding `docs/secrets.md:420` at hit #55 of a survey that had been truncated to 40; **W3-5** overturned "structural, every run" for the sidecar seal race on **both** halves (`plan:108`, `:115`) — the ordering is real but the flush wins by microseconds against a 30 s tick, and the "logs have no accommodation" half is wrong because neither log endpoint is an F2 endpoint at all; **W3-6** corrected the artifact-PUT span (`plan:125`, `client.go:349-371` not `:352-360`) and then confirmed the window live; **W3-2** corrected the same span independently and filed it first; **W3-1** overturned `plan:61`'s "step fails → `markFailed`" (the cache path is lenient by explicit written policy and reports `Succeeded`), corrected `plan:59`'s payload-orphan characterisation (it is not dead storage, it is live authoritative content that is **still served**), and corrected `plan:59`'s explanation of the *benign* orphan (the miss came from `:162`, not from the expiry skip at `:244`); **W3-infra** settled `plan:143`'s sidecar question doubly negative and corrected the brief's `test/ha/agent.Dockerfile`, which does not exist; **W3-4** confirmed the `seq`-is-global question the plan flagged (`plan:96`) from the migration, as instructed. **No task left the block untouched, and the plan file now carries `CORRECTED AFTER EXECUTION` blocks in place at `:85`, `:88`, `:108`, `:115`, `:124`, `:125`, `:126` and `:144`** — recorded *and* propagated, which is the distinction W2-3's `:739` drew and which the W2 checkpoint had to admit it got wrong once. **W3-4 is the one task whose corrections were against the brief and the campaign README rather than against the plan**, and both are worth carrying: `sideeffect.payload.json` emits **zero** log lines, not the 120 the brief and `test/edgecase/README.md`'s fixture table both claim (the `echo` is redirected to a file), and the bulk-log URI is `POST /api/v1/agents/{agentId}/runs/{runId}/steps/{stepIndex}/logs/bulk`, not the flat `/agents/*/logs/bulk` the plan sketched — which is why an exact-match nginx `location =` is impossible on that path and the overlay needs a regex `location`.
  - **THE REFINEMENT, AND IT IS WHAT W4 SHOULD ACT ON: it is the block's *mechanism* claims that keep failing, not its `file:line` claims.** Every constant, key, span and line number the block asserted survived checking (three were off by one or two lines and were corrected in place without changing a conclusion). What failed, every time, was an **inference drawn from correct constants** — which is exactly the failure mode the W2 checkpoint named (`:1508`, "the entries most likely to be wrong are the *inferences* drawn from correct constants") and which W3 confirms for the second time. **Two of this wave's planned mechanisms proved not merely wrong but structurally unreachable, and both still produced findings by substitution, which is the other half of the lesson:** W3-5's structural sidecar race cannot exist on this rig at all (sidecars are unavailable by two independent mechanisms) *and* is not structural anywhere, and the scenario substituted **delayed delivery after a partition** — the producer the troubleshooting docs actually name — and hit it on attempt 1; W3-1's chartered delete-mid-restore race is real in the code and **unreachable against Garage v2.3.0**, which delivers an in-flight GET in full after the key is deleted (measured twice, once with no unified-cd and no proxy in the path), and the scenario substituted **severing the connection** and produced the torn extract on the first attempt. **The instruction for W4+: treat the facts block's constants as checkable-in-one-grep and its mechanisms as hypotheses that must be probed before a scenario is designed around them — and when a mechanism turns out unreachable, substitute a fault that reaches the same state, label it a stand-in, and enumerate the ordinary faults that reach it (`:1516`'s discipline, which W3-1 paid in full at `:1984`). A scenario whose planned window does not exist is not a failed scenario.**
- **2. What the process cost, stated plainly, because it recurs and because each failure yields a one-line rule. Four tasks failed something, two of them on spec compliance for evidence traceability.**
  - **Task 3 (W3-infra) quoted four nginx log lines, a `step_reports` table and a duration for the 413 that appeared in NO capture.** The finding was corroborated in the capture, so this was a presentation failure rather than a fabrication — but verbatim-looking log text and a duration must be backed by a capture, so the rig was rebuilt and the whole block re-captured, reproducing the original byte for byte on the message text and differing, as durations do, on the two timings (0.015 s vs an uncaptured 0.012 s; 0.749 s vs an uncaptured 0.863 s). **Rule: if a block looks like pasted output, it must be pasted output — and the capture must exist before the entry quotes it, not after.**
  - **Task 4 (W3-2) stated numbers its own captures contradicted — seven of them, corrected in place at review**: a 59 s archival baseline that was the interval from the *trigger* rather than from terminal (28.4 s); a "~105 s" leader-rotation spacing that appears nowhere in the data (the real spacing is 89-92 s with one 120 s gap); "5" single-process retries where the window boundary gives 4; "≥ 18 s" of lock hold rounded up from a measured 17.46 s; "44-47 s" per failing `Put` against a true 42.8-45.2 s; a `ContentLength` digit quoted from one capture against another capture's citation; and a run census short by two — the two being **exactly the Part B runs later deleted by raw SQL**, i.e. precisely the runs a census exists to catch before deletion removes them. **Rule: re-derive every number from the capture you are about to cite, in the same pass in which you write it — and take the census before anything deletes rows.**
  - **Task 6 (W3-5) filed a re-file of an existing entry.** Its already-ruled check greped `docs/` passages and never greped `FINDINGS.md` for the *finding*, so it re-filed W2-2's cancelled-run-leaves-a-`Running`-step defect as a new I7 entry. It was withdrawn at review and survives as a cross-reference (`:1936`) contributing exactly one thing — a **fourth reproduction, on a controller built with PR #113 present**, confirming `MarkRunStepsInterrupted` still has one caller. **Rule: the already-ruled check has two halves — grep `docs/` for the passage AND grep `FINDINGS.md` for the finding — and the second half is the one that catches a re-file.** W3-1 is the model: its check (`:1973`) greped `FINDINGS.md` too, broke the 21 hits down in full, and corrected its own earlier three-way characterisation of them rather than restating it.
  - **Task 5 (W3-6) claimed a class fully enumerated while a third producer sat unevaluated in its own capture.** Its violation entry said the orphan class's producers "are named here: W3-2's failed compensation and W3-6's artifact-prefix TOCTOU" — and `docs/cli.md:164`, the job-delete leak, was **line 80 of that entry's own docs survey**, printed before the entry existed. It was found at review and spun out as its own entry (`:1864`), which the sibling now names and scopes to explicitly. **Rule: a completeness claim must be checked against your own captures before it is written — and if you find a producer that is worse than the entry you are writing, spin it out rather than folding it in, because folding an unmeasured, windowless, higher-severity producer into a measured race entry makes the entry's severity claim wrong and not just its completeness claim.**
  - **Task 2 (W3-3) piped a docs survey through `head` and did not disclose it** — 40 of 55 hits kept, and hit #55 was the one that turned "the docs are silent" into the wave's second major violation. Caught at review by re-running the identical command and comparing line counts. Both captures are archived (`w3-3/docs-greps-ORIGINAL-TRUNCATED.txt` beside the re-captured `docs-greps.txt`) because how it failed is part of the deliverable. **Rule: never pipe a survey through `head`, and print `| wc -l` beside the output before writing "the docs are silent" into an entry or a plan.** This is now a standing method rule and every later W3 scenario printed its counts (W3-2 231/54/210/27, W3-6 64/169/30/5, W3-5 35/49/84/1, W3-1 97/33/87/11).
  - **Two capped arms never reported their attempt count, against the wave's own explicit rule.** Every W3 runbook says "**report every capped arm's attempt count either way, with the cap stated**", and four scenarios paid it (W3-4 4-of-10, W3-5 1-of-3, W3-6 Part A 1-of-6, W3-2 Part B 2-of-6 and 1-of-6). **W3-3's Part D1 and W3-6's Part C4 each declared a cap and reported no count**, and W3-1's *delete-route* attempts are reported only as "negative" with no number. **Rule: a declared cap creates a reporting obligation that survives a hit on the first attempt — "1 of 6" is the result, not "it worked".** An unreported count is indistinguishable from an unbounded one, which is the whole reason the rule exists.
- **3. The wave's own review found and withdrew two classifications and one contract citation, and all three withdrawals are more instructive than the entries they corrected.** W3-infra's 413 was withdrawn from major violation to minor observation because **this branch had already ruled the other way on the same sentence** in W3-4's Notes and filing the broad reading would have made the branch say two incompatible things about `docs/high-availability.md:253-254`; W3-1's headline was reclassified from violation to observation because it disclaims both violation limbs by its own upheld rulings (see above); and W3-5's I7 re-file was withdrawn outright. **The one-line rule that covers all three, and it extends W2's `:1509`: before filing, grep this branch for every doc line and every finding you are about to cite, and read what it already decided — the campaign is now large enough that its own prior rulings are a source of contradiction, not only the product's docs.**

- **4. A NEW failure mode this checkpoint found, which no previous wave had: the runbooks and `FINDINGS.md` have DRIFTED, always in the same direction — the runbook is the stale side, because review corrections were applied to the entry and not propagated back.** Every W3 runbook carries an execution-notes section with its own results table, and this checkpoint re-read all six against the entries. **Six drifts, none of which changes a measurement, and one of which would have corrupted this tally if it had been trusted.** *(Nothing below is fixed by this checkpoint — the entries are authoritative and the drifts are recorded here so W4 knows which side to read. They are listed in descending order of how much damage trusting the wrong side would do.)* **ALL SIX HAVE SINCE BEEN RESOLVED in a follow-up commit on this branch, which is why the runbooks now carry struck-through superseded text where this list points. This list is kept as the record of what drifted and why, not as a live to-do; no severity, classification or measurement was changed in resolving them.**
  - **(i) W3-1's runbook states a tally that the file contradicts, and it is the one the checkpoint would have inherited.** `w3-1-cache-delete-vs-restore.md:686-687` (was `:608-614`; the runbook has grown since) says "**2 violations (1 major, 1 minor) and 2 observations (both minor)**". The file holds **1 violation (minor) and 3 observations (one of them major)**, because the headline entry was reclassified at review and the runbook was not updated. **The tally in this checkpoint is taken from the entries, mechanically, and is 9/13/1.**
  - **(ii) W3-4's runbook still instructs a future reader to do work already done.** `w3-4-bulk-append-duplication.md:707` and `:934` (were `:651-653` / `:855-867`; the runbook has grown since) say Part E "**is not measured and must not be written up as if it were**" and "**must be re-run after Task 3**". It was re-run — `FINDINGS.md:1557` carries the AMENDED bullet with the measurement (`line_count=8 max_seq=20`, run `46e21b34`, all 8 records including the 4 duplicates), the labelled caveat that the duplicates were SQL-planted, and the instruction not to cite that sub-bullet as an independent reproduction. **None of that nuance is in the runbook.**
  - **(iii) W3-2's runbook says its Part A outage was "8 min held".** The entry measures the attempt window at `03:03:37Z – 03:18:21Z` (**14.73 minutes**, and the arithmetic at `:1752` depends on that boundary) inside an outage running `03:02:15.838Z → 03:21:54.42Z` (**19 m 38 s**). Eight minutes cannot be reconciled as rounding on either reading; the entry is right and the runbook's step text was not updated when the hold was extended.
  - **(iv) W3-2's runbook says "both Part B arms hit on the first attempt", dropping the qualifier the entry keeps** — "*with that lever*". Arm 1 took **2** attempts against a cap of 6, the first with the `s3-latency` lever that did not work. The entry is right and the distinction is the whole reason `s3-latency`'s large-value failure is on record.
  - **(v) W3-6 states two different end instants for one session, and the file does it to itself.** The Repro line (`:1816`) says "Executed 2026-07-31 `04:36:29Z – 04:49:24Z`" while `:1835` scopes a negative claim against "the whole `04:36:29Z – 04:57:27Z` session". **The capture settles it and neither number is wrong**: `w3-6/teardown.txt` is stamped `04:57:16.881Z` and runs to `04:57:27.724Z`, so `04:57:27Z` is the session and `04:49:24Z` is the *measurement* window, ending with Part C's DELETE return. ~~**Deliberately not edited**~~ — both readings are defensible, `:1835`'s is the load-bearing one and is correct as written, and picking one silently is exactly what a checkpoint should not do, **so the resolution was recorded here first and applied afterwards rather than silently: both lines have SINCE been edited to say which span they name — the Repro line is now labelled the *measurement window* and `:1835` the *session* — and neither figure changed.** **W4: read `:1835`'s figure as the session.**
  - **(vi) W3-6's runbook fuses a client-side duration with a server-side timestamp** — "DELETE 204 in 13 ms at `04:45:28.891Z`" — where 13 ms is curl's and `04:45:28.891Z` is the access log's completion stamp for a **10 ms** handler. The entry keeps them apart. Trivial in size and exactly the class the wave otherwise polices.
  - **The rule for W4+, and it is a merge gate rather than advice: when a review changes an entry, propagate the change to the runbook in the same commit — and at the wave checkpoint, re-read every runbook's results table against the entries before tallying anything.** A campaign whose scenarios and findings are separate documents will drift, and the drift is invisible from either side alone. **`FINDINGS.md` is authoritative; a runbook's execution notes are a record of what was done, not of what was concluded.** (W3-3 is the model for how to handle it when the conclusion moves: its correction banner at `:3-13` and `:65-94` explicitly withdraws the pre-execution framing — though even there the un-struck body text at `:104-121` still reads "a conformance measurement, not a hunt for a contradicted contract", which the scenario's own major violation refutes.)

### Tooling and asset notes carried forward

- **THE ARM RULE, WHICH IS THIS WAVE'S MOST TRANSFERABLE OUTPUT AND WHICH W4, W5 AND W6 ALL INHERIT: a verb is verified when SOME CAPTURE MEASURES ITS EFFECT — not when its comment carries a measurement, and never when "the file is present, `s3-show` lists it, `nginx -t` passed and the `arm=` stamp appears".** `inject.sh s3-slow` was verifiably **loaded** — three independent checks passed — and did nothing at all. The verb table stands verified today, arm by arm: **`s3-block` is the best-verified arm in the table**, because it runs a per-arm effect probe *at arm time* parameterised on the actual method and prefix plus a control that must not be blocked, and W3-2 confirmed it live and prefix-scoped; **`steplock` shares `s3-slow`'s failure class and its own comment admits it** (a silent no-op against the wrong nginx conf) and is effect-confirmed by **execution** rather than by its comment, via W2-5's probe-confirmed 403 and the agent-originated 403s in the nginx log; **`s3-latency`** is the one verb whose comment carries its own measurement. **The standing requirement is forward-looking and is a merge gate, not advice: every NEW or CHANGED arm must ship with an effect measurement — a capture, a probe the verb itself prints, or the comment, in that order of preference.**
- **Rig facts W4-W6 need, each paid for once this wave.** **(i) `docker compose down -v` is mandatory** — the `ha-garagedata` volume is persistent and a leftover cache object turns a miss into a hit. **(ii) The nginx overlays do NOT stack, and there are FOUR of them, not three** — ~~"the three nginx overlays"~~ **corrected at branch review, because this fact is presented as complete and an incomplete "here is the whole set" is worse than no list at all.** Every file mounting `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` **on the `nginx` service**: `bigbody.override.yaml:31`, `logfault.override.yaml:18`, `steplink.override.yaml:18` and **`oneway.override.yaml:7`** (`nginx-edge.conf` — the W1-5 one-way-partition overlay, still in the tree and still the base every `nginx-block` scenario needs). Compose merges volumes by target path, so **the last file listed silently wins** — silently, which is the whole hazard. **One of the four collisions is deliberate and must not be "fixed":** `steplink` is *designed* to be stacked on top of `oneway` and to override its `nginx.conf` while inheriting its `blocklist` volume (`steplink.override.yaml:1-14`), so `-f oneway -f steplink` in that order is correct. Every other pairing is an accident. **`s3proxy.override.yaml:28` also mounts `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` but is NOT in this set** — it mounts it on the separate `s3proxy` container, which is why `bigbody` *does* stack with it. **(iii) `s3-latency` breaks a `Put` rather than widening it at large values.** The arm depends on a connect to `192.0.2.1` **hanging**; if anything on the path answers instead, nginx sees `connect() failed (111: Connection refused)`, which is `error` and not `timeout`, `proxy_next_upstream` never fires, and the request **502s**. **Name the errno, not a guess at the packet: `111` is `ECONNREFUSED`, produced on a TCP connect by a RST — an "ICMP unreachable", which an earlier version of this item blamed, surfaces as `EHOSTUNREACH` (113) or `ENETUNREACH` (101).** The rig fact W4-W6 need is the errno and nginx's classification of it; the emitter was not captured. Measured at `s3-latency 30`: a log-archive `Put` got `502 … rt=21.037`. The 3-second measurements are not withdrawn — at 3 s the connect deadline expires first — but **a scenario needing a wide window must use `inject.sh pause garage` behind the interposer**, which is a genuine hang bounded only by minio-go's 60 s `ResponseHeaderTimeout`. W3-2 hit both Part B arms on the first attempt with that lever after `s3-latency` failed. **(iv) minio-go retries a 503 ten times internally**, with backoff, so **choose the block status deliberately**: a `503` arm produces a slow retried failure that moves the timing, while `403` fails immediately. W3-2's Part C chose 403 on exactly this ground, because it was measuring a one-shot policy and not a retry policy. **(v) The Windows/MSYS `curl` trap, in both its forms.** W3-6 note 1: an MSYS-form `@`/upload path can upload an **empty body and still return 204** — the gate's first artifact was 0 B and the listing it backed was taken against it, and only the re-upload is the 4.0 KiB object. W3-5's mirror image is **loud**: `curl -D`/`-o` with MSYS-form output paths failed to open them, exit 23, `http_code=000`, and the request never left the client. **Both are avoided the same way: Windows-form paths for every `curl` file argument, and check `%{size_upload}` — never the status alone.** **(vi) Related, and it caught this checkpoint out too:** `%{size_upload}` on a chunked `PUT` counts the on-the-wire bytes **including chunk framing** — W3-6's orphan reads `upload_size=33558547` against an object of exactly 33554432 bytes, and the 4,115-byte gap is framing, not a short write.
- **Smaller rig facts, each of which cost time once this wave.** `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` must be exported before any compose command on Windows (all six runbooks do it, on the W2-5 path-rewrite lesson) — **and it is the direct cause of the `curl` trap above**, so the two are one fact, not two. `docker compose up -d --force-recreate` **erases that container's log history**: capture before you repair, which W3-3 did and says so, and which W3-2, W3-5 and W3-6 all record independently. `docker compose exec` costs ~200-400 ms, so 1 Hz is the practical sampling floor — do not design an arm that needs faster. **The `mc` image has no `sed`, no `ps` and no `grep`**, which cost W3-1 one VOID attempt (a `.meta` rewrite that silently produced an empty body). `inject.sh partition` **silently no-ops** unless the container is on `unified-cd-ha_default`. `DELETE /api/v1/agents/{id}` is an **agent-auth** route and the admin token gets 401 on it. `docker compose logs --since` still lags several seconds (wait ≥6 s, the W2-8 lesson, re-confirmed). **And a `curl -N` sampler launched without `-m` outlives the shell that started it and appears in neither the host `ps` nor `jobs`** — W3-4's teardown caught a live one (pid 169 in the nginx container, killed only by `down -v`), which is why the wave's sampler-hygiene check is now three-part: `jobs`, a host `ps` grep, **and an in-container `ps`**.
- **One standing README recommendation is now stale relative to the scenario it was written for, and W4-W6 will read the README before they read this file.** `test/edgecase/README.md:198` and the `artifact-large.payload.json` row at `:329` still present `s3-latency 3` as "the knob W3-6 should reach for first" for widening a large artifact PUT. **W3-6 as executed used neither it nor the interposer at all**, and for a reason that generalises: the DELETE it was timing itself calls `obj.Delete` and `obj.List`, so pausing the store behind the interposer would hang the instrument alongside the subject. It used `curl --limit-rate` against `proxy_request_buffering off` instead, which its own notes call "a better width knob than anything in `inject.sh` for this race". **The 9.702 s measurement behind the README row is real and is not withdrawn** — it just answers a different question (does `s3-latency` widen a large PUT rather than break it: yes, at small values). ~~**Recorded here rather than edited, because changing a verb-table recommendation is a campaign-asset decision this checkpoint was not asked to make.**~~ **TAKEN — the decision was made in a follow-up commit on this branch.** Both README passages are corrected in place: `:198`'s sentence is struck and rescoped to what the 9.702 s actually measures (`s3-latency 3` *delays* a large `PUT` rather than breaking it), the `artifact-large` row no longer calls it "the knob W3-6 should reach for first", and a **§"width-knob rule for W4-W6"** table was added immediately after the measurement — the place an author reaching for a width knob reads first — routing each side of a race to the knob that was actually measured to widen it: `pause` behind the interposer for a controller-side S3 call, `curl --limit-rate` + `proxy_request_buffering off` for a client→controller upload leg, `s3-slow` for a response-body stream, and prefix padding for the delete loop. **No measurement was withdrawn and no verb was removed from the table.**
- **Instruments this wave added and W4+ should reuse.** The **S3 interposer** (`compose/s3proxy.override.yaml` + `nginx-s3.conf`) is the wave's best instrument: an nginx between the product and Garage, side-selected by bucket (`unified-cd-logs/` is the controller's, `unified-cd-cache/` is the agent's), stamping `arm=` and a status onto **every** request, which is what let five of six scenarios bracket their claims per request instead of per wall clock. It resolves the W2-5 reload trap differently from `nginx-logfault.conf` and better for this path — `keepalive_timeout 0` rather than `worker_shutdown_timeout 1s`, so a reload is deterministic without **killing** in-flight multi-megabyte PUTs and cache-restore streams. The **`mc` service idles with its alias preconfigured** because `exec` costs milliseconds where `compose run` costs a container start, and injection timing matters; note it points at `garage:3900` directly and **bypasses the interposer**, so an arm must be measured through a job, never through `mc`. `tools/w3/fixcheck` parses fixtures through the real `dsl.Parse` offline and every W3 fixture that used it worked on the first API call. **The positive in-flight signal is the pattern to copy** — W3-6 fired its DELETE on `mc ls --incomplete` returning a multipart upload and W3-2 fired its on three consecutive granted `pg_locks` samples; both hit on the first attempt, where W2's unaided repetition scored 0/20 and 0/10.
- **Execution deviations, all six declared by their own runbooks, recorded so a re-runner is not surprised.** W3-2 ran **Part C before Part B**, because Part B deletes `runs` rows with raw SQL that would have polluted Part C's census — the ordering is a rule, not a preference. W3-5 partitioned **agent2**, not the `agent1` its runbook names, because agent2 claimed the run; the arm follows the claim. W3-4 **superseded its Part D1 in place** (SSE through the LB dies at the first arm, because `worker_shutdown_timeout 1s` severs in-flight streams) and re-took the capture directly against `controller1` from inside the nginx container, keeping the dead capture as the counter-example. W3-4 also **deliberately rejected** the brief's `inject.sh pause postgres` lever with three reasons on record — a re-runner should not reach for it. W3-1 **added a Part A'** after Part A's chartered delete route produced a negative, and **added a fixture** (`workloads/cache-torn.{yaml,payload.json}`) the task's file list did not name. W3-6 **skipped Part D** and argued the skip. **The pattern to keep: a deviation is fine and a silent deviation is not.**
- **The rig's intermittent-500 allowance was never spent in ANY of the six scenarios — and every runbook now labels that correctly.** Not one W3 scenario had to retry a step for a spurious 500. **The wording every entry uses is the point: that is an absence of trouble, not a measurement**, because no capture counts 500s across a session. W3-3 sharpens it into a rule the later waves need, because a 500 is its expected *result*: a 500 from `POST /api/v1/runs` is rig flakiness, a 500 from `POST /api/v1/agents/*/secrets/fetch` is the measurement, **and they are told apart by the path in the controller access log, never by the status alone.**
- **Statement logging was armed exactly once this wave, and that is a result.** W3-4 used `log_statement='all'` for one window and it answered the question nothing else could (2558 `INSERT`s, 0 `rollback`). Everything else came from per-request access-log brackets. **The cost comparison is the argument: W2 needed ~96 MB of evidence to answer its questions; W3 needed ~4.9 MB** (the block-allocated `du -sh` figure; the byte sum is **4,582,411 B** — see `:2124`). W2's two statement-log traps still apply when it is needed (pgx logs parameterised queries as `execute stmtcache_<hash>:` and arg-less ones as `statement:`; only the first physical line carries the `%m [%p] h=%h` prefix), as does the one-`ALTER SYSTEM`-per-`psql -c` rule.
- **Evidence archive.** `edgecase-evidence/w3/` now holds all six scenarios plus `w3-infra/` (**~4.9 MB is the block-allocated measure, `du -sh`; the byte sum is 4,582,411 B, `du -sb` — both are stated because the two differ by ~7 % on a tree of many small files and a re-measurer should know which one this figure is**), **all seven directories verified byte-identical against the session scratchpad with `diff -r`** — **true as taken, and now bounded: the branch review moved seven authored working copies (four `w3-2/entryN.txt`, `w3-5/entries.md`, `w3-6/entries.md`, `w3-3/apply_fixes.py`) out of the scenario directories into `w3/_not-evidence/`, so four of the seven no longer verify byte-identical and the difference is exactly those files. No capture was touched, none of the moved files backs a numeric claim, and none is cited by any entry** (the evidence root's own README records the move). The wave's one Postgres statement log is stored gzipped (`w3/w3-4/partB-pglog-raw.txt.gz`); the W3-4 entry cites the uncompressed name and its **71,852 lines / 4,964,400 bytes**, which `gunzip -c` reproduces with a matching sha256. **Credentials were scrubbed, and the way this was found is the rule.** W3-1 found a full `uca_` agent credential that W3-5 had left in a dotfile and scrubbed it mid-wave; **W3-6 then made the identical mistake in three files and nobody found it until this checkpoint swept the whole wave** — `.atok`, `.tokline` and `gate-g6-synthagent.txt` each carried the `w36-probe` identity's full access credential, and the last also carried its full `uce_` enrollment token. All are replaced in place by the prefix the entries cite plus a dated `<SCRUBBED …>` banner, both identities were destroyed with their stacks, and a full-token regex sweep over `w3/` now returns zero. **Rule: every wave checkpoint regexes the ENTIRE archive for credentials before copying, not only the scenario that happened to be reviewed.** Four capture-hygiene notes are recorded in the evidence root's own README rather than here, because they are about the captures and not about the findings: two `w3-2` samplers label a cadence they did not achieve (nominal 1 s and 2 s, actual ~1.59 s and ~2.59 s — every duration the entry states is timestamp-derived and unaffected, but "55 of 70 samples" spans ~111 s and not 70 s); **`w3-1`'s workspace samplers are the same class and were missed by the first pass of this list — `partA-torn.txt:15-17` and `partA-attempt1.txt:4-39` were described in the entry as "once per second" and are actually ~2.11 s apart** (`06:59:04.129 → :06.243 → :08.365`), which is why the descriptor is corrected at `:1952` and `:1984`; `w3-6`'s `upload_size` framing gap above, now reconciled inline at `:1820`; and `w3-1`'s two readings of one cache key at 16909275 B and 16909279 B, which is a real re-save between the two reads and not a discrepancy. **All four were checked at this checkpoint and none is an inconsistency between entries** — in every case the load-bearing claim is timestamp-derived or otherwise independent of the mislabelled cadence. *(The original checkpoint added "no W3 entry was modified by this checkpoint"; that remains true of the checkpoint itself, but entries have since been corrected in follow-up commits on this branch — see the drift list at `:2105` and the traceability corrections carried inline above.)*

## W4-0 — Kubernetes agent enrollment is impossible: the verifier reads the ServiceAccount UID from a TokenReview field the API server never populates
- **Invariant:** **none — this is filed on the documented-contract limb, not on an invariant.** `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:179` states as fact that the agent Pod "mounts a projected ServiceAccount token with audience `unified-cd-agent-enrollment`" and "exchanges that token for a short-lived access token in memory", and `:177` prescribes the controller-side verifier plus an enabled policy as the configuration that makes that exchange work. The exchange cannot succeed under any configuration. *(Earlier drafts filed this on I5 with I7; both are withdrawn as stretches, per the rule at `:1509` that an invariant must be contradicted by its own text rather than its spirit. I5's text is "after **fault injection** the system returns to steady state within documented bounds" — no fault is injected here and no documented bound is missed. I7's text is "run status, approval status, and audit rows never contradict each other or reality" — a 403 response string is none of those three.)*
- **Severity:** major per the band text — a total feature outage, but it fails closed with no data loss, no silent corruption and no security exposure, which is what the critical band requires.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-0-enrollment-spike.md`, steps 2-4, **in this order** (the kubeconfig is gitignored and must be generated before the overlay bind-mounts it, or Docker creates a directory at that path and the run fails *differently* — with the superseded 503 symptom):
  ```bash
  kubectl apply -f test/edgecase/k8s/w4-spike-identity.yaml \
                -f test/edgecase/k8s/w4-spike-controller-rbac.yaml
  bash test/edgecase/k8s/make-spike-kubeconfig.sh          # writes the gitignored kubeconfig
  MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker compose -f test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml \
                     -f test/edgecase/compose/k8senroll.override.yaml up -d
  ```
  Then mint a pod-bound token (`kubectl create token w4-spike-agent -n ci --audience=unified-cd-agent-enrollment --bound-object-kind Pod --bound-object-name w4-spike-agent-pod`) into the file named by `serviceAccountTokenFile`, and run the agent against `http://localhost:18080` with the committed config **`test/edgecase/k8s/w4-0-agent-config.template.yaml`** (copy it, fill the two placeholder paths). `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` is the standing W3 rule for this Windows rig and matters here because the overlay bind-mounts colon-bearing paths. The defect is also reproducible with **no unified-cd process at all** — a bare `kubectl create -f -` TokenReview is sufficient, see below.
- **Observed:** The one enrollment attempt the agent made was rejected 403; the mechanism was then reproduced twice more with direct TokenReviews (one `kubectl create token`-minted, one projected-volume) and no attempt of any kind has ever succeeded. *(The count is stated because it is small: one agent attempt, two direct TokenReviews. No capture bounds a larger population.)* Agent side: `{"level":"ERROR","msg":"bootstrap agent credentials","error":"kubernetes enrollment request failed"}`. Controller side: `{"method":"POST","path":"/api/v1/agents/enroll","status":403,"duration_ms":18}`.

  **403 and not 503 is the load-bearing detail, and what it licenses is an inference, not a proof**: `internal/controller/api_agent_enrollment.go:346-351` answers 503 when no verifier is registered, so a 403 means execution reached `verifier.Verify` — i.e. the config file was loaded, the kubeconfig parsed, and the verifier registered. What is *proved* live is the `TokenReviews().Create` at `agent_enrollment_kubernetes.go:70`: it must have returned successfully, since an error there yields `ErrKubernetesEnrollmentUnavailable` and a 503 (`:71-72`, handler `:354-356`). That single call establishes kubeconfig load, CA verification against the embedded cluster CA, and `create tokenreviews` RBAC for the controller SA.

  **`Pods().Get` did NOT run and must not be cited as evidence.** `Verify` returns at `:86`, upstream of the `Pods().Get` at `:93`, so in the failing request that call was never reached and is unreachable while the defect stands. `get pods` RBAC is confirmed separately by `kubectl auth can-i get pods -n ci --as=system:serviceaccount:unified-cd:w4-spike-controller` → `yes` (spike record `:170-174`) — **RBAC confirmed, call path not exercised.** *(An earlier version of this entry claimed both API calls succeeded; that was false and is corrected here and at spike record `:281-286`.)*

  The decision is made at `internal/controller/agent_enrollment_kubernetes.go:84-87`:
  ```go
  reviewedUID, hasReviewedUID := review.Status.User.Extra["authentication.kubernetes.io/serviceaccount.uid"]
  if claims.ServiceAccount.UID == "" || !hasReviewedUID || len(reviewedUID) != 1 ||
     reviewedUID[0] == "" || reviewedUID[0] != claims.ServiceAccount.UID {
      return ..., fmt.Errorf("%w: token review service account UID", ErrKubernetesEnrollmentRejected)
  }
  ```
  Issuing that same TokenReview by hand against the live cluster (Kubernetes v1.35.1) returns **no such extra key**. The block below is **not raw output**: `kubectl create -o json -f -` returns JSON, and a small Python reader parsed `.status` and printed the four fields plus a presence test — which is why `True` / `['…']` appear in Python repr form. A re-runner issuing the command alone gets JSON and should read `.status.user.uid` and `.status.user.extra`.
  ```
  authenticated : True
  audiences     : ['unified-cd-agent-enrollment']
  user.username : system:serviceaccount:ci:w4-spike-agent
  user.uid      : 'a7031b08-1c99-4348-994f-13b82ab66eb4'
  extra keys    : ['authentication.kubernetes.io/credential-id',
                   'authentication.kubernetes.io/node-name',
                   'authentication.kubernetes.io/node-uid',
                   'authentication.kubernetes.io/pod-name',
                   'authentication.kubernetes.io/pod-uid']
  serviceaccount.uid extra present? -> False
  ```
  The ServiceAccount UID **is** returned — in `review.Status.User.UID`, whose value (`a7031b08-...`) is exactly what the check wants to compare against, and exactly what the token's `kubernetes.io.serviceaccount.uid` claim carries. The code reads the wrong field.

  **What is measured, and what is inferred — stated separately, because the scope matters.**
  - **Measured:** on **Kubernetes v1.35.1, this one cluster, both token-mint paths** (`kubectl create token --bound-object-kind Pod` and a `serviceAccountToken` projected volume read from inside a pod), the `authentication.kubernetes.io/serviceaccount.uid` extra is absent and `review.Status.User.UID` carries the SA UID — the two captures quoted in this entry.
  - **Read from code, not measured:** `authv1.UserInfo.UID` is the documented location of a subject's UID in a `TokenReview` response, which is what makes `review.Status.User.UID` the correct field to compare against.
  - **Inferred:** that `hasReviewedUID` is therefore always `false`, so the branch rejects unconditionally for every token, in every namespace, on every cluster. *(Inferred; not measured on any other version, and no upstream source citation was obtainable offline — `k8s.io/apiserver` is not in this machine's module cache. The inference is very likely right, but this entry's own capture demonstrates that the extras set is **not** version-invariant: `node-name`/`node-uid` and `credential-id` are gated additions from different Kubernetes eras — ServiceAccountTokenNodeBinding / PodNodeInfo / structured authentication — so the set varies with version and feature gates even though the absent key is constant across both paths measured here.)*

  **The elimination argument, restated — the earlier version pointed at the wrong conditions.** Pod liveness, pod UID and `serviceAccountName` are checked at `:100-102`, and the requested-labels ⊆ `allowedLabels` check is not in `Verify` at all but in the handler at `api_agent_enrollment.go:363` — all **downstream** of `:86` and therefore incapable of causing this 403. What actually needed eliminating are the four conditions upstream of `:84` inside `Verify` (policy constraints parse `:65-67`, TokenReview authenticated + audience `:74-76`, `parseBoundPodClaims` `:77-80`, username-vs-claims `:81-83`), all confirmed satisfied for this attempt, **plus the three pre-verifier 403 exits in the handler**: `:319` (no bearer token), `:335` (policy nil / disabled / wrong provider), `:343` (unparseable `providerConfig`). Those three are excluded by the seeded, enabled `w4-spike-policy` row quoted under Step 2 of the record and by the agent having sent a bearer token at all. With the upstream conditions satisfied and the pre-verifier exits excluded, `:84` is the only **reachable** cause of the 403 — an inference from the code path plus the policy row, not something the 403 alone can prove, since (per the observation entry below) five 403 exits share one response string.

  **This is not an artifact of running the agent on the host.** The obvious objection — that `kubectl create token --bound-object-kind Pod` differs from the projected volume a real Deployment gets — was tested directly. A pod was created with a `serviceAccountToken` projected volume at the enrollment audience, its token read from inside the container and reviewed; the response is the same shape, same five extra keys, same absent `serviceaccount.uid`, same populated `user.uid`. **An in-cluster Deployment fails identically.**

  **The unit tests are green because the fake mirrors the implementation rather than the API server.** `internal/controller/agent_enrollment_kubernetes_test.go:175-181`'s `tokenReviewReactor` synthesises `extra["authentication.kubernetes.io/serviceaccount.uid"]` and never sets `UserInfo.UID`. `go test ./internal/controller/ -run TestKubernetesEnrollment -v` passes 100%, including a subtest named `RejectsMissingOrAmbiguousServiceAccountUID/missing_service_account_UID` that asserts the rejection which, in reality, is the *only* outcome. The happy-path tests pass solely because they inject a field Kubernetes never sends.
- **Expected:** A ServiceAccount holding a pod-bound projected token whose namespace and name match a seeded, enabled enrollment policy should enrol and receive an agent credential. The contradicted contract is `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:179` verbatim — "The agent Pod mounts a projected ServiceAccount token with audience `unified-cd-agent-enrollment`. It exchanges that token for a short-lived access token in memory" — a statement of what the product does, not a caveated option, and `:177` gives the controller-side configuration ("a Kubernetes cluster verifier and an enabled policy that binds the exact agent ServiceAccount and namespace") that is supposed to make it work. That configuration was supplied exactly as described and the exchange still cannot succeed. The `manifests/` Deployment ships the same path, and since PR #75 `4e8f315` removed static token auth it is the **only** way for a k8s agent to authenticate *(the exclusivity is from the code change, not from `:179`, which does not itself say "only")*. In practice **the Kubernetes agent has no usable authentication path whatsoever.**
- **Notes:** Fix shape is one line — compare `claims.ServiceAccount.UID` against `review.Status.User.UID` instead of the Extra map (retaining a non-empty guard, since `User.UID` is empty for non-ServiceAccount subjects, which preserves the existing `RejectsAuthenticatedNonServiceAccount` behaviour). **Phase 1 records only; no product code was changed.** The test fake must be corrected in the same change or it will re-certify the bug: it should populate `UserInfo.UID` and drop the fabricated extra. Consider also asserting against a real API server — the repo's CI already runs `go test -tags k8s ./internal/k8sagent/...` against a live kind cluster (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:80-89`), but that job never touches the controller's verifier, which is exactly the gap this defect fell through. Corroborating circumstantial evidence that this has been broken a long time: a `unified-cd-k8s-agent` Deployment on the test machine has been in `CrashLoopBackOff` for 14 days with 2983 restarts (it is a pre-#75 static-token build failing `http 401`, so it is not direct evidence about the enrollment path, but it does mean no working k8s agent has run here in at least two weeks).

## W4-0 — observation: enrollment 403 is undiagnosable — five rejection paths share one response and nothing is logged server-side
- **Invariant:** none. **Classified an observation, not a violation:** the "Expected" below cites no `docs/` promise and no invariant text — it is an authored expectation about what an operator should be able to tell apart, and the entry itself concedes that a coarse *client* response is a defensible security posture. *(An earlier draft filed this on I5. I5's text is about returning to steady state within documented bounds after fault injection; nothing here injects a fault or misses a bound. **Recording a divergence rather than leaving it as drift:** the W0-1 entry at `:44` makes the same `I5 (bounded recovery — diagnosability)` stretch for a structurally similar diagnosability finding and was accepted. The rule as written — `:1509`, and the classification rule at `:478` — governs here, so this entry is reclassified; `:44` is left as filed, and the inconsistency between them is therefore a recorded choice rather than an oversight.)*
- **Severity:** minor (observation — a defensible design, but it materially delayed root-causing the outage above)
- **Repro:** Same as the entry above. Compare the agent's error text and the controller's access-log line against the `http.Error(w, "enrollment policy rejected", http.StatusForbidden)` sites in `internal/controller/api_agent_enrollment.go`.
- **Observed:** The agent reports only `kubernetes enrollment request failed`; the controller logs only its routine access-log line (`"path":"/api/v1/agents/enroll","status":403`). **Five** rejection paths in `handleKubernetesAgentEnroll` return the identical response — `:319` (no bearer token), `:335` (policy nil / disabled / wrong provider), `:343` (unparseable `providerConfig`), `:359` (any non-`Unavailable` verifier error, itself covering seven distinct wrapped causes), `:366` (requested labels not authorized). *(Stated precisely because enumeration is this entry's whole subject: `grep -n StatusForbidden` on the file returns six hits, but `:499` carries a different message — "agent identity disabled" — and lives in a different function, so it is not one of these. Five sites, one message.)* The controller emits **no log record of why**, at any level: this is **read from code, not observed** — the handler at `:312-374` contains no `slog` call on any rejection path, so no log level could have produced one. *(For completeness, the controller's actual level during the capture was the default `info`: the rig sets no `UNIFIED_LOG_LEVEL` and passes no `--log-level`, `cmd/controller/main.go:202`. Only the *agent* ran with `--log-level debug`.)* `verifier.Verify` returns richly-typed wrapped errors distinguishing `policy constraints`, `token review`, `projected token claims`, `token review subject`, `token review service account UID`, `policy subject`, `pod` and `pod binding` — and the handler discards all of that at `:353-360`, mapping every non-`Unavailable` error to the same opaque string. `recordAgentAuth("kubernetes","failure","policy")` collapses them to a single metric label too. Diagnosing the defect in the entry above required reading the verifier source and then hand-issuing a TokenReview with `kubectl` to inspect a field the product never surfaces; the running system offered no signal narrowing the five reachable rejection paths down to one.
- **Expected:** An operator debugging a failing agent enrollment should be able to tell "your policy does not list this namespace" apart from "your token is not pod-bound" apart from "the pod was deleted" without source-diving. Keeping the *client-facing* message coarse is a defensible security posture (it denies an unauthenticated caller an oracle), but that argument does not extend to the controller's own logs.
- **Notes:** Cheap fix: `slog.Warn("kubernetes enrollment rejected", "policy", req.Policy, "error", err)` at the rejection site — server-side only, so the coarse client response is preserved. Widening the metric's `reason` label to distinguish the verifier's error classes would also make the failure alertable. Note this is not merely cosmetic: it materially delayed root-causing a total feature outage, and it is the reason the 403-vs-503 distinction had to carry so much diagnostic weight. **This entry constrains the one above:** because five paths share one response, a 403 cannot by itself *prove* which path produced it — which is why the entry above states the `:84` attribution as an inference from the code path plus the seeded policy row, and cites the TokenReview at `agent_enrollment_kubernetes.go:70` (not the unreached `Pods().Get`) for what the 403 does establish.

## W4-0 — Three controllers race to create the bootstrap PAT on cold start; the loser exits(1) and stays down
- **Invariant:** **none — filed on the documented-contract limb.** `docs/high-availability.md:227` prescribes `UNIFIED_TOKEN` | "Same on all replicas (admin static token)" (verbatim), and `:545`'s go-live checklist re-states it. The prescribed configuration is precisely the one that produces this race — every replica derives the same `token_hash` and they collide on the unique index. *(An earlier draft filed this on I5; withdrawn as a stretch per `:1509`. I5's text is about returning to steady state **after fault injection** within documented bounds; no fault is injected here — the cold `up` is the documented startup path — and no documented recovery bound is missed, because none is published for this.)*
- **Severity:** **major** — escalated from an earlier `minor`, on the band text verbatim: major is "incorrect visible behavior, **unbounded recovery**". The loser `os.Exit(1)`s and **stays down**; recovery is not slow, it is absent without operator action. **The distinguishing fact was checked, not assumed:** `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml` declares exactly one `restart:` key in the whole file — `restart: "no"` on the one-shot `agent-enroll` service at `:168` — and the controllers (`controller1: &ctrl` at `:79`, with `controller2`/`controller3` aliasing it) declare none, so Docker's default `no` applies and nothing restarts the loser. `k8senroll.override.yaml` adds none either. Cold-start-only, and the one-command workaround, are mitigations the band text does not discount. **Divergence from the W0-1 precedent, recorded rather than glossed:** the `store init` entry at `:43` is a minor of similar shape. The distinction that survives inspection is **loudness, not retry behaviour** — W0-1's dead replicas cascaded into `nginx` failing to start and `agent-enroll` exhausting its budget, so `docker compose up` itself reported failure and the stack was visibly unusable; here the two survivors serve normally behind the LB and the only symptom is a silently 2/3-sized cluster. *(The contrast "W0-1 crash-loops and keeps retrying, this exits once" would be wrong and is not relied on: W0-1's own body says both processes "exited(1) rather than retrying", the same shape as here, and only its title says crash-loop. If the band text is applied consistently, `:43` is arguably a major too; it is left as filed and the divergence is noted here as a choice.)*
- **Repro:** Cold `up` of the HA rig against a fresh database — observed on the very first `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker compose -f test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml -f test/edgecase/compose/k8senroll.override.yaml up -d` of this spike. Not specific to the overlay (which only adds `-f`, two bind mounts and a network) and not related to Kubernetes.
- **Observed:** `controller1` exited immediately and permanently:
  ```
  controller1-1 | {"level":"ERROR","msg":"sync UNIFIED_TOKEN as bootstrap PAT",
                   "error":"create bootstrap pat: ERROR: duplicate key value violates
                            unique constraint \"pats_token_hash_key\" (SQLSTATE 23505)"}
  ```
  ```
  $ docker compose -p unified-cd-ha ps -a
  controller1   Exited (1)
  controller2   Up
  controller3   Up
  ```
  All three replicas share one `UNIFIED_TOKEN` and each calls `pg.UpsertBootstrapPAT` at startup (`cmd/controller/main.go:277-281`). The upsert is not concurrency-safe against the `pats_token_hash_key` unique index: two replicas both find no row, both INSERT, and the loser's error is handled by `os.Exit(1)`. The rig declares no `restart:` policy, so the replica stays down and the stack silently runs at 2/3 capacity. It is **cold-start-only** — once the row exists a manual start succeeds:
  ```
  $ docker compose -p unified-cd-ha start controller1 && sleep 8 && docker compose -p unified-cd-ha ps -a
  controller1   Up 8 seconds
  $ docker exec unified-cd-ha-postgres-1 psql -U unified -d unified -c "select name from pats;"
         name
  -------------------
   env:UNIFIED_TOKEN
  (1 row)
  ```
- **Expected:** `docs/high-availability.md` presents running N identical controller replicas against one database as the supported topology. A benign write-write race between replicas doing identical idempotent bootstrap work should be absorbed (retry, or `ON CONFLICT` covering the `token_hash` index), not turned into a fatal exit. The exit is also the harshest available response to a condition whose desired end state — the row exists with the right hash — is *already true* by the time the error is observed.
- **Notes:** Distinct from the W0-1 `store init` crash-loop finding (that one is a DB-connectivity race with no retry; this one is an application-level uniqueness race that occurs *after* a successful connect), but the same root pattern: startup errors are uniformly fatal with no retry, and compose sets no restart policy, so any startup race permanently reduces replica count. Practical impact on this campaign: **any wave assuming three live controllers must verify all three are `Up` after a cold bring-up**, or it will silently measure a 2-replica system. Fix shapes: make `UpsertBootstrapPAT` conflict-tolerant on `token_hash`, or retry-then-verify instead of exiting.


## W4-rig — observation: a `podTemplate` whose containers do not include one named `job` parses, validates, schedules and builds a Pod, and then cannot execute a single step
- **Invariant:** none. **Observation, not a violation:** no `docs/` text promises that an arbitrary container name works, and the rule (the primary container is `job`) is real and internally consistent. What is recorded is that the rule is unenforced at every stage that could enforce it cheaply, and unstated at every stage that could state it.
- **Severity:** minor (observation — an authoring error that survives all validation and surfaces as a runtime message naming a container the author never wrote)
- **Repro:** Any Kubernetes job whose `podTemplate.spec.containers` supplies its own list without an entry named `job`, and whose steps set no `container:`. Encountered building the W4 baseline fixture, which copied its container name (`main`) from `test/edgecase/workloads/podcap-job.payload.json`.
- **Observed:** `dsl.Parse` with `KnownFields(true)` plus `Job.Validate` accept it (`test/edgecase/tools/w3/fixcheck` prints `OK`, `requiredCaps=[container]`), `POST /api/v1/jobs` returns **200**, the run is claimed, and `BuildPod` produces a live 2/2 Pod. The first step then fails:
  ```
  unified-cd: step "probe" failed to execute: unable to upgrade connection:
  container job is not valid for pod ucd-run-9c2e41c0-cc65-45
  ```
  and the run is `Failed` ~5 s after trigger. **Citation corrected at review:** the quoted line survives in `w4-2/final-logs/k8s-agent.log:5` (`"step exec error" … "container job is not valid for pod ucd-run-9c2e41c0-cc65-45"`), NOT in `w4-2/step6-baseline.txt` — that file was overwritten by the successful re-run, and the pod's phase history `Init:0/1 -> PodInitializing -> Terminating` for this first attempt **was never captured** and is dropped from this entry. (An identical phase sequence for a *different*, successful run is visible in `w4-2/step6-baseline.txt`; it is not evidence about this one.) `dsl.PrimaryContainerName = "job"` (`internal/dsl/container.go:23`) is the exec target for any step with no `container:`, and `internal/k8sagent/executor.go` falls back to it. `defaultPodSpec` injects `{Name: "job", Image: image}` only when the template supplies **no** containers at all (`internal/k8sagent/podbuilder.go:191`); when the author supplies a list, nothing adds one and nothing checks. *(Measured, not inferred: the built Pod had 2 containers — the author's `main` and the injected `unified-artifact` sidecar — so no `job` container was added.)*
- **Expected:** Either the DSL rejects a `podTemplate` that supplies containers without a `job` entry and without every step naming a `container:` (the same class of authoring error `validateStepTargetedWorkingDir` at `internal/dsl/container.go:130+` already catches at parse time), or the runtime error names the *author's* mistake rather than a container name that appears nowhere in their YAML. The reserved-name machinery to do this is already present — `IsReservedContainerName`, `PrimaryContainerName`, `DefName` and `PodTemplateContainers` are all exported and already used for adjacent checks.
- **Notes:** **`test/edgecase/workloads/podcap-job.payload.json` has exactly this shape** (`- name: main`). It has never been executed — W2-4 Part D uses it precisely because it is *unclaimable* on the `test/ha` agents — so this was latent in the campaign's own fixtures. It is left unmodified on purpose: `edge-podcap-job` staying claimable-but-unschedulable is W2-4 Part D's premise (`scenarios/w2-4-queued-reaper.md:207`). The W4 fixtures use `job`. Costs the campaign one wasted baseline run; would cost a real user one failed pipeline plus a source dive.

## W4-rig — observation: a run whose Pod is deleted mid-flight fails within ~1 s with exit code 137, and every recorded trace is indistinguishable from a step that exited 137 on its own
