## W4-2 — `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:491-521` publishes, as "Minimum permissions required for k8s-agent to operate", a Role whose `rules:` are byte-identical to those of the one that silently defeats `podTemplate.reuse` — the same page promises reuse at `:293` and `:341`, PR #50 fixed every copy of the Role it *ships* and none of the one it *publishes*, and the entire signal is one `WARN` per run reading "failed to mark pod idle, deleting"
- **Invariant:** **none — filed on the documented-contract limb, and no invariant is stretched to fit.** I1 ("every API-accepted run reaches exactly one terminal state; no phantom runs from duplicate fires/webhooks", `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-edge-case-testing-design.md:48`) was considered and is a **null limb**: every run under the restricted credential reached exactly one terminal state, `Succeeded`, no phantom run was created, and the jobs *did* succeed — what is lost is pooling and a `/workspace` build cache, not the correctness of the run record. *(Citation and quotation **corrected at review**: this entry previously cited `:45` — a blank line in the spec — and quoted "every run reaches exactly one terminal state, and that state matches what actually happened", **a clause that appears nowhere in the spec**; the same invented clause was carried by `scenarios/w4-1-podgc-skip-not-delete.md` and `w4-2-reuse-swallow.md` and is corrected at source in both. It is W4-local drift: `:1580` and the W2 runbooks all cite `:48` with the real text. **The null-limb call is unchanged and is stronger against the real clause**, whose subject is the arithmetic of terminal states rather than their deservedness.)* Filing I1 here would be the stretch `FINDINGS.md:1509` forbids, of the kind W2-5 and W2-7 were corrected for.
- **Severity:** **major.** Argued on this file's rubric (`:6-8`) rather than defaulted. This is "incorrect visible behavior" reached by *following the documentation*: the operator configures exactly what the Kubernetes integration guide calls the minimum permissions, enables a feature the same page promises twice, and the feature does not happen — every run, permanently, for the life of the agent process, because a credential does not change. There is no recovery path from inside the product (no retry, no re-check, no degradation notice) and no signal outside one process's stdout. Held **below critical**: no run fails, no status is wrong, nothing is lost or corrupted — the cost is pod churn, a cold `/workspace` on every run, and the loss of the persistent build cache `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:294` advertises. Held **above minor** because it is not a docs gap that merely misinforms: the documented configuration *produces the wrong behaviour*, and the wrong behaviour is invisible. **The reach, stated so the band is not read as broader than it is — the sibling entry at `:2407` does this for its own finding and this one should not have omitted it.** Two conditions must both hold: the operator must apply the **docs' hand-copied Role instead of the shipped `manifests/` bundle** (which grants the verbs correctly at HEAD — see the retraction cross-linked below), **and** some job must set `podTemplate.reuse: true`. Neither is exotic — `:2399` records that the RBAC section exists precisely for the reader not applying the bundle, and reuse is a feature the same page promotes twice — but the entry claims neither that the shipped manifests are defective nor that every k8s deployment is affected. **The severity argument does not depend on the size of that population**, only on the fact that the documented configuration silently defeats a documented feature for everyone in it.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-2-reuse-swallow.md` Parts A/B0/B1/B2 (`w4-2b/partA.txt`, `partA3-transition.txt`, `partB0.txt`, `partB1.txt`, `partB2.txt`, `partB-controller.txt`, `partC-rbac-docs.txt`, `partC-blame.txt`, `agent-logs/`). `kubectl apply -f test/edgecase/k8s/w4-2-reuse-denied-rbac.yaml` (whose `rules:` block is byte-identical to the documented example — the `diff -u` in `partC-rbac-docs.txt` prints nothing); mint a kubeconfig for that ServiceAccount with `test/edgecase/k8s/make-w4-2-restricted-kubeconfig.sh`; point the host-run k8s agent at it via `kubeconfig:` in `test/edgecase/k8s/w4-2-agent-config-restricted.yaml` (one field; everything else identical to the rig default); run `edge-w4-reuse` twice. **Control on the same rig, same fixture, same namespace, four minutes earlier:** the same runs against the ordinary privileged kubeconfig.
- **Observed:** **The control first, because without it the result means nothing.** Three runs of `edge-w4-reuse` with the ordinary kubeconfig all executed in **one** Pod `ucd-run-38dc9437-37b8-4d` — `W4-REUSE-MARKER=MISS`, then `HIT planted=08:24:03Z`, then `HIT planted=08:24:07Z` — with `unified-cd/pool-status` caught mid-flight going `idle` -> `in-use runid=0533d690` -> `idle` across three 0.7 s samples, and **zero** log lines containing the string `pool`. **Then the restricted credential, cold pool** (namespace cleared, agent restarted, `Restore` adopted nothing — verified, zero pool lines at startup): two runs, **two different Pods**, `W4-REUSE-MARKER=MISS` **both** times, **both `Succeeded`**. The complete `(level,msg)` enumeration for that window is six lines and three messages — `INFO k8s: executing Run` x2, `INFO running` x2, and `WARN pool: failed to mark pod idle, deleting` x2 — i.e. **the only difference between a working reuse feature and a totally defeated one, anywhere in the agent's log, is two WARN lines.** Verbatim: `{"level":"WARN","msg":"pool: failed to mark pod idle, deleting","pod":"ucd-run-c7031bdb-9ec9-43","error":"pods \"ucd-run-c7031bdb-9ec9-43\" is forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:ci:w4-2-reuse-denied\" cannot update resource \"pods\" in API group \"\" in the namespace \"ci\""}`. **`k8s: failed to release Pod` (`agent.go:317`) does not fire** — `delete` is granted, so `ReleasePod`'s fallback `DeletePod` succeeds and it returns `nil` (`pool.go:258`). **Nothing outside the agent process saw anything, measured not assumed:** `runs` shows all six session runs `Succeeded`; `step_reports` shows 12 rows, every one `Succeeded exit_code 0`; a case-insensitive grep for `forbidden|403|pool|reuse` across all three controller replicas returns 14 lines of which **every one is incidental** (`postgres pool configuration` at boot, and `http request` lines whose path contains the substring `403` because a run id does); and `grep -rlE 'prometheus|promauto|metrics\.|Metric' internal/k8sagent/` returns **0 across all 53 files** (`ls -1` = 53, `find -type f` = 53, `find -type d` = 1 — flat package, enumeration verified, and it corrects the "60 files" repeated by two earlier briefs). **The denial itself was proven three ways before anything ran through it** (`partB0.txt`): `kubectl auth can-i` gives `update no` / `patch no` and `get/list/create/delete/watch yes`; a live `kubectl replace` (HTTP PUT, the verb `ReleasePod` uses) returns `Forbidden ... cannot update resource "pods"`; a live `kubectl annotate` (PATCH) returns the `cannot patch` twin.
- **Expected:** `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:293`, verbatim: "With `reuse: true`, the Pod is returned to a pool after the run and reused by the next run." `:294` adds the consequence operators actually buy it for: "Build caches can accumulate in `/workspace`." `:341`, inside the numbered list of what the agent does per run — a *mechanism* claim, and the sharpest limb, because it presents pooling as an unconditional consequence: "4. After all steps complete, delete the Pod (or return to pool if `reuse: true`)". `docs/jobs.md:1657`, the field table: "| `reuse` | bool | Return pod to a pool after run and reuse it for subsequent runs |". **Not one of them qualifies the promise** — none says reuse can fail, none says it depends on the agent's `pods update` permission, and none says the run still succeeds when it doesn't. And the page carrying two of those limbs also carries, at `:491-521`, the section headed **"RBAC example"** introduced by *"Minimum permissions required for k8s-agent to operate:"*, whose `rules:` are `verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "delete", "watch"]` on `["pods", "pods/exec", "pods/log"]` — **no `update`, no `patch`**.
- **Notes:** **The provenance is the fix list.** `git log -L` shows `manifests/base/k8s-agent/rbac.yaml:13` last touched by `6b0bf8f` — *"fix(k8s): make podTemplate.reuse actually reuse pods (workspace/Library persistence) (#50)"*, 2026-07-15 — which changed exactly this line from the five-verb set to the seven-verb set and attached the comment *"Without update, that call is forbidden and the pool falls back to deleting the pod every run — reuse silently never happens."* `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:504` was last touched by `51b148d` (*"implement unified-cd"*, 2026-06-28, the initial commit) and still carries the five-verb set. `git show --stat 6b0bf8f` lists **ten** files — six under `internal/k8sagent/`, four under `manifests/` — and **no documentation file at all**. So the fix corrected every copy of the Role it shipped and left the copy it publishes, on the page that promises the feature. **This entry is the reason W4-2's re-charter was only half right, and that is recorded rather than buried:** the scenario was re-chartered because "the missing-verbs mechanism was fixed in PR #50". That is true of `manifests/` and false of `docs/`, and the re-chartered experiment turned out to be a live execution of the still-documented configuration rather than a synthetic one. The `rules:` block in `test/edgecase/k8s/w4-2-reuse-denied-rbac.yaml` was written as "the shipped manifest minus `update` and `patch`" and landed on the published example by construction. **Fixes, in order of cost.** (a) One line: add `"update", "patch"` to `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:504`, and carry across the shipped manifest's comment so the next reader knows why. (b) The message. `pool.go:257`'s `"pool: failed to mark pod idle, deleting"` describes a transient failure with a sensible fallback; the condition is permanent and the fallback silently substitutes pod-per-run for pod reuse. Distinguishing `apierrors.IsForbidden(err)` and saying so once, loudly, at the first occurrence — "pod reuse is disabled: the agent's credential cannot update pods" — would convert a per-run hiccup into a diagnosis. (c) `internal/k8sagent/` emits **zero** metrics (verified over all 53 files), so there is no counter to alert on; a single `reuse_release_failed_total` would make this visible to monitoring rather than to whoever reads `kubectl logs`. **Two of the seven verbs the shipped Role grants are dead at HEAD** — `grep -rn '\.Patch(' internal/k8sagent/` and `'\.Watch('` both return **0**; the three writers all use `Update` (`podmanager.go:91`, `pool.go:255`, `pool.go:336`). Not a defect (headroom is fine), but worth stating beside a finding about a missing verb: the shipped Role over-grants two and the documented Role under-grants the one that matters. **Related, not duplicated:** `FINDINGS.md:2260` (W4-rig) carries the **retraction** of the opposite claim — that the *shipped manifests* lack the verbs — which is false at HEAD; this entry is about `docs/`, a different file with the opposite status, and the two should be read together. **Every W4 finding runs against a controller whose enrollment was bypassed by test infrastructure** (`test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-rig.md`); nothing here depends on that path — the credential under test is the *Kubernetes API server* credential, which is independent of it. **Phase 1 records only; no product code and no `manifests/` file was changed.**

## W4-2 — `docs/configuration.md:458` gives the `poolIdleTimeout` default `0` as "(no reuse)"; measured, reuse is fully on at the default and what `0` disables is **eviction** — leaving idle pooled Pods that the pod GC declines by design, that no eviction goroutine ever starts to collect, and that are re-adopted across agent restarts, up to `maxConcurrent` per distinct pod shape
- **Invariant:** **none — filed on the documented-contract limb.** No invariant I1-I7 is contradicted by its own text: every run involved reached exactly one terminal state and it was `Succeeded`. What is contradicted is a published sentence about a default, and what it conceals is a resource with no reclamation path.
- **Severity:** **major**, argued rather than defaulted, and the reasoning is given so a reviewer can disagree with the band without disagreeing with the facts. The false sentence **alone** would be **minor** — `:8`'s "docs gap", the band W4-3's comparable `podStartTimeout` inversion (`FINDINGS.md:2282`) correctly took. What lifts it is the combination of three things. *(i)* The concealed behaviour is a resource **no component in the product ever reclaims**: `podGCDecision` (`podgc.go:19-24`) returns `false` unconditionally for pool-managed Pods and defers, in its own words (`podgc.go:99-100`), to "the pool's own idle-timeout/Restore logic" — which at `0` does not exist; `StartEviction` (`pool.go:130-133`) returns before launching its goroutine; and `Restore` (`pool.go:317-325`) re-adopts idle Pods rather than deleting them. That is `:7`'s "unbounded recovery" in its strongest form: not slow recovery, **no recovery path at all** short of `kubectl delete` by hand. *(ii)* There is no second source. `docs/configuration.md` is the **only** operator-facing page that mentions `poolIdleTimeout` (docs survey: 6 hits in 3 files; excluding `docs/superpowers/`, **2 hits in 1 file**), and `docs/kubernetes-integration.md` — the page that documents pod reuse — never mentions it, so an operator investigating accumulated `ucd-run-*` Pods is sent to the one page that tells them the wrong thing. *(iii)* `docs/high-availability.md:431` states the GC half as a **feature** — "Pods still owned by the Pod-reuse pool are never touched" — without noting that at the default nothing else touches them either. **Held below critical — and this was re-checked against the corrected bound in the Notes rather than inherited from the first draft.** The band turns on *kind*, not magnitude, and none of the kinds `:6` reserves for critical is present: nothing is lost, corrupted or exposed, no run fails, and the retained Pods are healthy and reusable, which is a pool's whole purpose. The corrected bound — up to `maxConcurrent` × distinct shapes, and `maxConcurrent` defaults to **100** (`config.go:207-208`) — is a far larger number than the "one per shape" this entry first asserted, and it does make one critical-adjacent path materially more plausible: enough retained Pods exhaust a namespace `ResourceQuota` or node capacity, after which subsequent runs fail to schedule. That path is **code-read and unmeasured** — every Part D config pinned `maxConcurrent: 1`, which forbade it structurally — and even measured it would land in `:7`'s "incorrect visible behavior, unbounded recovery", not in `:6`. The band is therefore unchanged at **major**, but it now rests on the rubric's categories rather than on a small number, because the small number was wrong.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-2-reuse-swallow.md` Part D (`w4-2b/partD1.txt`, `partD2-hold.txt`, `partD3.txt`, `partB3-docsurvey.txt`, `agent-logs/k8s-agent-partD-*.log`). Run the host k8s agent against `test/edgecase/k8s/w4-2-agent-config-pooldefault.yaml` — identical to the rig default except that `poolIdleTimeout` is **absent**, i.e. the product default. Trigger `edge-w4-reuse` twice (D4), then `edge-w4-poolkey-b` and `edge-w4-poolkey-c` once each (D1 — three fixtures whose only difference is pod shape, hence three `poolKey` buckets). Hold and sample. Restart the agent against the same config (D2). Restart against `test/edgecase/k8s/w4-2-agent-config-poolevict.yaml`, whose **only** difference is `poolIdleTimeout: 40s` (D3, the positive control).
- **Observed:** **D4, the direct refutation:** at the default the doc calls "(no reuse)", runs `f0b89939-...` and `62f508da-...` both `Succeeded` **in the same Pod** `ucd-run-f0b89939-bfd5-4f`, with `W4-REUSE-MARKER=MISS` then `HIT planted=08:28:33Z`. Reuse is fully on. **D1, accumulation:** three distinct pod shapes produced three separately-pooled Pods with three distinct hashes — `3c1d2612f14e2dd35233f878a28578b5`, `db63f75ad772fff085fd2b00d7836b73`, `5a495bb77d29c505ff339c7ad7f8c09f` — all `pool-status: idle`. **The hold, with its bound stated:** all three stayed `2/2 Running` and `idle` at every one of 8 samples over **7 m 03 s** of holding (`08:29:09.9Z` -> `08:36:13.3Z`), with **zero** agent lines matching `evict`; the oldest of the three Pods was **7 m 44 s** old at the final sample, having been created ~40 s before the hold opened (`partD2-hold.txt` prints both the sample clock and each Pod's age, and the two must not be conflated). That window exceeds the rig's own `poolIdleTimeout` (5 m) and does **not** exceed the documented example (10 m); it is not written as "never evicted" because the scenario ended the window itself. **The pod GC saw them and declined, ten times each:** the controller access log carries exactly **10** `GET /api/v1/runs/{id}` per pooled run id, counted over the **whole access log** — a window opening at Pod creation, ~40 s before the hold — and **not** over the hold alone, which `partD2-hold.txt`'s own header bounds at ~7 sweeps; there is no deletion and no GC log line, which is `podgc.go:99-100`'s deferral measured against a pool that has nothing to defer to. **The "one per sweep per Pod" reading is derived, not tagged:** the access log does not record which client issued a request, and the attribution rests on the agent's pod-GC ticker being the only plausible source of a repeating per-pooled-run-id GET at that cadence (`agent.go:139` passes `time.Minute` to `runPodGC`; the ticker is `podgc.go:101-106`) (independently corroborating `w4-1-podgc-skip-not-delete.md` §Part C on different Pods). **D2, the leak survives a restart:** SIGTERM and restart under the same config produced three `{"level":"INFO","msg":"pool: restored idle pod",...}` lines at `17:36:28.6008051+09:00`, one per Pod with its hash, and all three were still `Running` afterwards. **D3, the positive control — without it D1 proves nothing:** same rig, same three Pods, only `poolIdleTimeout: 40s` changed, and at `t=+60s` `pods=0` with three `{"level":"INFO","msg":"pool: evicting idle pod (timeout)"}` lines 6.3 ms apart — evicted on the second 30 s check, exactly as `pool.go:134-137`'s 30 s interval floor predicts. **So the rig can evict; at the default nothing does.** **One thing D3 exposed that nothing set out to look for:** the `idleSince` in all three eviction lines is `17:36:30.3255849+09:00`, byte-identical to that boot's `k8s agent registered` timestamp rather than each Pod's actual release ~8 minutes earlier, because `Restore` rebuilds every entry with `IdleSince: time.Now()` (`pool.go:322`). **The idle clock resets on every agent restart**, so an agent restarting more often than `poolIdleTimeout` evicts nothing even when the field *is* set — measured here as a side effect; mechanism code-read.
- **Expected:** `docs/configuration.md:458`, verbatim with its columns: "| `poolIdleTimeout` | string | No | `0` (no reuse) | Go duration an idle pooled Pod is kept for reuse before teardown (e.g. `10m`) |". The **Default** column asserts that `0` — which is the value of an unset field, i.e. the shipped default — means *no reuse*. The code trace, all at HEAD: `PoolIdleTimeoutDuration()` (`config.go:121-131`) returns `0` when the field is unset; `main.go:69-70` is `if d := cfg.PoolIdleTimeoutDuration(); d > 0 { pool.SetIdleTimeout(d) }`, so `SetIdleTimeout` is never called; `StartEviction` (`pool.go:130-133`) returns at `<= 0`; and `idleTimeout` is read **nowhere else** — `grep -rn 'idleTimeout' internal/k8sagent/` returns 7 lines, all in `pool.go`, all inside `SetIdleTimeout`, `StartEviction`, `evictExpired` or the struct comment, so `ClaimPod` and `ReleasePod` never consult it. The struct field's own comment (`pool.go:52`) reads `// 0 = no eviction` and `SetIdleTimeout`'s doc comment (`:122-123`) reads "A value of 0 disables eviction (default)" — **the code's author knew; the operator-facing table says the opposite.** *(Those comments are quoted to show the divergence; per the campaign's recording rules they are not the contract this entry is filed against — `docs/configuration.md:458` is.)*
- **Notes:** **The bound, stated so this is not inflated — and CORRECTED, because its first version claimed more than the evidence could carry.** What is measured is that the accumulation is **not one per run**: three fixtures produced three Pods, and two extra runs of `edge-w4-reuse` produced none. What this entry first added — that it is *one Pod per distinct pod shape* — is **withdrawn**, because the rig could not have shown otherwise. `ReleasePod` appends to `p.pods[pp.PoolKey]` **unconditionally** (`pool.go:263`) and `ClaimPod` pops exactly one (`pool.go:188-191`), so per-key pool depth is bounded by the **peak concurrency ever reached for that shape**, and the total by **`maxConcurrent` × distinct shapes** — `maxConcurrent` being a global semaphore (`agent.go:148-149`) that `Validate` defaults to **100** when unset (`config.go:207-208`) and that a negative value disables entirely (`agent.go:148`). **The concurrency multiplier was not measured and could not have been:** every Part D agent config pinned `maxConcurrent: 1` (`w4-2-agent-config-pooldefault.yaml:63`, `w4-2-agent-config-poolevict.yaml:62`, `w4-2-agent-config-restricted.yaml:72`), which structurally forbids a per-key depth above 1. The "× peak concurrency" factor is therefore **code-read**, and the same default configuration this entry is about carries `maxConcurrent` 100. The accumulation is unbounded in shape diversity and in time, and bounded in run count only by concurrency. It reaches only deployments where some job sets `podTemplate.reuse: true` while the agent config never sets `poolIdleTimeout` — which is the default configuration, and note that the two settings live in different files owned by different roles (job author vs cluster operator), so neither party necessarily sees both. **A partial self-correction worth acknowledging:** an operator who *wants* reuse and reads "(no reuse)" will probably set the field, and thereby accidentally avoid the leak. The population actually harmed is the one that enables `reuse:` in a job and never touches agent config. **Fixes.** (a) The Default column should read `0` (no eviction — idle Pods are kept indefinitely), and the Description should say what that costs. (b) `docs/kubernetes-integration.md`'s "Pattern 4: Pod reuse" (`:291-305`) should mention `poolIdleTimeout` at all — it is the only page a reader of `reuse: true` will find, and it is currently silent on the knob that governs the Pod's whole afterlife. (c) `docs/high-availability.md:431`'s "never touched" is accurate but incomplete; one clause naming the pool as the lifecycle owner *and* noting that at the default the pool never collects would close it. (d) If unbounded retention is not intended, a non-zero default (the docs' own `10m` example) is a one-line change; if it **is** intended, the doc should say so, because "keep warm Pods indefinitely" is a defensible design and "0 means no reuse" is not a description of it. **Secondary hit, recorded rather than filed:** `docs/configuration.md:395-396`'s comment "Unset = no reuse window" is ambiguous rather than false — "reuse window" can be read as "the window before teardown", which genuinely is absent at 0 — and is subordinate to `:458`. **Related but distinct, do not merge:** `FINDINGS.md:2282-2295` (W4-3) is about the **same table row** `:458` and a **different column and claim** — that its *Description* column omits the boot rejection of an unparseable value. Neither subsumes the other, and worth noting for the campaign's own process: W4-3 read that exact row closely enough to compare it against its neighbours `:456`/`:457` and did not notice the Default column was wrong, because it was hunting a different defect. **Correction to the campaign's own brief, recorded because the brief will be reused:** the W4 exploration brief states that `PoolIdleTimeoutDuration()` returns 0 for "unset, unparseable and literal `0` alike". The accessor does, but the **unparseable case is unreachable in the shipped binary** — `Validate` (`config.go:210-214`) rejects it and the agent exits first, which is exactly what `FINDINGS.md:2294` already established. Only *unset* and a value parsing to zero reach the accessor. This does not weaken the finding: the subject is the **default**, which is unset. **A second "correction to the brief" that this entry made and now WITHDRAWS.** It said the brief's survey figure was *wrong* — "`poolIdleTimeout` across `docs/` is 6 hits in 3 files, not 9". That is a grep-flag difference, not an error: `grep -rn "poolIdleTimeout" docs/` returns **6** lines and `grep -rni` returns **9**, in the **same 3 files**, so the brief's 9 is the case-insensitive count and is correct. The 3-line delta is four Go-identifier mentions of `PoolIdleTimeout` / `PoolIdleTimeoutDuration` in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-15-k8s-agent-resilience.md` (`:17`, `:130`, `:145`), all under `docs/superpowers/`. `partB3-docsurvey.txt` stated no flag for this survey and has been annotated to state it. The substantive claim needed no defence and holds identically under either flag: **2 hits in 1 file** operator-facing, `docs/configuration.md` alone, and `docs/kubernetes-integration.md` never mentions the field. **Every W4 finding runs against a controller whose enrollment was bypassed by test infrastructure** (`test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-rig.md`); this Part touches nothing on that path — the agent held the ordinary privileged kubeconfig throughout. **Phase 1 records only; no product code was changed.**

## W4-2 — observation: with `pods update` denied, `ClaimPod` announces a permanent 403 as `"pool: pod claim conflict, creating new pod"` — reachable on any agent restart that inherits an idle pooled Pod, which at the default configuration is every restart *once such a Pod exists*, and such Pods are created only while the agent can still update Pods
- **Invariant:** none. **Observation** — the wrong-shaped message costs an operator a diagnosis, not a run; every run in this arm reported `Succeeded`. Recorded because the reconnaissance for this scenario concluded, from a code read, that this branch is unreachable under an RBAC denial, and executing it proved otherwise.
- **Severity:** **minor (diagnosability)** — **observation**. The 403's text does survive into the `error` field, so the line is diagnosable by anyone who reads it in full; what is wrong is the `msg`, which names a condition with the opposite remedy. A claim conflict means another actor touched the Pod and retrying is correct; a 403 means retrying is futile for the life of the credential.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-2-reuse-swallow.md` Part B2 (`w4-2b/partB2.txt`, `agent-logs/k8s-agent-partB2-warm.log`). Leave one idle pooled Pod in the namespace (any `podTemplate.reuse` run under an unrestricted credential does this), then restart the agent under the restricted kubeconfig and trigger one run.
- **Observed:** `Restore`'s idle branch (`pool.go:317-325`) re-adopted the Pod **without calling `Update` at all** — it appends directly — so the restricted credential is never exercised at restore time: `{"time":"2026-08-01T17:25:55.5055937+09:00","level":"INFO","msg":"pool: restored idle pod","pod":"ucd-run-38dc9437-37b8-4d","poolKey":"3c1d2612f14e2dd35233f878a28578b5"}`. The pool was therefore non-empty on the first claim, `pool.go:188-189`'s `if len(idle) > 0` was true, and **1.02 s later**: `{"time":"2026-08-01T17:25:56.5304005+09:00","level":"WARN","msg":"pool: pod claim conflict, creating new pod","pod":"ucd-run-38dc9437-37b8-4d","error":"pods \"ucd-run-38dc9437-37b8-4d\" is forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:ci:w4-2-reuse-denied\" cannot update resource \"pods\" in API group \"\" in the namespace \"ci\""}`. The same run then emitted the ordinary `pool: failed to mark pod idle, deleting` **3.51 s** later, so the first run after such a restart emits *both* messages and the ordering is fixed. **A detail read off the live annotations that neither the plan nor the runbook predicted:** the replacement Pod carried `unified-cd/pool-status: in-use` right up to its deletion and **never** transitioned to `idle` — because that transition *is* the denied write. So under this failure `kubectl` shows a namespace of Pods permanently annotated `in-use` with an empty `pool-run-id`, which is indistinguishable from an in-flight run; the annotation is not a reliable readout of pool state.
- **Expected:** `pool.go:198-205`'s own comment says "conflict or fetch failure -> fall back to creating a new pod", and `UpdatePodAnnotations` (`podmanager.go:77-93`) genuinely does return a hand-rolled `conflict: resourceVersion of pod %s has changed` for the optimistic-concurrency case at `:83-85`. But it returns the API server's error **bare and unwrapped** at `:91-92`, and the log message at `pool.go:202` labels *every* error from that call a conflict. `apierrors.IsConflict(err)` / `apierrors.IsForbidden(err)` distinguish them in one line each.
- **Notes:** **This corrects a code-read conclusion in this scenario's own brief, and the correction is the point.** The brief argued that under an RBAC denial `ReleasePod` never appends to `p.pods`, so `ClaimPod`'s branch is never reached and its misattributed message is not what this scenario produces. That is right for a process that starts with an empty pool and wrong in general: `Restore` runs at every agent start (`agent.go:84`) and re-adopts idle Pods with no `Update`, so the pool is non-empty on the first claim after any restart that inherits one. **And per the `poolIdleTimeout` entry above, the default configuration guarantees that such Pods, once created, are never removed** — so on a default deployment every restart inherits them. **The reachability needs one further condition, and stating it costs the entry nothing.** An agent holding *only* the restricted credential never creates an idle pooled Pod at all: every `ReleasePod` `Update` is refused and the Pod is deleted instead of pooled (`pool.go:255-258`), which is precisely the violation filed above. This branch therefore requires a **credential downgrade or a mixed-credential history** — idle Pods left behind by a privileged agent generation, then a restart under the restricted one, which is exactly what Part A → Part B2 constructed. That is a realistic path (an operator tightening RBAC onto the documented "minimum permissions" example *is* that downgrade), but it is **not** "every restart" on a uniformly restricted deployment, and an earlier version of this entry said it was. **A third swallow on the same path, code-read and NOT EXECUTED, recorded here rather than filed separately.** `Restore`'s in-use branch calls `Update` at `pool.go:336`; that call sits inside `if err == nil { ... continue }` (`:337-346`), so on failure control falls through to `:349`, which logs `slog.Info("pool: deleting orphaned in-use pod", "pod", ..., "run", runID)` and deletes. That is **INFO** level, its text describes a deliberate cleanup of an orphan for a Pod that is neither, and **the error object is discarded entirely** — no `error` field, no use of `err`. It is the only one of the three swallows that loses the 403 completely. It is reachable whenever an agent restarts holding an in-use pooled Pod whose run has since finished; this scenario did not construct that state and does not claim to have measured it. *(A fourth, quieter still: `ReleasePod`'s `Get` failure at `pool.go:246-249` short-circuits to `DeletePod` with **no log line at all**. Also code-read, also not executed — `get` was granted in this arm, so it was never taken.)* **Related, deliberately not merged:** the two violations filed above from this scenario. This entry is about a message; those are about a documented Role and a documented default. **Every W4 finding runs against a controller whose enrollment was bypassed by test infrastructure** (`test/edgecase/scenarios/w4-rig.md`); nothing here depends on that path — the credential under test is the *Kubernetes API server* credential, which is independent of it. **Phase 1 records only; no product code was changed.**

W4-1 (`:2353`) is the campaign's second `major`-severity observation**, after W3-1's (`:1938`), and like that one the label is the point. **A 404 the controller did not mint makes the pod GC delete a live run's Pod** — measured, not argued: the run died 41.2 s into a 120 s job, was recorded `Failed` with a **NULL exit code** and no reason on any run-scoped surface, and its terminal status was written by the controller's **heartbeat reconcile** rather than by the agent that killed it. It recurs **once per sweep for every live Pod in the namespace** for as long as the condition lasts, so a minute-long routing fault takes out every run on the agent. It is held an observation, not a violation, for one reason stated plainly in the entry: `docs/high-availability.md:428-430` says a 404 means "definitively gone", so **the code does exactly what is published**, and the **trigger** — something other than the controller minting that 404 — is external to the product. *(Wording aligned with the entry's own correction: the trigger is external; the inability to attribute it is `client.go:107-108`, which is internal.)* `isRunNotFound` is a bare status-code test on a response the agent's own client has already stripped of provenance. **Severity and classification are orthogonal axes and this is the second entry that proves it.** What the label costs is the same thing it cost W3-1: an observation is easier to skip, and this one should not be skipped.
  - **W4-rig's three, none of which is a scenario finding.** A `podTemplate` whose `containers:` do not include one named **`job`** parses, validates, schedules and **builds a Pod**, and then cannot execute a single step — the rule is real and internally consistent, and it is unenforced at every stage that could enforce it cheaply and unstated at every stage that could state it, surfacing as a runtime message naming a container the author never wrote (`:2220`). A run whose Pod is deleted mid-flight fails within ~1 s with **exit code 137** and every recorded trace is indistinguishable from a step that exited 137 on its own — the status is *correct*, which is the desirable outcome; nothing anywhere says why, and this is the **third** W-wave entry of that shape (`:2233`). Under `podTemplate.reuse` a Pod's name **and** its `unified-cd/runId` label permanently identify the **first** run that used it, so a scenario locating "the pod for run X" by label finds nothing for runs B and C — only `unified-cd/pool-run-id` tracks the current occupant and it is cleared on release; this campaign's own injector had to be written around it (`:2246`).

A non-positive `UNIFIED_K8S_POD_START_TIMEOUT` **silently discards a valid config-file value** and substitutes 5m — the substitution itself is documented; that the file's valid value is discarded on the way is not, and **nothing anywhere logs the resolved duration**, which is what made D4 necessary to prove which one was in effect (`:2312`). A run cancelled while its Pod is still `Pending` ends with **zero log rows and zero `step_reports`**, so nothing tells its owner a Pod was created and destroyed — the agent's silence is the *documented* behaviour working (`docs/kubernetes-integration.md:207`), and the entry disputes not one line of it: what is at issue is that "not overriding the controller's **status**" has been implemented as writing **nothing at all**, and those are separable (`:2326`).

Nothing documented is contradicted: `docs/high-availability.md:351-352` justifies `replicas: 2` on the ground that "pod GC only touches pods whose runs are terminal or absent", and **that sentence held under test** — no Pod of a live run was deleted as a consequence of two agents sweeping, and the second agent correctly declined the first's pooled Pod on four consecutive sweeps. What is recorded is that it is safe **by predicate rather than by ownership**, and that both costs it carries are uncapped in the code (`:2366`). And the sweep interval is a **literal at its one call site** — no flag, no env var, no config field, **no test call site at all**, which makes `runPodGC`'s own `<= 0` guard unreachable code at HEAD; nothing documented promises configurability, and the practical consequence is that every trial in that scenario cost up to a full minute and the sweep phase could not be commanded (`:2374`).

Diagnosing the defect above required reading the verifier source and then hand-issuing a TokenReview with `kubectl` to inspect a field the product never surfaces (`:2182`). At the other end, with `pods update` denied, `ClaimPod` announces a **permanent 403** under the message `"pool: pod claim conflict, creating new pod"` — a message naming optimistic concurrency, whose remedy is the opposite of the real one: a claim conflict means retrying is correct, a 403 means retrying is futile for the life of the credential. **This entry exists because a code read said the branch was unreachable under an RBAC denial and executing it proved otherwise** (`:2409`).

### (a) The wave's two false premises, and the fifth-consecutive-wave verdict on the facts block

- **1. The campaign spec's kind-wiring sentence was wrong on four counts, and the wave's plan caught it before the wave began.** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-edge-case-testing-design.md:115-117` said the controller "stays on the compose stack, reachable from kind via host networking — **only the enrollment URL** changes, avoiding a second controller deployment." Refuted on four counts, each with its `file:line` at HEAD, at `plans/2026-08-01-edge-case-campaign-w4.md:13-17`: **(i)** no static token exists for the k8s agent — no `Token` field in `k8sagent.Config`, `enrollmentPolicy` mandatory, static k8s auth deliberately removed in PR #75; **(ii)** enrollment is **bidirectional** — `kubernetesEnrollmentVerifier.Verify` makes two live Kubernetes API calls (`TokenReviews().Create` and `Pods(ns).Get`), so **the controller must reach into the cluster** and needs a kubeconfig and RBAC; **(iii)** the compose controllers are configured with env vars only and load **no config file**, so the verifier map is empty and enrollment answers **503, fail-closed**; **(iv)** HTTPS is enforced agent-side unless `allowInsecureHTTP` or a loopback host, and the compose nginx serves plain HTTP on `18080`. Half the sentence was right — the controller did stay on the compose stack — and the half that was wrong turned "change a URL" into three tasks. **The spec now carries a `CORRECTED AFTER EXECUTION` block at `:115-117`, written at a preserved line count so the existing `...design.md:201-207` citation at `:496` still resolves.**
- **2. W4-2's charter was dead before the wave was written, and the stale premise then reached the wave twice more.** The charter — "verify the known missing `pods update/patch` RBAC verbs finding" — was closed by **PR #50 (`6b0bf8f`, 2026-07-15)**, the same day the campaign's own cross-session memory recorded the pre-fix diagnosis. That memory note carries a **`RESOLVED`** header. **The header did not travel with the claim.** It reached the W4 exploration brief, which chartered W4-2 around it; it then reappeared **inside Task 2's rig record**, which asserted that "the shipped `manifests/` Roles lack `pods update/patch`, so reuse is broken there" — unevidenced, false at HEAD, and attributed to W4-0, which records nothing of the kind. Task 2's own fix wave caught it (F7; the retraction is at `:2260`). **So one dead fact was published twice, in two documents, by two tasks, in one wave.** **The lesson, and it is the wave's main methodological output: a premise's provenance must travel with the premise.** A claim inherited from a note is worth exactly the freshness of the note, and a briefing that restates it **without its `file:line` at current HEAD** converts a dated observation into an apparent fact. The operational form is narrow enough to follow: *when a brief hands you a claim about the product, the first thing you do with it is re-read its `file:line` at HEAD and write down what you found — before designing anything around it.* **And the wave's strongest finding is what happened when W4-2 did exactly that**: re-charter in hand, it re-read the docs and found that PR #50 fixed every Role it *shipped* and **none of the one it publishes**, which is `:2393`. The dead premise was half right, and the live half was worse than the dead one.
- **The "verified code facts" pattern held for a fifth consecutive wave, and W4 makes it a three-way split rather than a two-way one.** W3 refined the rule to "the block's `file:line` claims hold while its *mechanism* claims fail". **Both halves held again — with one qualification added at the branch review, which weakens the cleaner half.** Every constant, key, span and line number in `plan:47-91` **resolved** correctly across all three scenarios, with one scope adjustment and no conclusion changed. *(Two corrections. **(1) The range.** This read `plan:47-99`, which runs past the facts block into "Facts NOT established" at `plan:93` — a list of declared open questions that cannot fail a check by construction, so including it inflated the denominator. The block is `:47-91`. **(2) The `file:line` half held on RESOLUTION and failed once on SUBSTANCE.** `plan:74` — "Both documented (`docs/configuration.md:456`)" — was counted below with the *mechanism* failures, and it is not one: `:456` exists, is the row the plan meant, and says the **opposite** of what it is cited for. That is a `file:line` claim failing in substance, a third failure mode the "line numbers hold, mechanisms fail" dichotomy has no slot for, and filing it under mechanism kept the "`file:line` half held for a fifth consecutive wave" record cleaner than the evidence supports. **The campaign should stop reporting resolution and substance as one number.** Reclassifying it also leaves the mechanism half at two executed refutations belonging to this plan plus one belonging to the Task 5 brief.)* And three mechanism claims were refuted **by execution**, which is the part that matters: the **Task 5 brief's** reachability claim (the "pod claim conflict" branch is unreachable under an RBAC denial, because a denied `ReleasePod` never appends to `p.pods`) is **wrong in general and a whole scenario part rested on it** — it is reached on any agent restart that inherits an idle pooled Pod, which at the default configuration is every restart once such a Pod exists, because `Restore` re-adopts **without calling `Update` at all**; *(attribution stated precisely rather than rounded to the plan: `plan:66` describes the two swallows accurately and makes no reachability claim, so this one belongs to the brief, and the plan's appendix records it under that name so a reader checking the block still finds it)*; `plan:74`'s "both behaviours are documented at `docs/configuration.md:456`" is not merely wrong but the **opposite** of what that line says, and became the W4-3 violation; and `plan:53`'s "the only non-test caller passes a literal" **understates** it, because there is no test call site at all. **What W4 adds is a third class the earlier waves folded into "mechanism": *environment* claims, which failed at a higher rate than mechanism claims did.** Four of the block's environment assertions were wrong or moot — **no `kind` CLI is needed and none is installed** (Docker Desktop's Kubernetes *is* kind, so the topology came free and a `kind create cluster` step every task would have repeated was never written); **`insecure-skip-tls-verify` was not required**, because the node certificate's SANs cover the name the kubeconfig uses; the `ci`-namespace question was already answered by the cluster; and the pod-bound-token question resolved **YES**, moving the enrollment failure strictly downstream of it. **The distinction is worth keeping because the cost profile differs**: a wrong mechanism claim costs a scenario design, a wrong environment claim costs bring-up time — and an environment claim is checkable in one command at the start of the first task. **W4-0's Step 1 is the model**: it spent its first ten minutes checking them and recovered an hour it had budgeted for a TLS workaround that was never needed. *(All of the above is now propagated to `plans/2026-08-01-edge-case-campaign-w4.md` §"CORRECTED AFTER EXECUTION", appended at the end of that file rather than inline, because `scenarios/w4-3-pod-start-timeout.md:46` cites `plan:71-84` and `:74` by line and an in-place banner would have silently invalidated those citations.)*
- **One thing the W4 plan did that no previous wave's plan did, and it should be copied: it corrected its own charter *before* execution, not after.** Both false premises are at `plan:11-19`, under the heading "Read this before planning anything: two chartered premises are false", each with its `file:line`. W1, W2 and W3 all corrected their facts blocks *during* execution. **The residual gap is the mirror image**: the plan's pre-execution corrections are exemplary and its **post-execution** ones were never propagated until this checkpoint — three tasks each recorded a `CORRECTION` in its own runbook and none of them reached the plan. That is the recorded-versus-propagated distinction `:739` draws, and W3's merge gate at `:2112` is what it violates.

### (b) What the rig cost, and what survives it

- **W4 was infrastructure work, and the ratio is the honest headline: three of six tasks built the rig, and the wave produced 21 entries against W2's 43 and W3's 23 — with six fewer scenarios than W2.** Nothing in this repo's automation had ever run a k8s agent against a controller. CI's k8s job runs `go test -tags k8s ./internal/k8sagent/...` on the runner host against kind's API with the default kubeconfig: it never applies a manifest, never enrolls, and never involves a controller. It proves kind can be created and nothing about the W4 surface.
- **What survives, all committed and all reusable as-is.** **(i) The kind wiring, which is that there is none to build** — Docker Desktop's Kubernetes *is* kind (node `desktop-control-plane`, a `kindest/node` container on a Docker bridge literally named `kind`), so the campaign gets kind's topology for free without installing the CLI and without a `kind create cluster` step every task would have repeated; `ci` and `unified-cd` both already exist and `ci` was free for use, with `manifests/` neither modified nor applied. **(ii) The controller config file and its RBAC** — `compose/controller-k8senroll.yaml` + `compose/k8senroll.override.yaml`, with `k8s/w4-spike-controller-rbac.yaml` granting **exactly** `create tokenreviews` + `get pods`, which is better than the admin kubeconfig the brief anticipated and doubles as documentation of the minimum RBAC a real deployment needs. **(iii) The kubeconfig *generators*, not the kubeconfigs** — `k8s/make-spike-kubeconfig.sh` and `k8s/make-w4-2-restricted-kubeconfig.sh`; both read the server URL out of the operator's own current kubeconfig, which is load-bearing because Docker Desktop publishes the apiserver on a **dynamic** host port and a hardcoded one breaks on the next restart. The generated files carry live bearer tokens, are gitignored, and are never archived. **(iv) The network bridge** — `docker network connect` onto the `kind` network **in addition to `default`**, which must be listed explicitly because naming any network replaces implicit default membership and would cut the controllers off from postgres, garage and nginx. No TLS workaround was needed. **(v) The k8s fault verbs** — `tools/w4/w4-k8s-inject.sh`, the first k8s fault tooling in this repo, because `inject.sh`'s verbs take compose **service names** and hardcode `unified-cd-ha_default`; six verbs, each with an effect measurement, and `block` now **asserts** its own arm rather than printing one. **(vi) The enrollment interposer** — `tools/w4/enrollproxy`, 427 lines of stdlib Go, forwarding everything except `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll`. **(vii) Seven fixtures and five agent configs** *(the count read "four" until the branch review; `ls test/edgecase/k8s/*agent-config*` returns five — W4-0's `.template.yaml` was omitted)*, every one validated through the real `dsl.Parse` twice — on the `.yaml` and on the YAML re-extracted from the `.payload.json`.
- **What was scenario-local, and should not be assumed by the next wave.** The **restricted kubeconfig and the `w4-2-reuse-denied` Role** are W4-2's and are regenerated, not reused. The **beacon Pods** W4-1 used to make GC sweeps observable are instruments, not product artifacts, and every one was removed by hand. The **second agent + second interposer** bring-up (a second credential for a different agent id, a second interposer on `:18098`, a config whose only edit is `server:`) is W4-1 Part D's and is cheap to redo but is not standing infrastructure. **The in-cluster Deployment route was deferred, not built** — every W4 capture is host-run.
- **The bring-up gotchas a re-runner will otherwise rediscover, in the order they bite.** **(i) The three bring-up commands are ordered and skipping one fails silently and confusingly**: the overlay bind-mounts `compose/kubeconfig-k8senroll.yaml`, and if that file does not exist **Docker creates a directory at the path**, all three controllers exit(1) on `is a directory`, and the empty directory **persists to poison the next `up`** until it is `rmdir`ed. It looks like the bootstrap-PAT race and is not — the race kills **one** replica, this kills **three**. If you do not need the 403 control, use the plain `test/ha` compose file, which is what W4-1, W4-2 and W4-3 all did. **(ii) `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` is not optional here** — the overlay's mounts are colon-bearing paths MSYS rewrites otherwise. **(iii) Verify all three controllers are `Up`, and do not assume failure either** (`:2270`). **(iv) The primary container must be named `job`** (`:2220`). **(v) Labels come from the enrollment token, not the agent config** — `handleAgentRegister` ignores the agent's requested labels and uses `principal.AuthorizedLabels`, so the label a job selector must match is the one on the *enrollment token*. **(vi) A `podTemplate` does not imply the `pod` capability** — three of four rig fixtures require `container`. **(vii) `-buildvcs=false` is required** in this worktree. **(viii) Two clocks**: agents and interposer log local `+09:00`, controller and Postgres log UTC, and captures alternate within a few lines. **(ix) `sidecarS3SecretName` is unset**, so cache steps are silent no-ops **reported `Succeeded`** and artifact steps fail — no W4 fixture depends on artifacts and none may. **(x) Clearing the `ci` namespace destroys `w4-spike-agent-pod` and any re-created Pod has a NEW UID**, so a captured token or a hand-written policy fixture pinning the old one is stale and will be rejected as a `pod UID mismatch`; re-mint rather than reuse. **(xi) The k8s agent re-enrolls on every process start**, so a scenario that swaps configs N times costs N+1 interceptions, not one per ~40 min. **(xii) A pre-#75 k8s-agent Deployment has been crash-looping on this machine for 14 days** (2983 restarts) and was left untouched — it is not this campaign's and will confuse a `kubectl get pods` that does not expect it.

### (c) The RBAC blind spot, and how much of it W4-2 actually closed

- **This repo's RBAC is exercised by no test and no CI job, and that is a coverage gap independent of any finding.** CI's Kubernetes integration job (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:80-89`) authenticates through `clientcmd.NewDefaultClientConfigLoadingRules()` — kind's admin kubeconfig, i.e. **cluster-admin** — **never applies `manifests/base/k8s-agent/rbac.yaml`**, creates no ServiceAccount and no RoleBinding (grep over the workflow: zero hits for any of them), and never starts a controller. Every permission the shipped Role grants or withholds is invisible to it by construction.
- **W4-2 closed part of it, and found the wave's strongest finding doing so.** It ran a live agent under a **token-scoped kubeconfig** for a ServiceAccount bound to a Role that denies `pods update`/`patch`, verified the denial two ways before measuring anything (`kubectl auth can-i` -> `no` for both, plus a live `PUT` and a live `PATCH` both refused, with `delete` granted as the control), and measured what a defeated `podTemplate.reuse` looks like from outside. That arm is what produced `:2393`.
- **What remains unexercised, stated precisely, because "W4 tested RBAC" would be the wrong summary.** **(i) The shipped Role itself has still never been the agent's identity.** W4-2 exercised the Role the **docs publish**; no wave has ever run an agent under `manifests/base/k8s-agent/rbac.yaml`. **(ii) The controller's enrollment Role is likewise unexercised** — W4-0 built a purpose-made least-privilege Role (`w4-spike-controller-rbac.yaml`) rather than applying `manifests/base/controller/rbac.yaml`. **(iii) Two of the seven verbs the shipped Role grants are dead at HEAD**: `.Patch(` and `.Watch(` return **0** across all 53 files of `internal/k8sagent/`, tests included — all three pool writers use `Update`. So the shipped Role **over-grants two verbs while the documented Role under-grants the one that matters**, and neither fact is reachable by any test. **(iv) The `pods/exec` and `pods/log` sub-resource grants** are untested as permissions, though exec is exercised functionally on every step. **(v) The in-cluster Deployment path is untested end to end** — every W4 capture is host-run under the developer's own cluster rights, which is why the entries say so and why no host-run capture is evidence about the shipped manifests **in either direction**. **The cheapest thing that would close most of this is not a scenario**: apply `manifests/base/k8s-agent/` into a namespace in CI's existing kind cluster and run the k8s tests as that ServiceAccount instead of as admin. It reuses a cluster CI already creates.

### (d) `internal/k8sagent/` has no Prometheus instrumentation at all — every W4 signal was a log line

- **Verified as an enumeration rather than asserted, twice, and both times the pre-execution figure was wrong.** `internal/k8sagent/` is **53 files** — `ls -1 | wc -l` and `find -type f | wc -l` agree, and `find -type d` returns 1, so the package is flat and there is nothing a recursive count could miss. `grep -rnE 'prometheus|promauto|metrics\.|Metric'` over all 53, **tests included**, returns **0 files and 0 matches**. The figure was stated as **60** in two briefs and was **corrected twice by execution** — `scenarios/w4-1-podgc-skip-not-delete.md:121-127` (CORRECTION 2, "53 files, not 60") and `scenarios/w4-2-reuse-swallow.md:856-861`, which records it as confirming the first and refuting the 60 "a second time". The wave's plan (`plan:59`) had scoped the claim narrower — "excluding tests" — and the executed enumeration is strictly stronger.
- **The consequence is not abstract and W4 paid it in every scenario.** The pod GC's entire observable surface is four `slog` calls; the pool's is three, one of which is `"pool: pod claim conflict"` announcing a permanent 403; the reuse defeat is **one `WARN` per run**; and the log-loss finding at `:2334` is a *silence*, detectable only by counting what the workload emitted against what the store holds. Three of the wave's five scenarios instrumented by tailing a single process's stdout, and the rig's route decision (host-run rather than in-cluster) turned on it — reason #1 of 3 was that a host process writes its stdout to a file the rig already tails, where an in-cluster Deployment puts it behind `kubectl logs` and a pod that restarts on crash.
- **Input to W6, stated as a scoping fact rather than a recommendation.** W6 owns the observability work, and it should know before it starts that the Kubernetes execution path contributes **zero** metrics to whatever it measures — so any W6 conclusion about metric coverage that does not name this exclusion is wrong by construction. The four candidates W4's own findings would have used, each corresponding to an entry: a pod-GC deletions counter split by `runFound` (`:2353`, `:2366`), a pool claim/release/evict counter split by outcome (`:2393`, `:2409`), a stdout-log-lines-dropped counter (`:2334` — the one that would have turned a silence into a signal), and the resolved `podStartTimeout` as a gauge (`:2312`).

### (e) The enrollment bypass, as a standing limitation on the whole wave

- **Every W4 scenario after Task 1 ran against a controller whose `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll` was answered by campaign test infrastructure rather than by the controller**, because the real Kubernetes enrollment path is unconditionally broken (`:2128`). This is recorded as its own entry at `:2275` precisely so a reader of the findings alone, who never opens `scenarios/w4-rig.md`, still learns it — and it is repeated here for the same reason.
- **What it does NOT invalidate, and the reason is a measurement rather than an assurance.** The credential served is **not synthetic**: it is a real `uca_` issued by this controller through the product's ordinary `"enrollment"` method and re-minted through the product's own `POST /api/v1/agents/token/refresh`. Nothing on the request path cross-checks `enrollment_method` — `agent_auth.go:38-100` reads only the token, kind, status, expiry and hash, and `GetAgentCredentialForAuth` does not even select the column; it is *compared* in exactly two places, both credential issuance. That was **confirmed live across six request paths** — register (204), heartbeat (204), claim (200), log-bulk (400 body-shape, i.e. authenticated and inside the handler), finish (404 run-not-found, likewise), refresh (200) — with not one 401 or 403. And the necessity is a measurement too, not a citation: the control was taken on the same stack at the same moment with one pod-bound token and one body — **403 direct to the LB, 200 through the interposer**. So everything downstream of authentication — claiming, pod lifecycle, execution, logging, reporting, pooling, GC — is the unmodified product path, and every W4 finding about those stands on its own.
- **What it DOES invalidate, stated plainly: no W4 finding is evidence about the Kubernetes enrollment path**, beyond what W4-0 itself recorded. **A second, narrower caveat travels with the route decision rather than with the bypass**, and it must not be collapsed into the first: the agent ran **on the host with the developer's kubeconfig**, so **no W4 host-run capture is evidence about the RBAC the shipped `manifests/` grant** — in either direction. `podTemplate.reuse` works on this rig *because the kubeconfig is privileged*, and that observation is silent about the manifests. See (c). **One asymmetry corrected at the branch review, and it was backwards.** The per-entry disclosure boilerplate had been applied to exactly three entries — `:2399`, `:2407`, `:2415`, all W4-2 — where it matters **least**, because the credential under test there is the Kubernetes API server's and is independent of the bypass. The eleven W4-1 and W4-3 entries carried none, **including `:2334`, whose "22.024 s controller blip" was injected by the interposer itself**, so a reader of `FINDINGS.md` alone who landed on it saw no indication that the agent's entire request path runs through campaign infrastructure. **The result was never confounded** — this section and `:2275` cover it, and `:2334`'s mechanism is code-read — but relying on a standing disclosure that a reader may not have reached is not the same as disclosing. All nine W4-1/W4-3 entries now carry the clause, each stating what its own evidence does and does not owe to the interposer.

### Cross-wave carry-forward

- **1. `RunGitResolver` is STILL OPEN and W4 did not take it — this is the third consecutive deferral, and the W3 checkpoint said a third should be read as a decision to drop it rather than as scheduling.** W3's carry-forward item 2 recommended W4 take it "if W4 has a task to spare, and W5 otherwise". **W4 had no task to spare**: three of six tasks went to a rig that did not exist, and a git-over-HTTP fixture would have been a fourth infrastructure task in a six-task wave. So the recommendation stands **unchanged and now explicitly to W5**, with W3's narrowing intact: what carries forward is the **git resolver's** instance of `docs/operations.md:53` and the **run-retention sweeper's**, not the log archiver's, which W3-2 already falsified live and filed at `:1736`. Everything queued behind the fixture is untouched — **W1-7** (AppSource reconciler), **W2-4's** un-run git variant, **W2-9's** git amplifier and its second independent hardcoded 50, and the resolve-deadline `AppendLog` that N replicas can each write to one run's log with no lock and no CAS. **The honest statement for the operator is that this item has now cost nothing and delivered nothing across three waves, and W5 should either build the fixture in its first task or the campaign should record it as dropped.**
- **2. The W2-6 3-hour promotion-free schedule observation is still unrun, and it is still the campaign's best cost-to-consequence ratio.** One unattended ~3-hour promotion-free window on an otherwise idle stack settles whether a `* * * * *` schedule reaches the silent-skip cliff **with no fault at all**, which would make `:1005` **critical rather than major**. Both validity conditions are unchanged and non-negotiable (the window must be promotion-free, because promotions *heal* the lag; the sampler must be continuous at 30 s, because the intermediate fingerprint survives only 60.36 s). **W4 could not have run it** — its rig has no scheduler exposure and its stacks lived in 20-90 minute windows — but that is an explanation, not a defence: the item has been open since W2 and every wave since has had a stack idle for long enough somewhere. **W5 or W6 should arm it as a background sampler on whatever stack they bring up first and simply let it run**, since it needs one loop and no attention.
- **3. The `LogPusher` disk-spill gate remains owned by W6-S2, and W4 added a FIFTH shape to the family that must be kept distinct when triaging.** The four W3 named are: **F9** (loss at the 1 MiB `p.pending` byte cap, never approached), the **W1-2 major** (loss at the bounded 5 s step-end `Flush` budget), **W1-6** (pure wasted request volume, O(t^2), no loss), **W3-4** (permanent *surplus*, and the only one where the controller is the party that gets it wrong), and **W3-5** (bytes accepted with a `204` and discarded server-side). **W4-1 (`:2334`) is the fifth and it is none of them**: the Kubernetes agent's stdout path has **no pusher at all** — no buffer, no retry, no cap, no marker, one `POST` per line with the error discarded — so every mitigation the other four are argued against is **absent rather than insufficient** on this backend. **The consequence for W6-S2 is concrete and it changes the shape of the task**: a spill/coalesce design that fixes `LogPusher` fixes the host agent and does **nothing** for the Kubernetes one, and W6 must measure both backends or it will report a fix that covers half the product. Note also that the drop **marker** `docs/troubleshooting.md:889-898` promises exists on one backend and not the other, which is why `:2334` is filed on that passage.
- **4. The campaign's invariant-set coverage gaps: W3 found two, and W4's entries argue for a third. The recommendation is again a single generalised clause rather than a narrow one.** W3's two are open and unchanged — **no secret-store integrity clause** (W3-3) and **no cache-integrity clause** (W3-1) — with W3's recommended fix being to restate I4's subject as *stored-state integrity* over the object classes the system persists on a run's behalf. **W4 asks the question its checkpoint was told to ask, and the answer is yes, from the entries rather than from theory.** **Six of W4's seven violations are filed on the documented-contract limb with no invariant reached, and two of those six state in their own Invariant lines that they cover a defect no invariant's text touches:** `:2383` (nothing outside `podgc.go` reaps a live orphan Pod — "nothing here concerns run accounting, side effects, locks, log integrity, recovery bounds or state display") and `:2401` (idle pooled Pods that **no component in the product ever reclaims**, up to `maxConcurrent` per shape, re-adopted across restarts). **Both are the same class: an execution resource the product provisions on a run's behalf, outside its own database, that outlives the run with no reclamation path.** I3 is the nearest invariant and its subject is *locks* — `mutex_holders` and `named_lock_slots` rows, which are the product's own tables. A Kubernetes Pod is not one, and stretching I3 to reach it would be exactly the move `:1509` forbids and W2-5 was corrected for. **What makes this load-bearing rather than academic is the same accident W3-3 escaped by:** both entries survive as violations only because a `docs/` sentence happens to be wrong. Had `docs/agents.md:513-514` been silent, and had `docs/configuration.md:458` been *correct* about the default, **both would have been observations** — and the second one describes an unbounded, unreclaimed cluster resource. **Recommended amendment, and it is one clause, not a fourth narrow one:** generalise **I3**'s subject from *locks* to *resources the system acquires or provisions on a run's behalf* — advisory locks, mutex rows, named-lock slots, **and externally-provisioned execution resources (Kubernetes Pods, pool entries, and whatever the next backend adds)** — retaining the existing predicate that each is released when the run that acquired it ends, or is reclaimed by a documented owner within a documented bound. **Whoever takes it must re-run the classification of exactly two entries and no others**: `:2383` and `:2401` each gain an invariant limb **without changing disposition** (both already stand on a contract, which is why this case is weaker than W3-1's and is stated as weaker), and W4-rig's pooled-Pod naming observation at `:2246` must **not** be disturbed. **The pattern across four waves is now the thing to report, not any one gap:** W1 refined I1-vs-I7, W2 amended it again, W3 found two holes in the coverage, and W4 found a third — and in all three of W3's and W4's cases the gap was found the same way, by an entry with a real, permanent, silent defect looking for the invariant that covers it and finding none. **Until the I-list is amended, W5 and W6 must not read "no invariant contradicted" as "nothing is wrong": check whether the invariant's *subject* reaches the object before concluding anything from its silence.**
- **5. W3's cheap unfinished items, checked at this checkpoint rather than forwarded silently.** W3 carry-forward 6 asked W4 to run the `DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{name}` measurement that `:1864` — the campaign's only unexecuted violation at the time — rests on, "as a warm-up on its first stack". **W4 did not run it**, and it was a defensible omission for a wave whose first stack had no object store wired and whose first task was a spike that came back NO, but it is now **two waves deferred on a measurement the entry itself says takes minutes**. W3 carry-forward 7 (W3-6's production window: does `cancelRun()` kill a long in-flight operation or does it run to completion?) is likewise untouched, and it is the **same discriminator** W2 carry-forward 2 asks for on the approval fence. **All three should be scheduled on one arm in W5**, because one long-running post-terminal operation answers all of them, and **W4 now supplies a second reason to want the answer**: `:2233` shows a Kubernetes run's container SIGKILLed within ~1 s of its Pod's deletion, which is a datapoint about how hard the k8s backend's teardown actually is and is the opposite end of the same question.

### Forward questions answered

- **(a) Did the enrollment spike's NO cost the wave its scenarios? No — it cost the wave a task and bought it three entries.** The spike was chartered as allowed-to-fail and budgeted at an hour precisely so this answer would be cheap, and the design worked: the failure was found before an image was built, a manifest written, or the compose stack's steady state disturbed. It produced two violations and an observation of its own, it forced the interposer (which every later task used unchanged), and it is the reason the wave's scope disclosure at `:2275` exists rather than being an unrecorded assumption. **The transferable form: a spike that comes back NO is a successful spike if it comes back NO cheaply and the wave is re-planned rather than pushed.**
- **(b) Does the Kubernetes backend change any earlier wave's finding? One, and only in scope.** W2's forward question (a)(6) told W4-1 not to budget W1-5's zombie, on the ground that W2-7 measured every soft fence at 0.939-4.938 s. **W4-1 did not need a zombie budget at all** — the k8s teardown is harder than either: a deleted Pod kills the container in **~1 s with exit code 137** (`:2233`), so this backend has no zombie window of the W1-5 kind to instrument. That does not overturn W2-7's measurement, which is about the *host* agent's cancel poller; it bounds it to that backend. **The general instruction W4 adds: a claim about agent-side fencing is backend-scoped until measured on both, and this campaign has now measured host (W1, W2) and Kubernetes (W4) and found them different in kind.**
- **(c) Is the rig good enough for a W5 or W6 Kubernetes arm? Yes for anything downstream of authentication, and no for enrollment or for RBAC-as-shipped.** The bring-up is two commands plus a kubeconfig regeneration, the fault verbs assert their own arms, the fixtures are pre-validated, and no limb of the rig failed. Two hard limits carry: **enrollment is broken in the product**, so a wave wanting to test enrollment must either fix the one line first (outside Phase 1's scope) or use the interposer and disclose it; and **the in-cluster Deployment route was deferred, not built**, so a wave wanting to exercise the shipped Role or the shipped Deployment pays that cost, which W4-2 estimated but did not spend. **And it needs its own object store if it needs one at all** — W3's checkpoint predicted at `:2089`(c)(iii) that the compose Garage does not transfer, and it was right.
- **(d) Was the campaign's own review still earning its keep in a fourth wave? Yes, and this checkpoint is where it earned most of it.** The single most consequential thing found here is not in any entry — it is **between** documents that were each internally correct. See the inconsistency list.

### Methodological findings — three, and the first is the one to act on

- **1. THE DRIFT DIRECTION REVERSED, AND THE REVERSED FORM IS WORSE. W3 found six drifts in which the runbook was stale and the entry was right; W4's is one in which the ENTRY was stale and the runbook was right, and the runbook stated in writing that it had already been fixed.** `scenarios/w4-2-reuse-swallow.md:574-591` records the first observed **failure** of the bootstrap-PAT cold-start race and said the datapoint was "**Recorded as a frequency datapoint on the existing entry, not re-filed**". **It was not.** The entry at `:2270` still read "3/3 survived, twice" and cited two bring-ups, having never received either W4-1's third survival or W4-2's failure. **Why this is worse than W3's six:** `FINDINGS.md` is the authoritative document and a runbook's execution notes are "a record of what was done, not of what was concluded" (`:2112`), so W3's drifts were all in the direction where the authoritative side was right. Here the authoritative side carried the superseded figure, and the runbook that superseded it **asserted its own fix** — which is the shape that defeats a reader checking either document alone. **The rule, and it is a checkpoint step rather than advice: grep every runbook for claims of the form "recorded on the existing entry" / "not re-filed" / "amended in place", and verify each one landed. A claim to have propagated is not propagation.** Resolved at this checkpoint by amending `:2270` in place at a preserved line count, so every `FINDINGS.md:NNNN` self-citation in the campaign stays accurate. **And a second time at the branch review, which found this finding half-applied — the checkpoint corrected the authoritative side and left the false runbook sentence uncorrected, so a reader of the runbook alone still met the claim that defeated the last one.** The runbook now strikes its own sentence and the three surviving 3/3 mentions (`w4-0-enrollment-spike.md` item 6, `w4-rig.md` §Bring-up, this runbook's findings table) are each scoped to the bring-ups their author observed. *Rule extension, and it is the sharper half: fixing the stale side of a drift is half the fix — the document that made the false claim must be corrected too, or the next reader meets it unchanged.*
- **2. An asset-verification lesson does not transfer by being read — it transfers by being *measured against*, and W4 is the proof.** W3's most transferable output was the ARM RULE: a verb is verified when some capture measures its **effect**, never when its state checks pass. W4's own fault verb then **shipped inert in exactly that way** (`:2262`) — armed, three state checks passing, and the agent claimed and ran a job 17 s inside the armed window — written by an author who had that rule in front of them. It was caught by an effect measurement and fixed. **And then the same verb did it a second time in the same session**: `block hang` shipped with a comment describing its behaviour and no capture measuring it, and its `probe_proxy` ended in a no-op `if ... then : fi` that would have printed `ARMED` against an interposer with no arm file at all. **The conclusion is not "try harder".** It is that the rule needs a mechanical enforcement point, and W4 built one worth copying: **the verb now asserts its own arm** — it probes through the interposer and **exits non-zero** unless the probe failed in the shape the mode promises, and `unblock` requires a 200 back, verified in all three modes **and against a negative control**. A verb that can fail its own arm check cannot ship inert. **W4 also generalised the mechanism**: the failure was a long poll that had entered the handler before the arm, so **any arm placed in front of a long-poll endpoint must sever established connections, not merely reject new requests** — which `inject.sh nginx-block` and `steplock` still do not do.
- **3. What the process cost this wave, stated plainly because each failure yields a one-line rule.** **W4-rig quoted `fixcheck` output for four fixtures from a capture covering three** — the fourth was validated live and never captured, and the record pasted its output under "Output, verbatim" anyway. Caught in review; the block was **re-run and re-captured** covering all four on both sides, and the earlier claim proved true: **the claim was right and the evidence did not exist**, which is the W3-infra failure repeating exactly. *Rule, unchanged and now paid twice: if a block looks like pasted output, it must be pasted output.* **W4-rig also published a false enumeration in three documents** ("the column is read in exactly three places and nowhere else"), corrected to *compared* in two and *selected* by several more, with the GO decision unchanged. *Rule: `:2100`'s completeness rule applies to enumerations of code sites, not only to enumerations of defect producers.* **W4-1's docs survey ran case-sensitive first and missed two hits**, and both were the addendum violation at `:2383` — recorded because "never truncate a docs survey" is worth nothing if the **pattern** is the thing that truncates it. *Rule: run docs surveys case-insensitively and print the count both ways.* **W4-2 filed a correction that was itself wrong and withdrew it** (it called the brief's `poolIdleTimeout` survey figure an error; the two numbers were the same survey under two `grep` flags, both correct), and **withdrew a bound it had asserted** ("one Pod per distinct pod shape") for a corrected and much larger one, then **re-checked the severity band against the corrected bound rather than inheriting it**. *Rule: when a number changes, re-run the argument that rested on it — and if the band survives, say it survives on the rubric's categories rather than on the number.* **W4-1 disclosed a deviation from its own pre-execution runbook** (an annotation its runbook says was read "while the sweep window is open" was in fact read before and after) and described the capture rather than the plan. *Rule, unchanged since W3: a deviation is fine and a silent deviation is not.*

### Inconsistencies found at this checkpoint — five, each between documents that were individually correct

*(Listed in descending order of how much damage trusting the wrong side would do. All five are resolved; none was resolved silently.)*

- **(i) The stale tally in the authoritative document — `:2270`.** Full account in methodological finding 1 above. **Resolved: the entry is amended in place** to 3 survivals and 1 failure across the four later cold bring-ups (five observed in the wave, 3 up / 2 down), with the superseded sentence struck rather than deleted and the false propagation claim at `w4-2-reuse-swallow.md:574-591` named — **and, at the branch review, corrected at source too, because naming it here left it standing there**. **`FINDINGS.md`'s line count was unchanged by the amendment, so no `FINDINGS.md:NNNN` self-citation anywhere in the campaign is affected.** This is the class the W3 checkpoint warned about — a document carrying a tally from before a supersession — found in the one direction W3 had not seen it.
- **(ii) The evidence directory names do not map to scenario ids, and every citation is nonetheless correct.** W2 and W3 both held `w<wave>-<n>/` <-> scenario `W<wave>-<n>`. **W4's directories are named after the *task*.** `w4-2/` is the **rig** (Task 2) and is cited by **six W4-rig entries and by no W4-2 entry**; scenario W4-2's captures are in `w4-2b/`; `w4-2-fixes/` is the rig's review wave; and `w4-1/` holds **two tasks** — W4-0's spike steps and W4-1's scenario parts, which is also why there is no `w4-0/` and nothing is missing (the W4-0 entries cite the spike record by line and no capture file). Every one of the **38 distinct `w4-*/...` paths (47 occurrences)** cited by the entries was resolved against the archive and **all 38 exist**. **Resolved by documentation, not by renaming**, and the reasoning is recorded: renaming to fix a readability trap would break 38 working citations to fix none. The evidence root's README now carries a trap table and it is the first thing a `w4-*` citation should be resolved against. **The rule for W5: name the directory from the scenario id at the first capture.**
