A pass therefore costs `len(p.pending) x 60 s`, confirmed by the two distinct `reqlen` values (5,143 and 29,184): `06:51:29` + `06:52:29` is one two-batch pass taking 120 s, and `06:53:29` + `06:53:35` is the next. Because `time.Ticker`'s channel is buffered, the next tick is already pending when a pass ends, so **`p.mu` is re-acquired immediately and is held essentially continuously** for as long as the fault lasts.
  - **The request cost COLLAPSES, which is the inverse of every other arm.** Six real requests in 195 s of black hole, against **11,326 in 300 s** of fast-failing outage on the same rig (Arm 1) — a factor of ~1,900. The hang regime is nearly free for the controller and near-total for the step; a request-rate alarm would show this outage as *quieter* than healthy.
  - **Nothing anywhere reports it.** Both agent containers emitted **66 log lines** across the whole 195 s, all `{"level":"ERROR","msg":"claim"}` and all stamped `06:50:19.92` — the instant of the arming nginx reload severing the long-polls, not the fault. **Zero lines mention the log path, a flush, or the stall**, in either agent, against zero in a clean control window. The run read `Running` throughout and `Succeeded` at the end. Per the enumeration re-verified for this scenario, there is no metric either: `grep -rn "ListenAndServe\|net.Listen\|http.Handle\|NewServeMux" cmd/unified-cd-agent internal/agent` returns **85** hits and **every one is in a `_test.go` file** (`w6-2b/codesurvey.txt`), so **the host agent binds no HTTP listener at all** and there is no surface on which a gauge could be exposed without adding a server first.
- **Expected:** nothing in `docs/` bounds how long a log flush may block a step, and the design intent visible in the code (`logPusherWriteFlushTimeout` exists at all) is that the writer should *not* be stalled by a partition. The measured behaviour is that it is, by the path the bound does not cover. Recorded as an observation because the promise lives in an unexported var's comment rather than in `docs/` or an exported API.
- **Notes:** **The fix is three lines and is the highest value-per-byte change this scenario found:** pass a `context.WithTimeout` per tick in `StartAutoFlush` — `logPusherWriteFlushTimeout`'s own 5 s is the obvious value — which turns 176.3 s of frozen step into ~5 s per tick. The cost is that a merely-slow controller will now have flushes abandoned that would have completed, so the deadline must sit comfortably above a normal round trip; note the same 60 s client timeout already applies per request, so nothing is being made less patient than it is today except in aggregate. **On the fault's fidelity, stated because a fake black hole is worse than none:** the agent image has no `iptables` and no `NET_ADMIN` (W1 established this), so this is an **HTTP-level** black hole — nginx forwarding to a container that accepts the TCP connection and never writes to it — not a packet-level one. It is equivalent in everything measured (accepted, sent, never answered, blocked for the full client timeout, `p.mu` held, step stalled) and **three things remain unmeasured**: `connect` never hangs here, so a packet-level drop would stall in Go's dialer under a different timeout; there are no retransmit or half-open dynamics; and the heal is instantaneous, so a *recovering* black hole — in particular whether a 60 s-blocked request that completes late races the batch that replaced it — was not exercised. A fix-verification pass on a real partition should re-check the first of those. **Cross-references, not re-filings:** `FINDINGS.md:465` (the quadratic amplification) is the *opposite* regime and this entry is its complement — the two together say the log path's cost under fault is bimodal, enormous under a fast-failing outage and negligible under a hanging one, with the harm inverted; `:179` (W1-2) is the loss path and is untouched here, since nothing was lost.

## W6-2b — observation: the `[N log line(s) dropped: controller unreachable]` marker is gated on the backlog being EMPTY, so it is structurally unable to fire in exactly the case where the loss is largest — measured as a `Succeeded` run with 2,002 lines emitted, **zero** delivered, and no marker
- **Invariant:** **none filed.** The data loss itself is already filed as the **W1-2 major** at `:179` (I4, the bounded 5 s step-end `Flush`) and is **cited, not re-filed** — this run is a further reproduction of that defect and adds nothing to it. What is filed here is a *different* property of the same machinery: the reachability of the announcement mechanism. `docs/` does not promise the marker fires in this case, so there is no contract limb either; it is an observation.
- **Severity:** **major (observation)** — the shape, not the loss, and **RE-ARGUED AT THE BRANCH REVIEW FROM `:6-8`'s OWN TEXT, at a preserved line count and with no change of band.** The earlier version of this line read *"W1-2 owns the loss and is already major. **This is filed at the same band because** it is the reason the loss is undetectable"* — which reaches a band by calibrating to another entry, the exact move commit `066e421` forbade and which `:2942` records as this wave's rule. **That argument is withdrawn and replaced; the band survives it.** The **major** band's first limb is *"incorrect visible behavior"* and it is met on the artefact itself. The drop marker is **not an out-of-band diagnostic** — it is a line the product inserts **into the log the reader reads** — so its absence does not make a true record harder to interpret, it makes the record **assert something false**: a run marked `Succeeded` whose log is served as a complete, uninterrupted record, with **2,002 lines emitted and zero delivered**, on every read surface, permanently, to every reader. **What decides it against the minor band — whose first word is *"diagnosability"*, and which is the serious counter-reading — is that the gate is structural rather than unlucky.** `len(p.pending) == 0` makes the marker **unable** to fire in precisely the case where the loss is largest; this is not a warning that happens to be missing, it is a warning the code cannot emit when it matters most, which is a property of the behaviour and not of its reportability. The *"unbounded recovery"* limb is **not** claimed here. It is not `critical` (*"data loss / silent corruption / security"*) — **and that is a question of scope rather than of band arithmetic: this entry does not own the loss.** The loss is filed at W1-2 `:179` and is **cited, not re-filed**; escalating this entry would double-count it (`:2931`). **What it legitimately does is upgrade W1-2's own account of the marker:** W1-2 records that in its case the precondition `droppedLines > 0` "was never even met, not merely unlucky timing on an otherwise-eligible marker" (`:188`) — i.e. the question was moot there. **This is the first live case in the campaign where the eviction path certainly did fire and the marker still could not**, which makes the `len(p.pending) == 0` precondition itself the defect rather than a coincidence of the earlier run.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-2b-logpusher-curve.md` Part E. `edge-w6-chatty lines=2000 pad_bytes=1024 interval_s=0` (~2.05 MiB of line text) with `tools/w6/w6-2b-fault.sh outage` armed **before** the trigger and **never cleared** while the run lived; at full speed the step finished in under 30 s, so the outage outlived it. Evidence: `w6-2b/partE/` — `bulk.csv` (the per-request table every number below is computed from), `logs.json` (`[]`), `timeline.txt`, `nginx.log.gz` and `nginx-window.txt`, run `120de00e`. **Citation corrected at review: this line previously named a `partE/analysis.txt`, which does not exist — Part E is the one arm whose per-arm analyser output was not written to the archive, so the headline numbers trace to `bulk.csv` directly and were re-derived from it at review (11,015 `502` + 1 `401` probe = 11,016 rows; peak second `06:17:52` = 1,070).** Source: `internal/agent/runner.go:396-424`, `:335-353`, `:429-435`.
- **Observed:**
  - `GET /api/v1/runs/120de00e/logs/stats` -> **`{"count":0,"maxSeq":0,"minSeq":0}`**. Run status **`Succeeded`**. Lines emitted **2,002**. Lines delivered **0**. Drop markers **0**. The paged log read returns an empty list; `chatty-begin` and `chatty-end` are absent along with everything between them.
  - **11,015 HTTP requests were spent to deliver nothing** — peaking at **1,070 req/s** (`06:17:52`) and sustained above 1,000 req/s for **six** consecutive seconds (`06:17:51`-`06:17:56`: 1029, 1070, 1044, 1040, 1030, 1006), from one step on one agent. **An earlier version of this line said five; it was conservative rather than wrong, and is corrected to the recount from `partE/bulk.csv`.** That is the amplification of `:465` running at full rate against a backlog that was then discarded in its entirety.
  - **`droppedLines` was certainly non-zero and is structurally unobservable.** 2.05 MiB of line text against the 1 MiB cap forces `appendPendingLocked`'s drop-oldest eviction (`:429-435`) many times over; it is stated as **derived from the arithmetic and the code**, not measured, *because it cannot be measured* — the field is unexported (`:244`), has no accessor, no metric and no log line, and the single surface that would have reported it is gated on the backlog being empty. The claim "it was non-zero" and the finding "you cannot tell" are the same fact.
  - **The gate is one condition.** `flushLocked` step 3 is `if len(p.pending) == 0 && p.droppedLines > 0` (`:401`). It is evaluated at the end of every flush, and skipped whenever any backlog survives — so the marker announces drops **only after full recovery**. When the run ends first, the step-end `Flush` spends its 5 s budget (`:343`), `p.pending` is still non-empty, the pusher is discarded, and nothing retries.
  - **The contrast arm proves the mechanism rather than assuming it.** Arm 2 ran the same fixture with the outage **cleared before the step ended**: 1,800 lines emitted, 1,537 delivered, **263 missing in one contiguous range `211..473`**, and the marker fired **exactly once** reading `[263 log line(s) dropped: controller unreachable]`. 263 = 263, to the line. So the marker is correct and exact when it can fire; the finding is entirely about when it cannot.
- **Expected:** the marker exists precisely so that "operators see that logs were lost instead of the gap passing silently" (`runner.go:396-400`). It does that for a *recovered* outage and not for an *ongoing* one, and the ongoing case is the one where the gap is total rather than partial. The `:415-420` comment explains carefully why the marker must not be queued in `p.pending` — a queued marker would become the oldest entry and be evicted, losing the true count — which is sound, and orthogonal to this: the problem is not where the marker is stored, it is that the attempt is never made.
- **Notes:** **Two fixes, and they are independent.** (i) Change the precondition from `len(p.pending) == 0` to "`droppedLines > 0` **and** at least one request in this flush succeeded" — the marker's count then becomes a running total that may be superseded, which is why it should also carry the `seq`/time range it covers. That range matters for a second reason measured in the same arm: the marker landed **987 lines after the gap it describes** (between `chatty 1460` and `chatty 1461`, for a gap at `210 -> 474`), because it is emitted at the recovery point rather than at the discontinuity — so a reader meets an unexplained 263-line jump and finds the explanation a thousand lines later carrying no indication of which range it refers to. (ii) For the case where no request ever succeeds — this one — the only possible answer is agent-side: a `slog.Warn` at teardown when `p.pending` is non-empty. Note that would be the **first log statement in the entire `LogPusher`**: `runner.go:207-446` contains no `slog.`, no `log.` and no `fmt.Print*`, the only `fmt` use being `Sprintf` building the marker's own text at `:404`. The silence is uniform, not an oversight in one branch. **Bearing on the disk-spill gate (`:496`), and this entry is one of its two decisive inputs:** the byte cap is the **only** one of this scenario's three loss paths that already announces itself correctly, and spill addresses that one. See the scenario's `THE DISK-SPILL GATE` section.

## W6-2b (campaign asset) — observation: `w6-reqshape.sh` had the SAME unstoppable-capture defect Task 2 fixed in `w6-idleload.sh`, and the black-hole arm's own verification probe destroyed the arm it verified
- **Invariant:** none — campaign instruments, not the product. Filed on the same reasoning as `:2622` and `:2262`: an instrument that passes its own state checks while producing wrong output is this campaign's recurring failure, and the record is worth more than the fix.
- **Severity:** minor (observation) — no product behaviour is involved. **Both were caught before any number was trusted**, and both fixes are verified live in the same commits.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-2b-logpusher-curve.md`, the instrument-defect section. Evidence: `w6-2b/harness/verify.txt`, `w6-2b/arm4-void/timeline.txt`, `w6-2b/arm4/timeline.txt`.
- **Observed:**
  - **(1) The leak was fixed in one instrument and left in the other.** `w6-reqshape.sh follow -d` used `dc logs -f ... > out &` and killed `$!` — and `dc` is a shell function, so the surviving writer is the docker-compose CLI plugin two levels down, exactly as `:2622` describes for `w6-idleload.sh`. Measured: `follow -d 5` printed **`captured 34 lines`**; eight seconds and twenty unrelated requests later the same file held **56**. **And it never stopped.** The same file was archived at the end of the session at **44,151,788 bytes** — a capture that reported 34 lines had absorbed the entire scenario, every arm of it, and only died when the stack was torn down (`w6-2b/harness/leaktest-truncated.txt`, truncated for archival with the size recorded in its header). This is the instrument W6-2b's entire request-count curve rests on, so every number in that scenario would have been taken off a still-growing file.
  - **(2) The black hole was fake on its first use, and the arm's own probe is what had made it fake.** `logsink` was first written as `while true; do tail -f /dev/null | nc -l -p 8080 >/dev/null; done`. It **passed `hangprobe` at 06:03:56** — `curl` exit 28, a genuine 12 s hang — and then **fast-failed with a 502 in 2.5 ms** when Arm 4 armed it at 06:42:48, i.e. the black-hole arm had silently degraded into the ordinary outage arm. Plain `nc -l` is single-shot, and the `tail -f` placed there to hold stdin open never exits, so the pipeline never completes and the `while` loop never iterates: **the sink served exactly one connection in its life and the verification probe was the customer.** The first Arm 4 run is kept at `w6-2b/arm4-void/` and its numbers are used for nothing.
- **Expected:** a capture that ends when its window ends, and an arm that is armed when its probe says it is. **Both fixed and verified live.** (1) `w6-reqshape.sh` gains a `window` verb — sleep, then a bounded `docker compose logs --since T0 --until T1` with no background process — plus a `-window.txt` sidecar so an old file can bound its own re-analysis; `follow -d` now **exits 5** and names the replacement. Verification: two consecutive 12 s windows against a 1 Hz probe are **disjoint** (`06:05:57.426` against `06:05:58.512`), both non-empty, and window 1's file was byte-identical before and after window 2 ran. (2) `logsink` becomes `nc -lk -p 8080 -e sleep 3600`, which has no per-connection state to exhaust; **three consecutive `hangprobe`s pass**, and Arm 4's own in-line probe passed immediately before the measurement. **Blast radius of (1), enumerated at review rather than dated — and it is zero.** `grep -rc reqshape scenarios/` returns **0** for `w6-2a-log-write-amplification.md` (W6-2a used `w6-idleload.sh`, a separate fix), **1** for `w6-1-connection-pressure.md` and **5** for this scenario; W6-2b's arms are all bounded by `-window.txt` sidecars, and W6-1's three `step5-reqshape*.txt` captures are self-bounding (60 of 60 fired requests, 15 of 15 ticks, URI-filtered), so **no published number moves.** `README.md`'s standing warning previously scoped the exposure by date — "any W6 number taken with `follow -d` **before 2026-08-02**" — which **excluded the entire exposed set**, since every W6 capture was taken on 2026-08-02 and the fix landed the same day; it now carries this enumeration instead. **The leak also survives in bare `follow`**, which only warns (`w6-reqshape.sh:133-134`); just `follow -d` is refused (`:126-131`), so a plain `follow` capture is still not window-bounded.
- **Notes:** **The generalisable rule, and it sharpens the campaign's existing one.** The standing rule is "an arm is verified when some capture measures its effect, not when its comment carries a measurement". Defect (2) satisfied that rule and was still wrong: the arm *was* verified by a capture, once, at setup — and the verification consumed it. **A verification that is not idempotent must be re-run at the point of use, and an arm whose probe is destructive is an arm that is armed exactly once.** W6-2b's arms all re-probe in line for this reason, which is why the degradation was caught in the timeline rather than in the numbers. **A second, smaller note carried forward for whoever next writes a fault into `compose/`:** `nginx-logfault.conf` fixes `proxy_connect_timeout` inside the bulk location, which means an arm cannot set its own without nginx failing `-t` on a duplicate directive — `compose/nginx-w62b.conf` moves it out to the include for that reason, and both files say so.

## W6-1 — `docs/high-availability.md:289` tells the operator that `/readyz` rotates a DB-broken replica out of the load balancer; measured IN-WINDOW across four independent arms, `/readyz` returns **200 in 143 of 144 saturated replica-readings — 47 of 48 sample instants** — while Postgres refuses every new connection and the same replica is answering **31.8 % of requests with 401 on a valid admin PAT** — and the controllers log nothing at all
- **Invariant:** filed on the **documented-contract limb**, not on an invariant, and the alternatives are named rather than left open. **I5 is not reachable and was checked rather than assumed**: the spec's text (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-edge-case-testing-design.md:52`) names *"leader re-election ≤ seconds"*, and leader re-election under exactly this fault was measured at **89 ms** (`controller1` `received shutdown signal, draining...` 07:55:50.644 → `controller2` `scheduler became leader` 07:55:50.733, `D3-after.txt`). Citing I5 here would be the stretch `FINDINGS.md:1509` forbids. **I7** ("run status, approval status, and audit rows never contradict each other or reality") is arguable — a readiness endpoint is a state display and it contradicts reality — but I7's own text enumerates run/approval/audit rows, so it is offered as secondary and the entry does not rest on it.
- **Severity:** **major.** Argued from this file's bands (`:6-8`) and **not** by analogy to `:2517` or `:2541`. The **major** band reads *"incorrect visible behavior, unbounded recovery"*, and both limbs are met independently. **(1) Incorrect visible behaviour.** `/readyz` is not prose, it is a machine-consumed control surface whose stated purpose is to gate traffic: `docs/operations.md:154` says verbatim *"A `503 db unavailable` response means the controller must not receive traffic even if `/healthz` is still `200`"*, and `docs/high-availability.md:241` instructs *"Use `/readyz` (see below) as the LB routing health check target."* An endpoint whose documented job is "answer 503 when the DB is unusable" answering 200 while the DB refuses every connection is that endpoint behaving incorrectly, visibly, to the consumer it exists for. **(2) Unbounded recovery.** The saturated state persisted **≥ 9 min 39 s** with no self-recovery (07:49:50 first refusal → 07:59:29 operator restart, `D5-recovery.txt`) and **no upper bound is established, because that window was ended deliberately** — see the Notes. **The counter-case, stated so the operator can judge:** this can be read as `docs/high-availability.md:289` being one wrong sentence about a `/readyz` that does exactly what `docs/operations.md:154` describes, which would be the **minor** band's "docs gap" and the W4-3 / W6-2a shape. What decides it against that reading is that the endpoint's *own* documented failure semantics — the 503 clause quoted above — are the thing that does not happen, and that the consequence lands on live traffic rather than on a reader.
- **Repro:** `scenarios/w6-1-connection-pressure.md`, Part C1. Rig: `test/ha` + `compose/ctrlports.override.yaml`, stock `max_connections=100`, `superuser_reserved_connections=3` (measured, `A1-ceiling.txt`), so the client-backend budget is **97**. Any of five arms reaches the state; the cheapest is Part E's, below. Evidence: `edgecase-evidence/w6/w6-1s/` — `B-B1.txt`, `B-B3.txt`, `B-B4.txt`, `E-60.txt`, `harnessfix-pgsample.txt`, and the paired `*-pg.csv.health.csv` series.
- **Observed:**
  - **The pairing is a measurement, not a juxtaposition.** `w6-pgsample.sh -p` probes `/readyz` and `/healthz` **inside the same loop iteration** as the `pg_stat_activity` query, so every backend count carries the health codes read beside it. This is the reading `FINDINGS.md:2525` says does not exist anywhere in the W6-1 archive: *"No `/readyz` sample exists inside any load window, so the in-window behaviour of the health surface is UNMEASURED here."* It exists now.
  - **143 of 144 saturated in-window replica-readings read 200 — 47 of 48 sample instants** — across four arms that reach saturation by different mechanisms: **E-60** 42 of 42; **B4** (200 workers, 1,960 req/s) 15 of 15; **B3** (200-wide bursts, 20 req/s average — **and the one arm that did not start from a reset stack: floor 80 against the others' 65-68, 17 connections from the budget, so its saturation is confounded by carry-over from B2**) 57 of 57; **B1** (8 workers, 2,451 req/s) **14 of 15**; a standalone post-load window 15 of 15. `/healthz` was 200 in every one. **The health reading itself is not weakened by B3's floor** — a replica answering 200 while `psql` is refused is the same observation however the saturation was reached — and it holds independently in the three arms that did reset. **Two arithmetic corrections at review, and both were the entry's own.** (i) The published total was `144 of 145`; the per-arm figures above are each right and every one was recomputed from the raw captures, but they sum to **143 of 144** — the headline was wrong on both sides. (ii) **The unit was wrong too, and it triple-counted.** `w6-pgsample.sh` printed "in 42 of 42 samples" where one row is **one port at one sample instant**, so 42 = 14 instants x 3 replicas, 15 = 5 x 3 and 57 = 19 x 3. The honest denominators are **48 distinct sampling instants** and **144 replica-readings**; of the 48 instants, **47** read 200 on all three replicas, the exception being B1's first instant. The tool inherited the word "samples" uncritically while this entry was otherwise scrupulous about units (`db_backends` vs `total_backends`); `w6-pgsample.sh` now prints both denominators and calls neither a "sample" on its own.
  - **The single 503 is explained rather than counted as a rebuttal — and the explanation is INFERRED.** It is port 18081 during B1 — the one replica taking 2,451 req/s — and it is **read as** the api-pool `Acquire` losing the 3 s race in `server.go:318-332`, i.e. a symptom of concurrency on that replica, not of Postgres exhaustion. **The label is "inferred" because the response body was not captured**: `server.go:318-332` returns 503 for **both** `shuttingDown` and a failed `Ping`, and the capture records only the status code. Nothing was draining at 08:32, so the `Acquire` reading is very likely right, but it rests on a code read plus an absence. It did not recur in B4, which put **25x the concurrency** on the same replica. So the health surface flickers under local load and is steady under the condition it is documented to detect: **the wrong way round.**
  - **What the 200 was concurrent with, on the same replica, in the same second.** B1: **6,242 of 19,623 requests answered 401 on a static, unexpired `ha-admin-token`** (31.8 %) and 321 answered 500; the per-second histogram (`B-histograms.txt`) shows 590-908 401s in **every** second of the 8 s window, not a spike. B4: 4,803 401s and 4,477 500s of 15,912.
  - **No `ERROR` line was observed — and that is weaker than what this entry first said, which was that background jobs did not starve.** The claim now made is exactly: in the window `C-bgstarve.txt` covers, the three controllers emitted **zero `"level":"ERROR"` lines**. **Four things that capture does not carry, all recorded at review in `w6-1s/C-bgstarve-LIMITS.txt` beside the unedited capture.** (i) **The liveness control is a different command**: the file reads `total lines last 4m: 604` and `ERROR lines last 12m: 0`, and this entry called those "the same command" — `--since 4m` against `--since 12m`, so the 604 does not bound the window the zero came from. (ii) **The window endpoints are not in the capture** — no capture timestamp, no command text, no service scope, no log-level configuration — so neither `--since` can be shown to cover B1 (08:32) at all; a 4-minute window ending at capture time would reach E-60 (08:37) and not B1. (iii) The error-class section is empty **with no positive control**. (iv) **And the substantive one: zero errors is consistent with zero ATTEMPTS.** B1's arm is **8 s** long (08:32:06.009-08:32:14.015) and the log archiver ticks at **60 s** — measured in `D3-after.txt`, where controller1 boots 07:55:52 and logs its first `log archiver error` at 07:56:52, with stuck-run reaper errors 30 s apart — so an 8-second window can contain no archiver execution whatever, and a job that never ran cannot log an error. **Outstanding measurement: an in-window count of background-job executions, successful ones included, so the zero has a denominator. It was not taken** (another scenario held the rig when this correction was made).
  - **What IS positively measured, and the section's conclusion rests on this rather than on the zero.** The only starvation observed anywhere in this scenario is on a controller that had **just restarted** and therefore had to open new connections — `log archiver error`, `stuck-run reaper list error`, `queued-run reaper lock`, `appsource reconciler: failed to list AppSources`, all naming `too many clients already`, all timestamped, in `D3-after.txt`. A pool that already holds its connections keeps serving from them, so only a component that needs a *new* connection sees the fault. **A warm pool hides the exhaustion from everything that does not need a new connection** — which is a mechanism statement supported by a capture that bounds itself.
- **Mechanism (code-read, and it is short).** `/readyz` calls `s.store.Ping` under a 3 s timeout (`internal/controller/server.go:318-332`); `Ping` is `p.pool.Ping(ctx)` (`internal/store/postgres.go:145-147`) — the **api pool**. `pgxpool.Ping` acquires a connection and pings on it, and when the pool holds an open idle connection that acquire never touches the server's connection limit. So `/readyz` measures **the pool**, not **the server**, and the one state in which the pool is guaranteed to be full of open connections is precisely the state in which the server is out of slots. `docs/operations.md:154`'s description is literally accurate and is exactly why the endpoint passes.
- **Expected:** `docs/high-availability.md:289`, verbatim: *"`/readyz` pings the DB, so replicas with a DB connectivity issue are automatically rotated out."* Measured, no replica is rotated out in any arm, and an LB configured exactly as `docs/high-availability.md:241` instructs keeps routing to a replica that is rejecting valid credentials a third of the time.
- **Notes:**
  - **This is the settled version of a question a prior entry deliberately left open, and it resolves in the direction that entry feared.** `FINDINGS.md:2532` says verbatim: *"Whether that second sentence is a contradicted contract is deliberately left open here and handed to W6-S1"*. `:2534` adds that its health leg *"is the weakest of the three and is deliberately stated at the strength of its one sample"*, and invites re-grading: *"If W6-S1 finds `/readyz` does fail inside the load window and only recovers afterwards, this leg weakens."* **It does not fail inside the load window.** The leg is now measured at **143 of 144** replica-readings — **47 of 48** sample instants — rather than 1/1, across four arms and three saturation mechanisms, so `:2517`'s band stands on stronger evidence than it had. **Cite `:2517`; it is not re-filed here** — this entry is about the health contract, which `:2517` explicitly declined to rule on.
  - **The recovery limb, at the strength of its capture.** ≥ 9 min 39 s of continuous saturation, ended by operator action. **No claim is made that it never recovers on its own** — that window was ended deliberately, and the rule against writing "never" for a window you ended yourself applies here. pgxpool's `MaxConnIdleTime` default of 30 m (pgx v5.9.2, `pgxpool/pool.go:22-23`) is a code read and is not traced by any capture.
  - **Rig scoping, which every claim borrowed from this entry must carry.** `test/ha` runs stock `max_connections=100` against 3 x 304 = 912 configured pool connections. The repository's own `docker-compose.yaml:30` starts Postgres with **`max_connections=1000`** and `docs/operations.md:173` tells operators so, and 912 < 1000. **The `/readyz` behaviour itself is not rig-scoped** — it is a property of pinging a pool rather than a server, and it holds on any deployment that ever reaches its connection ceiling — but the *ease* of reaching that ceiling here is.
  - **The cheap fix is not a code change of any size.** `pgxpool.Stat()` already exposes `AcquireDuration`, `EmptyAcquireCount` and `MaxConns`, and none of it reaches any surface. A `/readyz` that probed a **new** connection, or simply an `EmptyAcquireCount` gauge on `/metrics`, would have turned every arm above from silent into visible.

## W6-1 — observation: **sixty concurrent agent claim long-polls — three requests per second, every one answered `200` — pin Postgres at `max_connections`**, because the claim handler polls the database once a second from inside the request; this is the cheapest trigger found in the campaign and no surface reports it
- **Invariant:** none violated by its own text; recorded as an observation. It is a **capacity relationship** plus a diagnosability gap, and the incorrect behaviour it enables is filed above and at `FINDINGS.md:2517`.
- **Severity:** **major (observation).** Argued from `:6-8`, not by analogy — and **THE TWO LIMBS WERE SWAPPED AT THE BRANCH REVIEW, at a preserved line count and with no change of band, because the load-bearing one was resting on a window this entry's own Notes record as deliberately ended.** The limb that carries the band is *"incorrect visible behavior"*, and it is met **in-window and measured**: while the state is held, valid admin PATs are answered **401** (`:2517` and the entry above), SSE subscribers are answered **200 with a complete backfill and then a server-closed stream** (the entry below), and `/readyz` answers **200** on every replica while Postgres refuses every new connection (`:2680`) — each of those is a surface returning a wrong answer, each is **cited and not re-filed** here, and **none of them depends on how the window ended.** What *this* entry contributes is the **trigger**: that state is reached **with no fault injection, by agents doing the one thing agents exist to do**, at 60 long polls and ~3 req/s with every request answered 200. **The *"unbounded recovery"* limb is now claimed only at the strength of its capture, which is weaker than what stood here:** ≥ 9 min 39 s of continuous saturation with no self-recovery observed — **but that window was ended by operator action, so no unassisted-recovery time is measured and no "never recovers" is claimed** (§(d) `:2906`; pgxpool's 30 m idle default is a code read traced by no capture). **What was weighed against major, and it is real:** the trigger count is a property of `test/ha`'s stock `max_connections=100`, and on the reference compose's 1000 it would take far more; if this were only "a small test rig runs out of connections" it would be minor. **What answers that is the rig-independence of the mechanism — a polling loop inside the request re-acquires a connection every second at any budget — and NOT the absence of a warning: "nothing anywhere warns" is withdrawn as a severity argument, because *diagnosability* is the minor band's own subject and cannot lift an entry into major.** It stands instead as the reason the entry is worth reading: the API returns 200, the health surface returns 200 and the log is empty, so an operator's first evidence of the ceiling is 401s on valid credentials.
- **Repro:** `scenarios/w6-1-connection-pressure.md`, Part E. `test/ha` + `compose/ctrlports.override.yaml`, floor settled at **67** client backends. One agent identity enrolled through the product's own two-step enrollment (`tools/w6/w6-synth-agent.sh enroll`), then `tools/w6/bin/loadgen -url "http://localhost:18081/api/v1/agents/w6-1-sse/claim?timeout=20s" -method POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <uca_ redacted>" -c 60 -mode sustained -duration 45s -timeout 40s`. Evidence: `edgecase-evidence/w6/w6-1s/E-60.txt`, `E-60-req.csv`, `E-60-pg.csv.health.csv`, `B-histograms.txt`.
- **Observed:**
  - `requests=180 wall=1m0.348s  maxInFlight=60  meanInFlight=59.89  status 200=180 errors=0`. **One hundred and eighty requests. Three per second. Zero failures.**
  - Client backends went **67 → 100 and stayed at 100 for the whole window**; `psql` inside the Postgres container was refused with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` on one sample and the count read 100 on the other thirteen. Connections were read from `/proc/net/tcp` inside the container when `psql` could not run, the same fallback `:2523` used.
  - **`/readyz` 200 on all three replicas in 42 of 42 saturated replica-readings** — 14 sample instants x 3 replicas; no controller `ERROR` line was observed in the window, at the strength the entry above now states that.
  - **The contrast, and it is DOWNGRADED from what this entry first claimed.** The same rig, same replica, same session: **8 workers at 20 req/s for 60 s did NOT saturate** — 1,200 of 1,200 requests `200`, **zero 401s**, established TCP 68 → 77 with `db_backends` peaking at 78 (`B-B2.txt`). E-60's rate is **~8x lower than that** and it pins the server. **What was written here was "rate is not the variable". That is over-sold and is withdrawn**, for three reasons the matrix carries on its face. (i) **The decisive comparison changes two variables**: E-60 is `POST …/claim?timeout=20s`, a 20-second long-poll, while B2 is `GET /api/v1/runs?jobName=` at ~2 ms — so B2-vs-E-60 is **cross-endpoint** as well as cross-concurrency. (ii) **The one within-endpoint comparison is the arm the scenario itself discounts**: B2-vs-B3 holds the endpoint and the 20 /s average and varies worker count 8 → 200, and B3 saturates — but B3's arrivals are 200-wide bursts once every ten seconds, and B3 ran from a floor of **80** where the other arms started at 65-68, i.e. 17 connections from the 97-slot budget — B2 had ended at 77 nine seconds earlier and B3 got no reset, so **B3's saturation is confounded by carry-over** (`B-B2.txt`, `B-B3.txt`, floor lines). (iii) **On the published concurrency metric the matrix reads against the thesis**: the column was `meanInFlight`, and **B3 saturates at 0.69 — below B1's 7.99** — so no threshold in that metric orders the five arms, and the original argument silently switched to `maxInFlight` (8 vs 200). **The structural reason none of this is a tooling failure:** in-flight = rate x latency, so at a ~2 ms endpoint concurrency cannot be raised without raising rate, and the concurrency corner *had* to change endpoint. **Stated at the supported strength: concurrency at a latency-bearing endpoint is by far the cheaper route to `max_connections`; the clean single-variable isolation was not run.** **Outstanding measurement: a dose-response on one endpoint — E-20, E-40, E-60 from a common recreated floor.**
- **Mechanism (code-read, `internal/controller/api_agent.go:127-155`).** `handleAgentClaim` is a **polling loop inside the request**: `claimPollInterval = 1 * time.Second`, `maxClaimTimeout = 60 * time.Second`, plus one `UpsertAgentOnClaim` per request at `:150`. So an in-flight long-poll is **not** one connection held for the duration — it is one api-pool connection **re-acquired every second** for the duration, and N of them keep the pool permanently busy. The pool then does not shrink promptly (`:2527`), so the connections stay taken after the polls end. This is also why the claim surface is already **49 %** of the measured idle floor from just **two** agents (README §"The idle floor": `ClaimNextRun` 35.25 q/s of 72).
- **Expected:** `docs/operations.md:162-173` gives operators a connection-budgeting formula — `replicas x (API + background + lock + listen) + reserve < max_connections` — and it is the right formula. What is missing is any statement that **the api pool is driven by concurrent agents**, and any runtime signal when the budget is spent. An operator sizing from that table sees 128 API connections per replica and no way to know what consumes them.
- **Notes:**
  - **NO SIZING NUMBER IS OFFERED AND THIS ENTRY MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE.** "Fifty-nine agents" is not a product limit; it is what one laptop's `test/ha` with `max_connections=100` did on one afternoon. The transferable content is the **relationship**: concurrent long-polls consume api-pool connections, the pool does not give them back promptly, and the limit that binds is the **database's** `max_connections`, not the pool cap. **"In proportion to their number" was written here and is WITHDRAWN — it is a proportionality claim from a single point, and that point is not proportional.** On the one instrument read on both sides, established TCP to 5432 went **67 → 99** (`E-60.txt`): **60 concurrent long-polls added ~32 connections, not ~60. The scaling law is not measured.** Nor can it be recovered from this arm, because the observation is **right-censored** — the in-window `db_backends` series reads **100**, the server's own ceiling, on 13 of its 14 instants, so demand above the ceiling cannot appear. **+32 is a lower bound on what 60 long-polls wanted, not a coefficient.** The number an operator needs is arithmetic on their own `max_connections` against `replicas x 304`, and it should be computed rather than extrapolated from here.
  - **The instrument's own honesty check.** `loadgen` reports `maxInFlight` swept from 2N start/end events and guards **both** tails; this arm reports `maxInFlight=60 meanInFlight=59.89` against `-c 60`, i.e. the concurrency is measured, not assumed.

## W6-1 — observation: an SSE subscriber past the connection ceiling gets `200` and a **complete backfill** and then has its stream **closed by the server** with no error event, no status event, and no log line — settling the question `FINDINGS.md:2537` left explicitly open, and the answer is "silently EMPTY", not "silently dead"
- **Invariant:** none violated by its own text. I4 is not reachable — nothing is lost or reordered; the log rows are intact in the database and a reconnect that succeeds shows them all.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation).** Argued from `:6-8` and argued **against** inflation. Nothing is lost, nothing is corrupted, no request fails, and no state is written wrongly: the client receives a correct and complete view of the run as it stood at connect time. What is wrong is **entirely** that the client cannot tell a stream that died from a run that went quiet — which is the **minor** band's own first word, *"diagnosability"*. The visible-behaviour case (a `Running` run appears to stop logging) was weighed and rejected, because the same appearance is produced by a run that genuinely stops logging, and the view is recoverable by reload.
- **Repro:** `scenarios/w6-1-connection-pressure.md`, Part A / Part C3. From a floor of **59** client backends, `tools/w6/bin/ssehold -base http://localhost:18083 -run <live Running run> -token ha-admin-token -s 40 -hold 60s -stagger 250ms`. Evidence: `edgecase-evidence/w6/w6-1s/A3.txt`, `A3-sse40.csv`, `A3-sse40-events.log`.
- **Observed:** `requested=40 opened=40 aliveAtEnd=24 diedEarly=16 non200=0 totalEvents=1880`, `status 200=40`.
  - **The 200 is real and so is the backfill.** Each of the 16 streams past the cap received **14-18 log events** — a complete replay of the run to that point — and then `server closed the stream`.
  - **It is closed, not hung.** The response body ends and the client sees EOF. **That is the correction to the guess `:2536` recorded** (*"4 of 5 streams were seen to get a `200` with full backfill and then die after 2 events"*, uncaptured): the shape is right, but "silently dead" implies a stream that stays open and delivers nothing. It does not stay open. An `EventSource` will therefore reconnect automatically — into the same refusal — rather than hang.
  - **Nothing says why.** No `error` event, no `truncated` event (that one is reserved for backfill overflow, `sse.go:88`), status 200, and — per the entry two above — **zero controller `ERROR` lines** in the window.
  - **24 survive, which is the ceiling this scenario was asked to measure.** The wave plan assumed ~100 concurrent streams; `:2535` had already corrected that to ~26 by arithmetic. **Measured: 24.** Note this is not one connection per stream — 24 survivors consumed a 38-slot free budget, because each subscriber also spends **api-pool** connections per NOTIFY wake (`FINDINGS.md:2539`), so sizing from `ListenMaxConns` alone under-counts a subscriber.
- **Mechanism (code-read, and it is one assignment).** `handleRunEvents` writes the headers and the entire backfill at `internal/controller/sse.go:55-103` — `TailLogsRecent` at `:69`, `flusher.Flush()` at `:103` — **before** `:118` reaches `_ = s.store.ListenForNotify(r.Context(), channel, ...)`, whose first act is `conn, err := p.listenPool.Acquire(ctx)` (`internal/store/postgres.go:1665-1667`). Under exhaustion that acquire fails, the error is **discarded by the `_ =`**, `handleRunEvents` returns, and the response ends. `sse.go:118`'s `_ =` is what converts "the database is full" into "your log ended".
- **Expected:** `docs/high-availability.md:189-194` documents the endpoint's transport and says SSE clients may connect to any replica; **nothing in `docs/` states what a client should see when the stream cannot be established**, so this is not filed as a contradicted contract. The gap is that no surface — client-side or server-side — distinguishes the two cases.
- **Notes:** `FINDINGS.md:2537` says verbatim *"The '200 with backfill and then a silently dead stream' question is therefore still OPEN, and is handed to W6-S1"* and instructs that *"a re-runner must treat that question as unresolved."* **It is now resolved and the archived numbers are `aliveAtEnd=24 diedEarly=16 non200=0` in `A3.txt` with the per-stream table in `A3-sse40.csv`** — which also discharges the related note that `ssehold` had **no archived degraded-state reading**: it does now. Separately, this is **not** `FINDINGS.md:2614` (a stream whose run terminates *mid-stream* is never closed); that entry is about the opposite branch and is cited, not re-filed.

## W6-1 — observation: connection exhaustion is owned by a **single replica**, and restarting any other one returns its connections straight to the replicas still holding theirs — so the obvious operator remedy, and a rolling restart, fix nothing two times in three
- **Invariant:** none violated by its own text. **I5's re-election bound is met at 89 ms; the other bounds were not exercised.** This entry previously said "I5 was checked and is MET", which asserts a class on one of its members: the spec's text (`:52`) names leader re-election ≤ seconds, the stuck-run reap ≤ `staleAfter` 90 s + interval 30 s, **and** "the bounds in `docs/high-availability.md`". Only the first was measured (re-election under this fault took **89 ms**); the reap was never timed and `docs/high-availability.md`'s bounds were never enumerated, so **"MET" is corrected to "the one bound measured is met"**. No violation is claimed and none is available — an unexercised bound is not a missed one.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation).** Argued from `:6-8`. There is no data loss, no corruption and no incorrect state written; the cluster's recovery is achievable and was achieved in 11 s once the right replica was restarted. What is wrong is that **no surface anywhere tells the operator which replica to restart** — per-replica connection counts are not on `/metrics`, not in the log, and not queryable through the API — so the remedy is a guess with a one-in-three hit rate. That is the **minor** band's *"diagnosability"*. **The escalation case, stated for the operator:** if the "unbounded recovery" reading of the underlying saturation is taken (see the major entry above), this becomes the reason that recovery is hard rather than a separate defect, and the two should be read together.
- **Repro:** `scenarios/w6-1-connection-pressure.md`, Part D. Saturate one replica (40 SSE streams is enough), then restart a **different** one. Evidence: `edgecase-evidence/w6/w6-1s/D1-pre.txt`, `D2-restart.txt`, `D3-after.txt`, `D4-conn-owners.txt`, `D5-recovery.txt`.
- **Observed:**
  - **The distribution, read at 07:59:11 from `/proc/net/tcp` inside the Postgres container** — the only way to read it while `psql` is refused: **controller3 = 61, controller2 = 22, controller1 = 17, total established to 5432 = 100.** controller3 is the replica the SSE fan-out was opened against. **One replica of three holds 61 % of a 100-connection server.**
  - **Restarting the wrong replica moved the total not at all — and the "why" is INFERRED, with nothing measuring it.** `controller1` was restarted at 07:55:50 and was back with `/readyz` 200 by 07:55:53 (`D2-restart.txt`); it released its whole pool and the total was still **pinned at 100** at the next reading, 07:59:11 (`D4-conn-owners.txt`). **Those two readings bracket a 3 min 21 s gap containing no connection sample at all** — `D2-restart.txt` polls `/readyz` and container state only — so *"the survivors expanded into the freed slots faster than the sampling interval"* is a mechanism offered to join two endpoints, **stated as mechanism where it should have been labelled inferred**. What is measured is 100 before and 100 after. **The attribution itself is unaffected and is solid:** 61/22/17 = 100 read from `/proc/net/tcp` against an explicit IP→service map, corroborated by `D5-recovery.txt`, where restarting the *owning* replica drops the total to 43.
  - **Restarting the owning replica cleared it at once**: 100 → **43 established within 11 s**, `psql` answering again at **58** client backends (`D5-recovery.txt`).
  - **A prediction that was wrong, and the correction matters more than the prediction.** The runbook predicted the restarted controller would fail `store init` and stay down, since `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml` sets **no `restart:` policy on any controller** (verified by enumeration: the file's single `restart:` is on `agent-enroll`, `docker-compose.ha.yaml:168`). It came straight back — `RestartCount=0`, `ExitCode=0` — **because stopping the process is what frees the connections it then needs.** A controller holding ~304 pooled connections releases all of them on SIGTERM and its replacement opens into the space it just vacated.
- **Mechanism:** each replica opens four pools over one DSN (`internal/store/postgres.go:67-71`, caps at `:46-53`), and the pool that grows is the one on the replica the load lands on. Nothing rebalances across replicas and nothing releases promptly (`:2527`), so exhaustion is a **per-replica** property presented as a **server-wide** symptom.
- **Expected:** `FINDINGS.md:43` records controllers crash-looping with no DB-connect retry at startup, and `FINDINGS.md:2534` names restarting a controller as *"the obvious operator response in this state"* being *"the one with a documented failure mode"*. **Cite both; neither is re-filed.** This entry narrows `:43`'s scope: the crash-loop needs Postgres to be unreachable for a reason that is **not this controller's own pool** — a `pgbouncer` boot race, an external database — and in the self-inflicted case the restart is safe. It widens `:2534`'s: the restart is safe but, aimed at the wrong replica, useless.
- **Notes:** the saturation ran **≥ 9 min 39 s** without self-recovery (07:49:50 → 07:59:29) and was ended by operator action, so **no upper bound is established and "never recovers" is not claimed** — the window was ended deliberately. Also worth knowing for a re-runner: `docker compose down -v` / `up` **re-assigns container IPs**, so per-replica attributions are comparable only within one stack instance (`B-B4-maxrate-200w-pg.txt` resolves `172.20.0.7` to controller3 where an earlier capture resolved it to controller2). Totals are comparable across recreates; splits are not.

## W6-1 (campaign asset) — observation: `w6-pgsample.sh` could not survive the saturation it was built to measure, its own summary compared the number its README warns against, and `w6-synth-agent.sh heartbeat` failed the runs it was called to protect — plus a driver that outlived its own session and contaminated two captures while looking dead
- **Invariant:** none — instrument defects, filed so no future wave inherits them and so the voided captures are on the record.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation).** Diagnosability of the campaign's own tools; no product behaviour is implicated by any of the four.
- **Repro / evidence:** `edgecase-evidence/w6/w6-1s/` and its `void/` subtree; fixes in `tools/w6/w6-pgsample.sh` and `tools/w6/w6-synth-agent.sh`.
- **Observed — four defects, in descending order of what they cost:**
  - **1. The sampler died of the thing it measures, in two places.** `set -euo pipefail` plus a bare `rows=$(psql_ ...)` meant the first `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` ended the script. A 130 s grid over the 40-stream arm returned **2 samples**, both from before the exhaustion, and the `-p` health series — *the entire reason `-p` was added* — stopped with it (`A3-pg.txt`, `void/A2-partial-sweep/`). A second copy sat in the preamble's `max_connections` read, so a capture **started into** an existing saturation never reached its own loop at all. Fixed: `psql_ok` records `unavailable` and keeps sampling, `PG_MAXCONN_`/`PG_RESERVED_` let a capture be started into saturation, and the peak analyser counts `unavailable` rows instead of choking on them. **Verified by effect** (`harnessfix-pgsample.txt`): 5 of 5 samples `unavailable`, health probed on every one, summary reporting `UNAVAILABLE: 5 sample rows`.
  - **2. The same tool's saturation test was on the wrong side of its own README caveat.** Its closing summary compared `total_backends` — which includes Postgres background workers, NULL `datname`, consuming no `max_connections` slot — against `max_connections - 3`. It printed *"AT/NEAR max_connections in 156 of 180 samples"* for a window whose **client** backends were 93 of a 97-slot budget, i.e. not saturated (`void/A2-partial-sweep/A2-sweep.txt`). Now compares `db_backends` against `max_connections - superuser_reserved` and treats `unavailable` as saturated. **The README warned about exactly this over-read and the tool's own summary did it anyway.**
  - **3. `w6-synth-agent.sh heartbeat` terminalises the calling agent's own runs, and it voided two captures.** The verb sent `-d '{}'`. `handleAgentHeartbeat` gates reconcile on **body presence**, not on the decoded slice — `internal/controller/api_agent.go:88-91`, verbatim: *"gated on BODY PRESENCE (r.ContentLength != 0), not on the decoded slice being non-nil"* — so `{}` is `ContentLength=2` and reports an **empty** active set, which is the "the agent restarted and forgot its runs" signal. A 25 s keepalive loop written to protect a long-lived probe run **failed it 4 s into the first arm**, twice, and both sweeps then measured an already-terminal run and reported `diedEarly` figures that had nothing to do with connection pressure (`void/void-heartbeat-kill/`, `void/void-run-failed-2/`). **The product behaviour is correct and its own comment documents it; the harness was wrong.** The verb now takes run ids and its body carries the warning.
  - **4. A driver outlived its session and contaminated two captures while its own output file made it look dead.** A `nohup driver.sh &` kept running for ~6 minutes after the call that started it returned, and stdout was **block-buffered**, so its log showed only the first of four arms. It was in fact running a **200-worker max-rate arm** at the exact moment a "zero-load control" and a three-controller restart were taken on the same rig — producing an apparent stack that went from 23 to ≥97 client backends **in 12 s with no load**, which would have been a spectacular and entirely false finding. The orphan's own output files, timestamped inside that window, are what identified it (`void/void-B4-orphan/`). Every arm was re-run in the foreground. **Two archival corrections made at review.** (a) **The driver's own output was still in the LIVE archive.** `w6-1s/B-results.txt` **is** that driver's log — it runs B2/B3/B1/B4 from 08:01:14 to 08:08:05, including the 08:07:44 B4 arm named above as the contaminant — and only its `B-B4-*` pg files had been moved. It sat under the most inviting filename in the directory carrying four superseded arms with different numbers (B3 floor 76 and 100 after with **91 of the 100 on one replica**, an `11 of 12` readyz line, and a `readyz 000=1` triple discussed nowhere), **contradicting this entry's own closing corollary that any window-overlapping capture is void.** It is now at `void/void-B-orphan-driver/` with the driver (`B-driver.sh`) and a `NOTE.txt` enumerating the superseded numbers and excluding the `000` readings — `curl`'s no-response code, seen on all three ports at the same instant, i.e. a probe starved on a laptop running a second driver's 200-worker arm, not three replicas failing together. **No number in it is published anywhere.** (b) **The B-arm commands, absent from every capture, are archived**: `w6-1s/B-arm.sh` is the foreground one-arm-per-invocation replacement the published arms come from, and it carries the URL and headers that only survived as a flag string before. It also settles a sentence the scenario got wrong: its reset is `docker compose restart controller1 controller2 controller3` plus a 70 s settle, **not** a recreate.
- **Expected:** an instrument that outlives its fault, a summary that compares the quantity its own documentation says to compare, a keepalive that keeps things alive, and a driver whose death is observable.
- **Notes:** **the generalisable rule, and it is the third variation on one theme this wave.** W6-2a found a capture that would not stop; W6-2b found the same defect in a second tool and an arm whose verification consumed it; W6-1 finds a sampler that stops when the fault starts and a driver that does not stop when its session does. The unifying statement is worth writing down plainly: **an instrument's failure mode and its subject's failure mode must not be the same event, and "the process looks finished" is never evidence that it is.** The corollary for this campaign: **any capture whose window overlaps another arm's window is void**, and the only reliable defence found so far is to run arms in the foreground, one per invocation.

---

## W6-3 — observation: a Postgres connection-pool failure inside `GetJob` is reported to the client as `404 job not found: <name>` for a job that provably exists — 225 of 5,000 measured — and the same code path serves the agent's `call:` child-run route, where it is not retried at all
- **Invariant:** none breached by its own text (I7 covers run/approval/audit state, not resource-existence responses), and no `docs/*.md` statement to contradict: an untruncated survey of the 17 `docs/*.md` files outside `docs/superpowers/` returns **9** hits for `404` (all about OIDC, `/ui/*` and `GetRun`) and **0** for `job not found`. Filed as an **observation**.
- **Severity:** **major (observation)**, argued from `FINDINGS.md:6-8`'s own text and not by analogy. The band's major limb is *"incorrect visible behavior"*, and this is the API asserting, with a 4xx that means "the thing you named is not here", that a job **is not here** while the same job answered 2,790 successful lookups inside the same 2.964 s window. It is not `minor` — the minor band is *"diagnosability, docs gap, cosmetic"*, and this is not a message that merely fails to help: it is a message that is **false and actionable in the wrong direction** (an operator or a CI wrapper reads "job not found" and re-checks or re-applies the job YAML, while the real fault is database saturation). It is not `critical` — no data is lost or corrupted and there is no security impact.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-3-trigger-flood.md` Part A. `loadgen -url http://localhost:18081/api/v1/runs -method POST -c 16 -n 5000 -mode sustained` with a **developer** PAT against the `test/ha` rig plus `compose/{logfault,ctrlports}.override.yaml`, body `{"jobName":"edge-mutex-hog"}`, the job having been applied and exercised beforehand.
- **Observed:** of 5,000 requests in 2.964 s, **225 (4.50 %)** returned `404` with body `job not found: edge-mutex-hog`, captured verbatim by `loadgen -error-bodies`:

      09:15:10.198 seq=78  code=404 body="job not found: edge-mutex-hog"
      09:15:10.209 seq=107 code=404 body="job not found: edge-mutex-hog"
      09:15:10.209 seq=105 code=404 body="job not found: edge-mutex-hog"

  The job existed throughout: `SELECT ... FROM jobs WHERE name = $?` ran **2,790** times in the same window and the run table gained **2,241** rows for that job name. The count reconciles exactly against the statement census: 3,015 `pats` lookups (5,000 minus the 1,985 requests whose auth lookup never reached Postgres) minus **225** equals the 2,790 `jobs` lookups — i.e. **the 404s are precisely the requests whose `GetJob` never issued a statement**, because the pool could not hand out a connection. The mechanism is one line: `internal/controller/api_runs.go:49-52` is `job, err := s.store.GetJob(ctx, jobName); if err != nil { return nil, http.StatusNotFound, "job not found: " + jobName }` — **any** error becomes 404, the error value is neither inspected (no `errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows)`), nor logged, nor included in the body. Twenty-nine lines further down the same function, `CreateRun`'s error is surfaced honestly at `api_runs.go:84-86`, which is why 549 requests that failed one statement later got a truthful `500 create run: ... FATAL: sorry, too many clients already (SQLSTATE 53300)`. **Three failure points in one handler, three different status codes, and only the last one is true.**
- **Expected:** `404` on a trigger means the named job does not exist. A controller that cannot reach its database should say so — the same handler already proves it can (`api_runs.go:84-86`) — and a `503`/`500` is what lets a client distinguish "fix your job name" from "retry later".
- **Notes:** **The compounding is the reason this is not merely cosmetic, and it is measured code rather than speculation.** `createRunFromJob` has exactly two callers (`internal/controller/api_runs.go:36`, the human trigger, and `internal/controller/api_agent.go:800`, `handleAgentCreateChildRun`), so a `call:` step creating its child under DB pressure receives the same `404 job not found`. On the agent side `internal/agent/callstep.go:50-53` wraps it with **no retry whatsoever** — `childRun, err := client.CreateChildRun(...); if err != nil { return nil, "", fmt.Errorf("create child run for job %q: %w", ...) }` — so the parent run fails immediately and permanently with a message naming a job that exists. This is a sharper instance of the family the **W1-5 4xx-permanent-abandonment major** describes: that entry's Notes (`FINDINGS.md:327`) list *"a `404` window while an ingress route is reconfigured"* as a hypothetical intermediary-minted trigger, and this finding shows **the controller itself mints exactly that 404, with no intermediary involved**. Cheapest fix, entirely local: distinguish `pgx.ErrNoRows` from every other error at `api_runs.go:49-52` and return 503 (or 500 with the error, matching `:84-86`) for the rest. The 401 half of the same phenomenon — a valid PAT rejected because `GetPATByHash` could not get a connection (`internal/controller/auth.go:76-79`) — is **already filed at `FINDINGS.md:2517` and is cited, not re-filed**; it recurred here at 1,985 of 5,000 (39.70 %) at only **16 in flight**.

## W6-3 — observation: nothing on the run-creation path is rate limited, and the price is not the flood but its aftermath — one developer PAT bought 2,241 permanent runs, `max_connections` exhaustion, 55.18 % self-inflicted rejection, and a cluster left running at 14.9x its idle query rate after the client disconnected
- **Invariant:** none breached by its own text — I1 held on both clauses this arm could test (see the runbook's Part C). **One bound on the double-write check, stated here because the entry leans on it:** the pre-restart terminal-transition sum (7 = `runs_finished_total` 1+2+2+2, i.e. one `Failed` on `controller1` plus one `Succeeded` on each of the three) was scraped at `09:18:25`, **30 s before** the `09:18:55` restart that reset the registries, so a transition inside that gap would not be counted — and `controller2` was later SIGKILLed in Part C2 and its registry lost outright. **The gap biases the counted total *downward*, i.e. away from masking a double write, so the I1 conclusion survives it**; a gap that could have hidden a surplus would not. Filed as an **observation** about a design gap and its measured cost.
- **Severity:** **major (observation)**, argued from `FINDINGS.md:6-8` — and **SHARPENED AT THE BRANCH REVIEW, at a preserved line count and with no change of band, because the limb was resting on a window this entry's own Notes record as not waited out.** The `minor` band is *"diagnosability, docs gap, cosmetic"* and none of the three fits: the outcome is a cluster-wide availability failure, not a reporting weakness. The `major` band's second limb is *"unbounded recovery"*, **and what makes it an argument rather than an extrapolation is that the persistence has a MECHANISM and not merely a duration.** What is measured: **95 s of flat 14.9x idle-query load with no decay at all, while the client was gone**, and Postgres still refusing every connection **3 min 17 s** after the client disconnected. What accounts for it: **nothing on the run-creation path is rate limited** — the limiter inventory below is an enumeration, 3 hits, all in `enrollment_limiter.go` — so the input carries no cap; and the aftermath does not decay because the **2,241 runs are permanent** and the scheduler re-attempts the unqueueable ones **every 200 ms with no backoff** (`:2784`, cited and not re-filed), i.e. the cost is bound to a backlog that does not drain rather than to a client that has left. **The bound the window carries is stated rather than papered over:** that 3 min 17 s reading is the last unattended one, the operator restarted the three controllers rather than waiting, **the unassisted recovery time is therefore UNMEASURED, and no "never recovers" is claimed here or anywhere in this wave** (§(d) `:2906`) — this entry's own Notes record that pgxpool's `MaxConnIdleTime=30m` default would eventually reclaim the connections, which is a code read traced by no capture and which does not touch the scheduler-driven query load at all. **So the limb rests on measured non-decay plus a code-read reason for the non-decay, not on a window that was ended.** It is not `critical`: the critical band is *"data loss / silent corruption / security"*, and nothing was lost, nothing was corrupted, and the actor held a legitimate credential — although the last point is the uncomfortable one, since the credential is the **lowest** role that can trigger anything.
- **Repro:** as above. `w6-pgsample.sh -i 2 -d 110 -p 18081,18082,18083` and `w6-idleload.sh -d 110` recording across the same window.
- **Observed:** `loadgen [w6-3-floodA] mode=sustained requested_c=16 requests=5000 wall=2.964s / maxInFlight=16 meanInFlight=15.97 / status 200=2241 401=1985 404=225 500=549 errors=0`. **1,687 req/s from one client process against one controller, and zero `429`.**
  - **The limiter inventory is enumerated, not assumed.** `grep -rn "rate.NewLimiter|golang.org/x/time/rate" internal/ cmd/ --include=*.go` (excluding `_test`) returns **3 hits, all in `internal/controller/enrollment_limiter.go`** (`:11`, `:25`, `:44`). That one limiter is `rate.Every(6*time.Second)` burst 5 keyed on provider+IP+policy and is reachable from exactly three sites, all agent-credential routes (`api_agent_enrollment.go:271`, `:313`, `:408`). A second `*Limiter` type exists — `credential_touch_limiter.go:30`, one touch per credential per 5 minutes — but it suppresses a **DB write**, never a request, and returns nothing to the client. The router-wide middleware stack (`internal/controller/server.go:285-293`) is `Recoverer`, `RealIP`, `accessLogMiddleware`, `metricsMiddleware`, `securityHeadersMiddleware`, `originCheckMiddleware` — **six middlewares, no limiter**. There is no per-principal quota, no queue-depth cap, and no `Retry-After` outside enrollment.
  - **What one developer PAT cost in 2.964 s.** `requireMinRole("developer")` (`server.go:359`, `:370`) is the floor for `POST /api/v1/runs`. That credential produced: **2,241 permanent `runs` rows** and **2,624 `audit_logs` inserts inside the 110 s capture window** — a *window* figure, not a table figure, and not solely flood traffic: the table itself read `audit_rows=2655` at the C1 census and **3,057** at teardown (`c1-census.txt`, `final-census.txt`), and those rows are permanent under stock retention (Part E); Postgres pinned at `max_connections` from sample 3 of 29 onward, still refusing at **09:18:30** (3 min 17 s after the last request — the last unattended reading, **not waited out**); and **55.18 %** of its own requests rejected. Per accepted run the measured cost was **5.49 statements** (12,302 attributable statements / 2,241 runs) against a code-read prediction of 4 synchronous + 1 asynchronous.
  - **The aftermath, per-second and flat.** The 110 s statement capture contains only 2.964 s of client load. Across the **95** post-flood seconds the stack ran at **mean 1,071.6 statements/s (min 1,042, max 1,158)** — **14.9x** the published 71.8 q/s idle floor — with **no decay**, while the client was gone. Peak second during the flood was **5,076 statements/s (70.7x)**. The composition of that aftermath is the subject of the next entry.
  - **Nothing reported it.** `/readyz` and `/healthz` read **200 on all three replicas at all 29 sample instants — 87 of 87 replica-readings *for each of the two endpoints* (174 readings in total), 81 of the 87 taken at or above `max_connections - 3`** — taken in-window by `w6-pgsample.sh -p`. The two endpoints are counted separately deliberately: `a-pgsample.txt` records `readyz=200` **and** `healthz=200` per port per instant, and folding them into one 87 would be the same port-readings-as-samples conflation a sibling scenario was corrected for this wave. Three `ERROR` lines were logged by the controllers across the entire session, two of them genuine (`queued-run reaper list error` at 09:15:46, `log archiver error` at 09:18:46), i.e. roughly one line per two minutes of total database unavailability.
- **Expected:** an authenticated client holding the least-privileged role that can trigger anything should not be able to exhaust a shared cluster resource in three seconds, and the resulting degradation should not be shed from every other client on every replica. Nothing in `docs/*.md` promises a limiter, which is why this is an observation and not a violation — but `docs/operations.md:154` does tell operators to watch `/readyz`, and `/readyz` was 200 for all of it.
- **Notes:** **Scope.** The 9x pool over-commit arithmetic behind this belongs to `FINDINGS.md:2517` and is **rig-scoped**: `test/ha` runs stock `max_connections=100`, while the repository's own `docker-compose.yaml:30` starts Postgres with `max_connections=1000` and `docs/operations.md:173` documents that for operators (3 x 304 = 912 < 1000). On a 1000-connection deployment the same *shape* needs proportionally more load; the shape is what transfers, not the number. **What is new here relative to `:2517` and W6-1** is (a) that the trigger is **16 in flight**, not 8-at-2,554-req/s, on a *write* endpoint rather than a cheap GET; (b) that the credential is **developer**, not admin; and (c) the aftermath measurement, which no prior entry has. **What is deliberately not re-filed**: the 401-on-a-valid-token mechanism (`:2517`), the pools' failure to release promptly (W6-1), and the `/readyz`-does-not-degrade result (W6-1's `:2680`), all corroborated here and all cited rather than counted. **What is NOT known**: which of the four pools crossed the line. `w6-pgsample.sh` could not connect for 27 of its 29 samples — recorded as `UNAVAILABLE`, a saturation reading rather than a gap — so the per-pool peak table covers only the two pre-flood samples and this entry makes no claim about pool attribution under saturation.

## W6-3 — observation: the scheduler re-attempts runs it has already found unqueueable on every 200 ms tick with no backoff, so a mutex-blocked backlog costs a permanent 250.0 futile `INSERT INTO mutex_holders` per second — 93.3 % of a steady state 14.9x the idle floor — and bloats a one-row table to 776 kB
- **Invariant:** none breached by its own text. `docs/operations.md:53` documents an exponential backoff (1 min doubling to 1 h) for *"the log archiver, run-retention sweeper, and git resolver"* — the scheduler's queue attempts are **not** in that list, so there is no contradicted statement and this is an **observation**, not a violation.
- **Severity:** **major (observation)**, argued from `FINDINGS.md:6-8`. The `minor` band (*"diagnosability, docs gap, cosmetic"*) cannot hold a 14.9x sustained load multiplier that no surface reports. The `major` band's *"unbounded recovery"* limb fits: the elevated rate does not decay while the backlog exists, the backlog is created by an unprivileged client in seconds, and the only thing that ends it is the blocked runs draining at the blocking job's own pace. **The counter-argument is recorded so a reviewer can re-band**: the queue *does* drain — one holder per 600 s for this fixture — so the churn is finite in principle, and one could argue for `minor` on the ground that no behavior is visibly incorrect. It is banded `major` on the **fixture-independent** quantity only: **250.0 futile inserts/s for as long as more than 50 blocked runs exist**, borne by every co-tenant of the same database, with no decay and no surface that reports it. **The ~15.7-day drain figure is explicitly NOT load-bearing for the band**, because it derives from `mutex-hog`'s own `sleep 600` — a one-second job drains the same backlog in ~40 minutes, and the churn rate is identical in both cases. The drain time is reported as a property of this fixture; the band is argued from the rate.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-3-trigger-flood.md` Parts A and B. Apply `test/edgecase/workloads/mutex-hog.payload.json` (`concurrency.mutex: edge-mutex`), create more runs of it than can hold the mutex, and record a bounded window with `w6-idleload.sh`.
- **Observed:** per-second histogram over the 110 s capture, the client having disconnected at second 09:15:13:

      second(UTC)              stmts mutexIns
      2026-08-02 09:15:06        366       75    <- pre-flood, only 15 blocked runs
      2026-08-02 09:15:12       5076      166    <- flood
      2026-08-02 09:15:17       1064      250    <- steady state, client gone
      2026-08-02 09:16:55       1063      250

  **95 post-flood seconds at mean 1,071.6 statements/s (min 1,042, max 1,158), flat**, and `INSERT INTO mutex_holders` sits at **exactly 250.0/s** — which is `internal/controller/scheduler.go:58`'s `TransitionPendingToQueued(ctx, 50)` times the loop's 5 ticks/s (`RunScheduler`'s 200 ms default, `scheduler.go:24-26`). Each attempt is a full write transaction that accomplishes nothing: the top four statement classes are `begin`, `SELECT status FROM runs WHERE id = $? FOR UPDATE`, `INSERT INTO mutex_holders(mutex_name, run_id) VALUES ($?, $?)` and `rollback`. **Two windows, kept apart, because mixing them is how a span average gets read as a rate.** *Steady state* (per-second histogram, `a-churn-persecond.txt`): **250.0/s each = 1,000.0/s**, against the post-flood steady rate of **1,071.6 statements/s** = **93.3 %**. *Whole 110 s capture* (totals, `a-idle-report.txt`): **26,578 / 26,577 / 26,577 / 26,577 = 241.6/s each = 966.4/s**, against the whole-window **1,149.88 q/s** = **84.0 %** — lower purely because the window also contains the 2.964 s flood, during which the backlog had not yet reached its 50-row ceiling. The 93.3 % is the steady-state figure and both of its terms are steady-state. All of it is on the single replica holding the scheduler lock (controller1 1,101.25 q/s against controller2's 24.90 and controller3's 23.70). The dead-tuple cost is visible in the object itself: at teardown `mutex_holders` held **1 row occupying 776 kB**. Even the pre-flood state shows the mechanism cleanly — **15** blocked runs already produced 75 inserts/s and 368 statements/s, five times the idle floor.
- **Expected:** a run the scheduler has just found unqueueable is unqueueable for a reason that will not change within 200 ms (the mutex is held by a run that is executing). Re-testing it five times a second, in its own transaction, forever, is pure waste; the product already has the pattern to avoid it, documented at `docs/operations.md:53` for three other sweeps.
- **Notes:** **This is NOT a second count of `scheduler.go:58`, and the direction matters.** `FINDINGS.md:1398` files the hardcoded `limit = 50` as the defect that starves newer runnable runs, and `:1399` states plainly that *"`scheduler.go:58` is one defect and must not be double-counted"*. The 50-row cap is what **bounds** the churn described here: without it the same tick would re-attempt all 2,255 blocked runs and the rate would be ~11,275 inserts/s rather than 250. The defect here is the **absence of any backoff or negative-result memory on a failed queue attempt**, which is a different line of code and a different fix. Both were re-triggered by the same flood, which is how they were found together. **Starvation is `:1398`'s and is cited, not re-filed** — including this session's measurement of it, an unrelated probe `Pending` at **975.5 s** against a 0.807 s median baseline with an idle agent long-polling, which appears in the runbook's Part B as an operator number for `:1398` rather than as a finding. Cheapest fix directions: cache the failed `(mutex, tick)` outcome for the tick so 50 candidates blocked on one mutex cost one attempt rather than 50; or exclude runs whose declared mutex is currently held from the candidate query itself, which also happens to free the 50-row window for exactly the runnable runs `:1398` is about.
