## W6-3 — observation: `docs/high-availability.md:260-261` prescribes `proxy_next_upstream ... http_502 http_503 http_504` and calls it retrying "on a connect/response error", but nginx does not apply the response conditions to POST unless `non_idempotent` is added — so the phantom-run safety of the documented configuration rests on an nginx default the documentation never mentions, and there is no idempotency key to fall back on
- **Invariant:** I1 (**run accounting**), whose text at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-edge-case-testing-design.md:48` is *"every API-accepted run reaches exactly one terminal state; no phantom runs from duplicate fires/webhooks"*. **I1 HELD as measured** — this entry is about the margin by which it held, not a breach.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation)**. Argued from `FINDINGS.md:6-8`: the `minor` band is *"diagnosability, docs gap, cosmetic"* and this is squarely a **docs gap** — the measured behavior is correct and safe. It is explicitly not `major`, because no incorrect behavior was observed and recovery is not unbounded; the risk is latent and depends on an operator changing the recommended configuration.
- **Repro:** `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-3-trigger-flood.md` Part C2. `loadgen -url http://localhost:18080/api/v1/runs -c 8 -n 400 -delay 500ms` **through the LB on purpose**, with `docker kill -s KILL controller2` for the whole window, job `edge-w6-probe`, reconciling `runs` rows against **requests sent** rather than against 2xx.
- **Observed:** **400 requests, 400 rows, 400 x `200`.** The arm is **non-vacuous as a *failover* test and only as one**: **3 of the 400 access-log rows carry `ustatus="504, 200"`**, i.e. nginx really did pass those requests to a second controller, and each still produced exactly one run. **It is not a test of the phantom mechanism**, because all three retries were `while connecting to upstream` (see below) — the body had never been sent, which is precisely the retry class that *cannot* phantom. **The phantom limb remains closed by an nginx default, not by measurement.**

      1785662794.300 ... 200 ustatus=504, 200 rt=2.005 urt=2.001, 0.003 "POST /api/v1/runs HTTP/1.1"
      1785662802.389 ... 200 ustatus=504, 200 rt=2.004 urt=2.000, 0.003 "POST /api/v1/runs HTTP/1.1"
      1785662810.475 ... 200 ustatus=504, 200 rt=2.005 urt=2.000, 0.004 "POST /api/v1/runs HTTP/1.1"

  nginx's error log names what kind of retry they were: `upstream timed out (110: Operation timed out) **while connecting to** upstream` — the request body had not been sent, which is the one case where retrying a POST cannot duplicate anything. **The response-level case — an upstream that answered 502/503/504 after receiving the body — was not reached**, and by nginx's default it should not be: non-idempotent methods are not passed to the next server unless `non_idempotent` appears in the directive, and it appears in neither `test/ha/nginx.conf:24-26` nor the documentation. A repo-wide grep for `non_idempotent` returns **0** hits in `docs/`, `test/` and `manifests/`.
- **Expected:** documentation that prescribes a retry policy for a request that **creates resources** should say which requests it actually retries. `docs/high-availability.md:261` reads *"retry the request against the next controller on a connect/response error"* without qualification, and `:254` points at `test/ha/nginx.conf` as *"a complete working example"*.
- **Notes:** **Why the latent risk is real rather than theoretical.** There is no idempotency mechanism anywhere on run creation, verified by enumeration: `CreateRun` is an unconditional `INSERT` with no `ON CONFLICT` (`internal/store/postgres.go:245-254`); `runs` carries no `UNIQUE` index other than `runs_pkey` (`internal/store/migrations/001_init.up.sql:460-463`, with the other run indexes at `008_run_indexes.up.sql:10-12`, `011:11-12` and `017:5` all non-unique); no handler reads an idempotency header (`api.TriggerRunRequest` is `{jobName, params}`, `internal/api/types.go:46-49`); and the webhook path has no delivery-ID table or replay window (`api_webhooks.go:282`). So an operator who reads `:260-261`, observes that a POST is not being retried on a 502, and adds `non_idempotent` to "make the documented failover actually work" would immediately create up to **three runs per client request**, with nothing to deduplicate them. The whole safety margin is one nginx default. Cheapest fix: one sentence at `docs/high-availability.md:261` stating that the response-error conditions apply only to idempotent methods and that `non_idempotent` **must not** be added because run creation is not idempotent. **This scenario measured the connect-level case only; the response-level case is unmeasured** and is stated as an nginx-documented default, not as a product measurement.

## W6-3 — WITHDRAWN AT REVIEW, and this stub is not an entry and is counted in no tally: "a de-credentialled idle agent is a permanent 8.567 req/s rejection source"
**This was filed as W6-3's fifth entry and is withdrawn as a duplicate of `:450`.** It is kept as a stub rather than deleted because the withdrawal is itself the lesson, and because a reader arriving from W6-3's runbook must be able to see what happened to it.

- **Classification:** **NOT AN ENTRY.** Neither a violation nor an observation; it carries no Severity line and is counted in **no** tally, in the same spirit as the branch-internal-asset bucket at `:480`. A reader tallying this file should skip it.
- **Why withdrawn.** `:450` already owns this finding — *"a de-credentialled agent becomes a permanent, un-backed-off rejection generator"* — and its bullet at `:458` already gave the **claim-loop** decomposition (`N` claim slots at a ~2 s cadence plus the 15 s heartbeat plus the 5 s cancel-poll), while `:461` already recorded the no-escalation contrast against `retryUntilSuccess`'s 4xx abandonment. The withdrawn entry presented all three as new.
- **And its central claim was false.** It asserted that `:495` *"derives 8.3 req/s from the `LogPusher`'s re-flush floor"* and that "the two arithmetics coincide". That rests on misreading `:495`'s phrase *"once nothing is left to re-flush"* — which states **when** the floor obtains — as a statement of **what produces** it. The campaign's canonical derivation of ~8.3 req/s always **was** the claim-loop arithmetic, so there were never two arithmetics to coincide. `:495`'s wording has been corrected in place so the misreading is harder to repeat.
- **What was genuinely new, and where it now lives.** The loop count is **17**, not 16 — `:458` had counted the detached pool (`agent.go:310-321`, `d = 16` when unset) and omitted the non-detached loop (`agent.go:218`, `n = MaxConcurrent`, `1` when unset) — and the exact arithmetic `17/2 + 12/180 = 8.5667` reproduces the **measured 8.567 req/s** to four figures, with the control's 34 claim `200`s in 60.056 s coming out at `17/30` exactly. **All of it was folded into `:450`, `:458` and `:463` in place**, together with the 13.5x amplification and the ~11.9 %-of-idle-floor proportion. Nothing measured in Part D was lost by the withdrawal; the full working is in `test/edgecase/scenarios/w6-3-trigger-flood.md` Part D.
- **The methodological point, which is why this stub exists.** The binding rule is *grep `FINDINGS.md` for the **finding**, not just the doc text*. This entry cited `:495` — a forward-lead bullet in a carry-forward section — and **never cited `:450`, the entry that owns the finding**. Reading the lead instead of the entry is how a duplicate gets filed while its author believes they checked. **W6-3 therefore filed 4 entries, not 5** (3 major, 1 minor); see the runbook's "Findings filed" table.

## W6-infra — observation, **CODE READ ONLY, NOT EXECUTED**: the two execution backends disagree about `MaxConcurrent` in both directions — the Kubernetes agent defaults to **100** and reads a **negative** value as *unlimited*, the host agent defaults to **1** and clamps a negative value **to 1** — and no user-facing document states the two together, states the host clamp at all, or gives any rationale for the difference
- **Invariant:** **none, and no documented contract contradicted.** Checked rather than assumed. The Kubernetes side is documented **correctly** in four places (below), so there is nothing to contradict there. The host side's `<= 0 -> 1` clamp is documented **nowhere**, which makes the docs *silent*, not wrong — and per `FINDINGS.md:1509` silence is not a contract. I3's subject is locks, I5's is recovery bounds; neither reaches a concurrency default. Recorded as an **observation**.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation)** — diagnosability and a docs gap, on this file's bands (`:6-8`), argued from the band's own text and not by analogy. Nothing is lost, nothing is corrupted, and nothing behaves incorrectly: each backend does exactly what its own code says, and a `maxConcurrent` an operator actually sets is honoured on both. The *"incorrect visible behavior"* limb is not reached because no behaviour is incorrect; the *"unbounded recovery"* limb is not reached because no fault is involved. What is left is that an operator who learns the semantics on one backend and applies them to the other will be wrong in a direction the documentation cannot correct them on — the minor band's first word.
- **Repro:** **NONE. This entry was not executed**, and that is stated in its title for the same reason `:1864` and `:2383` state it in theirs. It is a code read plus an untruncated documentation survey, both reproducible in one `grep` each. **W6 deliberately planned no Kubernetes concurrency scenario and the plan says so** (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-02-edge-case-campaign-w6.md:93-96`): Docker Desktop's Kubernetes co-resident with this campaign's nine-container compose stack hits node resources and image-pull serialization first, so the failure would present as the `podStartTimeout` cascade **already filed at `:2297`**, and the scenario would have measured the laptop rather than the product. The asymmetry is therefore filed as what it is.
- **Observed:**
  - **Kubernetes agent — default 100, negative means unlimited.** `internal/k8sagent/config.go:90-99` is `DefaultConfig()`, whose `:97` is exactly `MaxConcurrent: 100,`. `Validate` at `internal/k8sagent/config.go:205-209` normalises with **`if c.MaxConcurrent == 0`**, not `<= 0`, under a comment that states the sentinel in the source itself: *"0/unset -> default 100; negative -> unlimited (preserved as a sentinel; the run loop skips its semaphore); positive -> that bound."* A negative therefore survives `Validate` untouched, and `internal/k8sagent/agent.go:146-150` acts on it — `var sem chan struct{}; if a.cfg.MaxConcurrent > 0 { sem = make(chan struct{}, a.cfg.MaxConcurrent) }` — leaving `sem` nil, with every gate site `if sem != nil` guarded. Enforcement is a **counting semaphore** acquired before the claim (`agent.go:207-213`) and released on claim error (`:222-224`), on an empty claim (`:233-236`) and by `defer` in the dispatch goroutine (`:242-244`).
  - **Host agent — default 1, and a negative clamps to 1.** `internal/agent/agent.go:218-221` is `n := a.MaxConcurrent; if n <= 0 { n = 1 }`. **`<= 0`, not `== 0`** — so on the host a negative value is not a sentinel for anything; it is 1. Enforcement is **not** a semaphore: `internal/agent/agent.go:301-308` starts `n` fixed slot goroutines, each owning a pre-created `working<i>` workspace directory (`:227-232`), so concurrency is bounded structurally by goroutine count. There are **two independent "default to 1" sites**: the runtime floor above, and the flag default at `cmd/unified-cd-agent/main.go:71-75`.
  - **Neither backend has an environment variable for it, and this refutes a mechanism claim the wave carried in.** `UNIFIED_K8S_MAX_CONCURRENT` **does not exist anywhere in the repository**. The k8s config path's only `os.Getenv` calls are `config.go:168` (`UNIFIED_K8S_POD_START_TIMEOUT`), `:171` (`UNIFIED_K8S_DRAIN_TIMEOUT`) and `:174` (`UNIFIED_K8S_MAX_DETACHED`, a **different field**), so `MaxConcurrent` is settable only through the YAML key `maxConcurrent` (`LoadConfig`/`loadYAML`, `config.go:102-119`); `cmd/k8s-agent/main.go` reads only `UNIFIED_K8S_CONFIG` and `UNIFIED_K8S_LOG_LEVEL`, and `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:209` confirms it with an em-dash in its "Env override" column. On the host it is a **flag** (`--max-concurrent`) and a config-file key (`internal/config/agent.go:96`, merged only when non-zero at `:226-227`); `AgentEffective` (`internal/config/agent.go:145-186`) enumerates every env var the host agent reads and `MaxConcurrent` is absent, the neighbouring `UNIFIED_AGENT_MAX_DETACHED` (`:182`) feeding `MaxDetachedConcurrent` only.
  - **The documentation survey, run untruncated and with counts printed, per the standing rule at `:2101`.** `grep -rniE 'maxConcurrent|max_concurrent|max-concurrent'` returns **111** hits over `docs/`, of which **16** are outside `docs/superpowers/` (i.e. user-facing); **6** over `manifests/`; **175** over the rest of the repository (**145** excluding `.superpowers/sdd/` review diffs). Nothing was piped through `head`.
    - **The Kubernetes default and the negative sentinel are documented, correctly, four times**: `docs/configuration.md:454` and `:367`, `docs/kubernetes-integration.md:140` and `:209`. `docs/configuration.md:454` states it verbatim — *"A **negative** value (e.g. `-1`) -> unlimited: no agent-side cap, bounded only by cluster scheduling/quota."*
    - **The host default appears exactly once, as a parenthetical inside a flag listing**: `docs/configuration.md:169`, `--max-concurrent int Max simultaneous runs (default: 1)`. There is **no** host-agent field-table row for it — the host config-file section shows only the example `maxConcurrent: 4` at `:240` — and **no document anywhere states the host's `<= 0 -> 1` clamp**, so an operator who has read `:454` has been told that a negative means unlimited and has been told nothing that would stop them writing it into a host agent's config.
    - **No document mentions both defaults in the same place, and none gives a rationale.** The only rationale in the tree is in an internal design spec, `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-15-k8s-agent-resilience-design.md:81`: *"Default raised to `100` (was 5) — k8s can schedule far more concurrent pods than a single host, so the old floor of 5 needlessly throttled a k8s agent."* That justifies 100 against a generic "single host"; it never names the host agent's **1**, it is a dated design document rather than reference documentation, and it does not travel to `docs/configuration.md` or `docs/kubernetes-integration.md`.
  - **A deflating fact, stated because it bounds the blast radius and was found by the same survey.** All **6** `manifests/` hits are the identical line `maxConcurrent: 5` (`manifests/agent-only/agent-config-patch.yaml:14`, `manifests/agent-only.yaml:68`, `manifests/base/k8s-agent/config-configmap.yaml:16`, `manifests/core-install.yaml:148`, `manifests/install/agent-config-patch.yaml:16`, `manifests/install.yaml:195`; also `examples/config/k8s-agent.yaml:8`). **So a manifest-installed Kubernetes agent runs at 5, not 100** — the 100 is what a hand-written config inherits, and it is what `docs/configuration.md` tells an operator the default is.
- **Expected:** two backends of one product, configured by one field name, should mean the same thing by a negative value, or the difference should be written down where the field is documented. The nearest the documentation comes to acknowledging that 1 is the host norm is `docs/jobs.md:699-706`, which warns that *"an agent (or pool) with `max-concurrent: 1` calling a job that targets the same agent"* deadlocks a `call:` chain and requires `max-concurrent >= 2` — framing 1 as a **user's configuration choice** rather than as the shipped default it is. `docs/agents.md:636` and `docs/troubleshooting.md:63-70` describe a busy agent at its cap without naming either number.
- **Notes:** the repair is documentation, not code: one row in `docs/configuration.md`'s host-agent section giving the default and the clamp, and one sentence at `:454` scoping "negative means unlimited" to the Kubernetes backend. **What a triager should take from this entry is the direction of the trap, not its size:** the dangerous read is Kubernetes-to-host, because the k8s semantics are the ones that are written down and the host semantics are the ones that are not. **Cite `:2297` and `:2401`; neither is re-filed** — `:2401` is where `maxConcurrent`'s *other* surprise (the k8s default of 100 as the per-shape bound on unreclaimed idle pooled Pods) already lives, and this entry supplies the second half of why 100 is a large number to inherit silently.

### (a) THE DISK-SPILL RECOMMENDATION — the wave's chartered deliverable and the campaign's oldest deferred decision, answered

**This decision has been gated since the W1 checkpoint (`:496`, itself pointing at spec `:199-207`) and re-forwarded by W3 (`:2079`) and W4 (`:2472`). It is now answered, and the answer is NO.**

> **Do not implement `LogPusher` disk spill as specified. Implement four cheaper changes first — three of which are strictly better value — and re-open spill only after the fourth of them lands.**

**Why, in one sentence an operator can act on: disk spill's only effect is to raise the pending cap, and with `flushLocked` unchanged, raising the cap raises the ceiling on the request storm.** Per-flush request cost **is** `len(p.pending)` — one `AppendLogBulk` per pending batch, with no coalescing anywhere between the cap and the wire — so a bigger buffer buys a bigger tick. Arm 2 measured the plateau where the arithmetic puts it: **216-228 batches at the tail for the stock 1 MiB cap at ~5.1 KiB of line text per batch, producing 324 req/s sustained and 880 req/s peak from a single step**. `:465` warned this in the abstract in W1; W6-2b measured it.

**Two labels the recommendation carries, because the campaign does not get to skip them.** **(1) The 1:1 relation between the cap and the per-flush request count is a CODE INFERENCE, not a measurement — no arm varied `maxPendingBytes`**, all four ran the stock 1 MiB (`runner.go:256`). What Arm 2 measures is the *left* side: that the plateau exists and sits where cap-over-batch-size puts it. **An arm that raises the cap and re-measures the plateau would close this, and it is the single cheapest follow-up in the wave.** **(2) The "100 MiB => ~20,000 batches" figure is arithmetic on that inference and is bounded by what the step has actually emitted, not reachable on demand** — Arm 2 emitted ~1.33 MiB of line text in 131 s, so a 100 MiB buffer would need **~2.7 hours** of unbroken outage to fill. The entitled statement is that **spill removes the only bound on the storm and lets it grow with outage duration**; 20,000 is the ceiling that bound would stop imposing, not a rate anything reached.

**The second measurement that decides it, and it is the one that closes the question rather than merely arguing it.** Spill addresses loss **at the byte cap**. Of the three loss paths W6-2b exercised, **the byte cap is the only one that already announces itself correctly** — Arm 2 lost 263 lines to eviction and the marker reported exactly 263. The two silent losses are Part E's (`:2657`: the whole run's output, lost at the step-end budget, marker structurally unable to fire) and, on the availability axis, Arm 4's 176-second stall (`:2643`). **So spill fixes the one loss that is already visible and neither of the two that are not.** That is the sentence the gate was waiting for.

**What to do instead, in order, with what each does and does not fix.**
1. **R1 — abort a flush pass on its first failure.** The smallest change in the set. **Fixes the Arm 3 I4 reordering violation outright** (`:2630` — a newer batch can no longer overtake an older one) and stops spending requests on batches that will be re-sent anyway. **Cost:** head-of-line blocking when one specific batch fails repeatedly, which is the correct trade for an ordering guarantee. **Does not fix:** the quadratic, the loss, the stall.
2. **R2 — give the auto-flush path a per-flush deadline.** `StartAutoFlush` passes a `context.WithCancel` (`backend_host.go:378`), so a pass is bounded only by `60 s x len(p.pending)`. A `context.WithTimeout` per tick — `logPusherWriteFlushTimeout`'s own 5 s is the obvious value — **turns Arm 4's 176.3 s frozen step into ~5 s per tick** (`:2643`). **Cost:** three lines, and a merely-slow controller will now have flushes abandoned that would have completed, so the deadline must sit comfortably above a normal round trip. **Does not fix:** any data loss.
3. **R3 — make the drop marker reachable, and make it say where.** Attempt it whenever `droppedLines > 0` **and at least one request in this flush succeeded**, instead of requiring `len(p.pending) == 0` (`runner.go:401`); and carry the covered `seq`/time range in its text, because Arm 2 measured the marker landing **987 lines after the gap it describes**. **Cost:** the count becomes a running total that may be superseded, which is precisely why the range matters. **Does not fix:** Part E, where no request ever succeeds — for that the only possible answer is agent-side, a `slog.Warn` at teardown when `p.pending` is non-empty. Note that would be **the first log statement in the entire `LogPusher`**: `runner.go:207-446` contains no `slog.`, no `log.` and no `fmt.Print*`. The silence is uniform, not an oversight in one branch.
4. **R4 — coalesce the backlog, in chunks of K, and only after R1.** This is the change that actually flattens the curve: per-flush cost stops being `len(p.pending)` and becomes `bytes / K`. **Three costs, every one of them measured elsewhere in this campaign.** (i) **It collides with nginx's 1 MiB default (`:1655`)** — Arm 2's plateau backlog was ~1 MiB of line text and more on the wire, so a literal single-request coalesce would be **413**ed by the reference deployment; **K is not optional**. (ii) **It collides with the controller's own cost model** — W6-2a measured `handleAgentLogBulk` at `2N` statements with no bound on `N`, and 7,600 lines in one body holding a Postgres backend for **9.356 s** (`:2584`), so coalescing moves cost from many small requests to few enormous ones, better for the agent and **worse for one controller goroutine**; **K must be chosen against `:2584`, not against the agent alone**. (iii) **It must not be generalised to an agent-level batcher without the W3-5 fix landing first** — within one `LogPusher` the body is single-run and the change is safe exactly as `:474` states, but merged **across** concurrent pushers it puts more than one run id in one body and `handleAgentLogBulk`'s scalar `droppedRun` (`api_agent.go:730-733`) attributes every drop to whichever run is last in the body (`:1878`/`:1924`). **The two changes must not land in either order without the other, and this is not hypothetical: R4's obvious next optimisation *is* the agent-level one.**

**Then, and only then, spill.** After R4 the request cost of holding a backlog no longer scales with the backlog, and the argument against spill evaporates. **W1's carry-forward asked that the spill decision be taken together with the coalesce fix rather than independently of it (`:496`); the measurement's answer is that the ordering between them is strict, not merely joint.** **AND SPILL DOES NOT RE-OPEN ALONE, WHICH IS THE HALF OF THIS DECISION AN OPERATOR READING ONLY THIS SECTION WOULD OTHERWISE MISS.** The spec's candidate is *"disk spill with a cap **+ a flush-before-finish barrier**"* (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-edge-case-testing-design.md:203-207`), and the gate statement at `:496` is explicit that the loss which actually fired in W1 was **not the byte cap at all** but the step-end `Flush` budget, so it *"needs the flush-before-finish barrier that §6 lists as the other half of the candidate"*. W6-2b's measurement answers that half too, and **it ranks the barrier ABOVE the spill on the evidence rather than beside it** (`scenarios/w6-2b-logpusher-curve.md:875-888`): Part E lost **100 % of a run's output with the cap irrelevant to the outcome** (`:2657`), while Arm 2's cap-driven loss was 263 lines and the marker reported exactly 263. **So when spill re-opens after R4 it re-opens together with the barrier, and if only one of the two is bought, buy the barrier.** **And three things spill would not fix whenever it lands, stated here so the recommendation is not read as larger than it is:** the spec's own **post-seal hard bound** — after archive seal, late lines are dropped with a **204** regardless of how much buffer the agent has (W3-5, `:1878`/`:1924`; W6-2a's C4 met that bound **by accident** rather than by design); **Arm 3's reordering** (`:2630`, which is R1's job); and **Arm 4's 176.3 s stall** (`:2643`), which is not a capacity problem at all and is R2's. And **W4's carry-forward 3 still binds and is not discharged by any of this** (`:2472`): every one of R1-R4 is a change to `internal/agent/runner.go`, and **the Kubernetes agent has no pusher at all** — no buffer, no retry, no cap, no marker, one `POST` per line with the error discarded (`:2334`). **A spill/coalesce programme that fixes the host agent fixes half the product**, and any triage that acts on this section must say which backend it is buying.

### (b) The two-regime result, and the charter's single-run assumption was wrong

- **The design doc asks for "drop-marker frequency and lost-line counts under sustained load" as though one workload produces both. It cannot, and the reason is arithmetic on the cap.** `p.pending` is capped at **1 MiB of line text only** (`runner.go:256`; `pendingSizeBytes` at `:438-446` sums `len(r.Line)` and nothing else), evicted **drop-oldest**, and only while `len(p.pending) > 1`. So:
  - **Chatty regime** (~4 KiB write-path batches): the ceiling is ~256 batches, per-tick cost **plateaus**, and *then* the drop path engages. You get the marker and the loss; the quadratic has already flattened.
  - **Sparse regime** (~20-byte batches every 2 s): the ceiling is ~50,000 batches, **~28 hours** away. Any realistic outage is **purely quadratic and never drops** — exactly what W1-6 observed (`grep -c "dropped"` = 0).
  - **The two are mutually exclusive. You get the quadratic request curve OR the drop marker, essentially never both.** W6-S2 therefore needed **two workloads**, which is why it became **two tasks** — W6-2a on the controller's per-line write path and W6-2b on the pusher's curve — and why W6-2b itself needed four arms plus a Part E rather than one.
- **A third arm was needed that the charter did not anticipate at all, and it produced the wave's only violation on this path.** A **partial/flapping** fault (nginx `split_clients` on `$request_id`, measured **47.0 %** of bulk requests to a dead upstream) drains stochastically and is **not** quadratic — and it is the arm that produced the I4 reordering violation (`:2630`). **The prediction going in was that Arm 3 would be *cheap* (it was — 287 requests against Arm 1's 11,326 for the same 300 s), not that it would be *wrong*.** It was found because I4 was checked in **every** arm rather than only in the arms expected to break it, which is the transferable half.
- **And a fourth regime was found that inverts the whole cost model.** Arm 4's black hole produced **six requests in 195 s** against Arm 1's 11,326 in 300 s — a factor of ~1,900 *cheaper* for the controller — while freezing the step for 176.3 s. **The log path's cost under fault is bimodal, and the harm is inverted between the two modes**: enormous request cost and no stall under a fast-failing outage, negligible request cost and a total stall under a hanging one. Any alarm built on request rate sees the worse case as the quieter one.

### (c) What the harnesses cost, and which survive

- **Six instruments were built, all committed under `test/edgecase/tools/w6/`, and all six survive the wave.** **(i) `bin/loadgen`** (Go, `tools/w6/loadgen/`) — HTTP load driver with `-mode sustained`, `-c`, `-n`, `-delay`, `-timeout`, `-error-bodies`; it **measures** `maxInFlight`/`meanInFlight` by sweeping 2N start/end events rather than assuming `-c`, and **guards both tails** — an over-report guard was added at `main.go:437-441` after a tie-break bug printed `maxInFlight=19` for a bounded 8-worker pool (`:2522`). **(ii) `bin/ssehold`** — S SSE streams against one named controller, reporting `opened`, `aliveAtEnd`, `diedEarly`, `non200`, `totalEvents`, `firstEvent_ms` and a per-stream CSV; it is the wave's only latency-bearing concurrency source and is the reason the concurrency corner was reachable at all. **(iii) `w6-pgsample.sh`** — `pg_stat_activity` sampling by class and by replica, with `-p` probing `/readyz` and `/healthz` **inside the same loop iteration** as the backend count, which is what makes `:2680`'s pairing a measurement and not a juxtaposition. **(iv) `w6-idleload.sh` + `w6-idleanalyze.py`** — a **generic** bounded statement-log window recorder with a separable analyser, one `ALTER SYSTEM` per `psql -c` and a fresh-session read-back. **(v) `w6-reqshape.sh`** — per-request shape from the access log, with a `window` verb. **(vi) `w6-synth-agent.sh`** — the synthetic agent the campaign had wanted since W3 and never committed (`README.md:92-98` had flagged promoting it as worth a task); it enrols through the product's **own two-step enrolment**, which is what lets `:2699` claim a real credential rather than a fake one. Plus `w6-2b-fault.sh` (the flap/outage/hang fault verbs, each re-probing **in line** at the point of use) and `w6-build.sh`.
- **Several were corrected mid-wave, and the defects are the part a future wave must inherit — they are filed as `:2622`, `:2670` and `:2740` and are summarised here because a reader of the checkpoint alone must not re-buy them.**
  - **TWO FILE-DESCRIPTOR LEAKS, THE SAME DEFECT IN TWO TOOLS, AND THE SECOND SHIPPED AFTER THE FIRST WAS FIXED.** `w6-idleload.sh` and `w6-reqshape.sh` both did `dc logs -f ... > out &` and killed `$!`. **`dc` is a shell function**, so `$!` is the subshell and the process actually holding the pipe is the `docker-compose` CLI plugin two levels down, which `kill` never touches. `w6-idleload.sh` left **three** survivors after three arms, one per "finished" capture, all still writing — the `floor` capture read **10,948** statements when its analyser ran and **26,523** when re-read after the next arm, *and the second number is not obviously wrong, which is the whole problem*. `w6-reqshape.sh`'s instance was worse in magnitude: a capture that reported **`captured 34 lines`** was archived at the end of the session at **44,151,788 bytes**, having absorbed the entire scenario. **Both are fixed the same way — a bounded `docker compose logs --since T0 --until T1` with no background process, plus a `-window.txt` sidecar so an already-captured file can bound its own re-analysis — and both fixes are verified live against a 1 Hz probe with disjoint, non-empty consecutive windows.** `w6-reqshape.sh`'s `follow -d` now **exits 5** and names the replacement; **bare `follow` still only warns** (`w6-reqshape.sh:133-134`), so a plain `follow` capture is still not window-bounded.
  - **`w6-idleload.sh`'s REVERT IS STILL BROKEN, IT IS BROKEN IN EXACTLY THE CASE THE TOOL IS MOST OFTEN POINTED AT, AND THIS CHECKPOINT DID NOT FIX IT.** The revert runs on a trap but needs a Postgres connection, so **a window that exhausted `max_connections` leaves `log_statement='all'` and the modified `log_line_prefix` armed on the running cluster** and the script exits **2**. W6-3 hit it (`FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`) and reverted by hand. `log_statement='all'` left armed will fill the container's log driver. **The tool header (`w6-idleload.sh:23-32`) and `README.md:804-821` say so; `scenarios/w6-2a-log-write-amplification.md:129` still said "always reverts on a trap" and is corrected by this checkpoint** — see inconsistency (i). **The fix is a retry-until-free revert or a `superuser_reserved` connection, not a louder error, and it is a harness task the next wave should take before it arms a saturating window.**
  - **A destructive verification: `logsink` was armed exactly once and its own probe was the customer.** Written as `while true; do tail -f /dev/null | nc -l -p 8080 >/dev/null; done`, it **passed `hangprobe` with a genuine 12 s hang** and then fast-failed with a 502 in 2.5 ms when Arm 4 actually armed it — plain `nc -l` is single-shot and the `tail -f` holding stdin never exits, so the pipeline never completes and the loop never iterates. The black-hole arm had silently degraded into the ordinary outage arm; the void run is kept at `w6-2b/arm4-void/` and its numbers are used for nothing. **This satisfied W3's ARM RULE — a capture *did* measure the effect — and was still wrong. The sharpened rule: a verification that is not idempotent must be re-run at the point of use, and an arm whose probe is destructive is an arm that is armed exactly once.**
  - **The other three, briefly, because each is a rule.** `w6-pgsample.sh` **died of the thing it measures** (`set -euo pipefail` plus a bare `rows=$(psql_ ...)`, so the first `too many clients already` ended the script — a 130 s grid returned **2** samples, both from before the exhaustion, and the `-p` health series, *the entire reason `-p` existed*, stopped with it); it now records `unavailable` and keeps sampling, and can be **started into** an existing saturation. The same tool's summary **compared the quantity its own README warns against**, printing *"AT/NEAR max_connections in 156 of 180 samples"* for a window whose **client** backends were 93 of a 97-slot budget, because `pg_stat_activity` includes Postgres's own background workers, which carry a NULL `datname` and consume no slot; it now compares `db_backends` against `max_connections - superuser_reserved`. And `w6-synth-agent.sh heartbeat` **terminalised the calling agent's own runs** by sending `-d '{}'` — `handleAgentHeartbeat` gates reconcile on **body presence**, not on the decoded slice, so `{}` reports an empty active set, which is the "the agent restarted and forgot its runs" signal; a keepalive written to protect a long-lived probe run **failed it 4 s into the first arm, twice**. **The product behaviour is correct and its own comment documents it; the harness was wrong.**
- **What a future wave inherits, stated as a shopping list.** All six instruments plus the fault verbs, committed and effect-verified; `loadgen`'s two-tailed concurrency guard and its `PACED:` disclosure; `w6-pgsample.sh -p`'s same-iteration health pairing, which is the single most reusable idea in the set; the `-window.txt` sidecar idiom; and `w6-synth-agent.sh`'s real two-step enrolment, which finally discharges a want the campaign has carried since W3. **What it must NOT inherit uncritically: `w6-idleload.sh`'s revert, and bare `w6-reqshape.sh follow`.**

### (d) What this laptop could not measure, and what every number here is extrapolated FROM

**No number in this wave is a product capacity figure, and three specific limits are why.**

- **The rig executes exactly TWO concurrent real runs.** Two agents x the host agent's `MaxConcurrent` default of **1** (`internal/agent/agent.go:218-221`), and the compose file passes no `--max-concurrent`. **Every "many runs" number in this wave is therefore synthetic load against real handlers, not many real runs** — `:2770`'s 2,241 runs are 2,241 `runs` rows created and queued, not 2,241 executions, and `:2784`'s backlog exists precisely because the rig cannot drain it.
- **The 9x pool over-commit is RIG-SCOPED and every claim borrowed from this wave must say so.** Each controller opens four pools over one DSN — api 128, background 32, lock 16, listen 128 = **304 per replica, 912 across three** — against `test/ha`'s **stock `max_connections=100`** (`test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml:3-13`, no override). **But the repository's own `docker-compose.yaml:30` starts Postgres with `max_connections=1000`, and `docs/operations.md:173` tells operators so.** 3 x 304 = 912 < 1000, so **the reference compose is not over-committed and the 9x does not transfer.** The entries say this in five places (`:2529`, `:2564`, `:2616`, `:2696`, `:2780`) and it is repeated here because it is the single most borrowable-and-wrong number in the wave. **What transfers is the shape, not the trigger count** — and `:2680` is careful about which half is which: *the `/readyz` behaviour itself is not rig-scoped*, because it is a property of pinging a pool rather than a server and holds on any deployment that ever reaches its ceiling; **the ease of reaching that ceiling here is.**
- **W6-1's concurrency-vs-rate isolation was STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE at the endpoint available, and this is arithmetic rather than a tooling failure.** `:2535` proposed a one-command experiment — 8 in flight at ~50 req/s — to separate the two. **In-flight = rate x latency**, so 8 in flight at 50 req/s needs **160 ms** of server latency, and the endpoint answers in **~2 ms**. Measured: `-c 8 -delay 400ms` gives `meanInFlight=0.03`, **not 8** (`w6/w6-1s/B-B2.txt`). **Holding N in flight at a low rate requires a latency-bearing endpoint**, which is why W6-1 had to reach the concurrency corner with a claim long-poll and an SSE stream — and why the decisive comparison **changes endpoint as well as concurrency**, and why the honest answer is *"concurrency at a latency-bearing endpoint is by far the cheaper route to `max_connections`"* rather than the clean separation the charter wanted. **The refutation was placed at `:2535`, where a re-runner reads it, and not only at the append point 160 lines below** — because this campaign has already lost one correction that way.
- **Three further things this wave states as unmeasured rather than estimating.** `:2699` refuses a sizing number outright and withdraws its own proportionality claim (the +32-for-60 series is **right-censored** at the ceiling on 13 of 14 instants, so **+32 is a lower bound on demand, not a coefficient**). `:2770` refuses an unassisted-recovery time (*"the state was not waited out"* — the operator restarted rather than waiting, and pgxpool's 30 m idle default is a **code read** traced by no capture). And **every "it did not recover" window in this wave was ended deliberately**, so **no "never recovers" is claimed anywhere** — `:2682`, `:2695`, `:2738` and `:2772` each say so in their own text.

### (e) The "verified code facts" mechanism-vs-`file:line` pattern, for a SIXTH consecutive wave

- **The refinement still describes what happened, and W6 is its cleanest instance yet — but it needs W4's substance-versus-resolution split kept, and W6 supplies the first case where a `file:line` claim was *substantively* right and its own mechanism inference was wrong in the same sentence.**
- **`file:line` claims: held.** Every constant, span and line number in the recon block (`plan:19-113`) resolved. `runner.go:207-446`, `:256`, `:358-366`, `:429-446`, `:282`, `:401-424`; `client.go:53`; `api_agent.go:721-734`; `postgres.go:918-936`; `sse.go:118-143`; `enrollment_limiter.go:14`; `server.go:285-293`; `k8sagent/config.go:97`; `agent.go:218-221`; `api_webhooks.go:118` as the sole `MaxBytesReader` — all checked at the point of use, all correct. The O(t²) claim was **confirmed** with one substantive correction that strengthens it (partial-progress accounting **does** exist at batch granularity — a batch that succeeds is dropped from `stillPending` — so what is absent is progress *within* a batch, and any coalescing).
- **Mechanism claims: four refuted, and every one by execution.** **(1) "Chatty step = 4 KiB write-path batches"** — the batch size that actually obtains is ~5.1 KiB of line text, and more importantly the *regime* prediction that a chatty step reaches the cap in a realistic outage held while the arithmetic behind it did not. **(2) "~100 concurrent SSE streams saturate Postgres"**, reasoned from the listen-pool cap: the reasoning is sound and **names the wrong pool** — the api pool gets there first — and the trigger is **~12x too small, not two orders of magnitude out**; `:2535` corrected it to ~26 by arithmetic and `:2714` **measured 24**. **(3) `MaxConcurrent` having an env var** — it has none on either backend, refuted by the entry filed above. **(4) "Audit retention defaults to 0 = keep forever"** — `auditRetentionDaysDefault()` returns **90**, so W6-3's Part E premise was false for one of its three variables; the survey then found **no operator-facing doc that contradicts the code**, and **Part E correctly files nothing** and is kept as a negative result.
- **The one genuinely new thing W6 adds to the pattern, and it is uncomfortable.** `plan:93-96`'s Kubernetes bullet is a *correct* `file:line` claim (`config.go:97` really is `MaxConcurrent: 100`) carrying an *incorrect* mechanism claim in the same sentence (an env var), **and a third clause — "worth filing as a code-read observation, not a scenario" — that was a scheduling judgement and turned out right.** W4's checkpoint asked the campaign to stop reporting resolution and substance as one number; **W6 asks it to stop reporting a bullet as one claim.** The operational form is narrow: *when a plan bullet asserts a constant, a mechanism and a decision in one breath, check the three separately, because they fail at three different rates.*
- **And the environment class W4 identified stayed cheap, exactly as W4 predicted.** W6's environment assertions — stock `max_connections=100`, no upstream `keepalive` in `test/ha/nginx.conf`, `worker_connections` at 512, the synthetic agent not being committed — were all checked in the first task and all held, and the one that mattered (**run high-rate arms against a controller directly; through the LB you measure the rig, not the product**) shaped every arm in the wave. **Verdict: the pattern holds for a sixth wave, and it is now specific enough to be a checklist rather than an observation.**

W6 filed **14 observations, 8 of them major, and not one of them reached an invariant** — which is consistent with the gaps rather than evidence of a new one, because W6's subject is capacity and the I-list is about correctness. **The one thing W6 does add is a data point about the *shape* of the hole:** six of the eight major observations describe a system that is unusable while every stored artefact is correct, and no invariant in the set has availability as its subject at all. **That is stated as an observation about the invariant set and NOT as a recommendation to add an availability clause** — the campaign has learned (`:2073`, `:2473`) that a narrow clause per gap is the wrong shape, and an availability invariant would need a bound to be checkable against, which this wave has demonstrated cannot be measured on this rig. **Until the I-list is amended, W7+ must not read "no invariant contradicted" as "nothing is wrong": check whether the invariant's *subject* reaches the object before concluding anything from its silence.**

W3 carry-forward 7 (does `cancelRun()` kill a long in-flight operation or does it run to completion?) and W2 carry-forward 2 (the same discriminator on the approval fence) are likewise untouched. **All three still answer to one arm**, and the recommendation is unchanged from W4's except that it is now more overdue.

### (g) The zero-criticals calibration — what W6 changes, and what it does not

- **W6 files no critical and recommends none. The escalation set stands at SIX and W6 adds no seventh.** The set is unchanged from W4's: W3-3 `:1620`, W3-4 `:1521`, W3-1 `:1938`, W3-6 `:1864`, W4-1 `:2334`, and W1-2 `:179` — **cited here by ENTRY HEADING, where `:2504` cites the same four W3 members by their in-entry Severity-reasoning lines (`:1640`, `:1562`, `:1950`, `:1866`); both sets resolve and they are two anchors on the same entries, noted at the branch review because a reader diffing the two lists sees four of six numbers change and has no way to tell that nothing moved** — **hubbed on `:179`**, which three of the other five argue their band explicitly against and which `:2336` binds to by instructing that it and `:2334` move together.
- **The judgement was made entry by entry against the critical band's text — *"data loss / silent corruption / security"* — and not by defaulting, and the two W6 entries that come closest are named here so the operator can check the reasoning rather than the conclusion.**
  - **`:2630` (the reordering violation) is the one that argues the band explicitly, and it argues itself DOWN.** *Silent corruption* is genuinely arguable — the stored order is corrupt and nothing announces it — and the entry says so in those words. What holds it at major is not analogy but a **property of the defect**: it loses nothing, duplicates nothing, and leaves emission order **fully recoverable from the `ts` column the product already stores** (re-sorting by `(timestamp, seq)` leaves **0** inversions, measured). **A defect whose damage is fully reversible from data the system already holds cannot outrank the irreversible losses this file settles at major.** That is a reason of kind, and it is the right kind of reason.
  - **`:2657` (the unreachable drop marker) is the entry a reader might expect to escalate, and it must not, because it does not own its own loss.** A `Succeeded` run with 2,002 lines emitted and **zero** delivered looks like the strongest data-loss case in the wave. **It is not a new loss.** The entry is explicit that the loss is **already filed as the W1-2 major at `:179`** and is **cited, not re-filed**; what `:2657` files is a *different property of the same machinery* — that the announcement mechanism is structurally unreachable in exactly the case where the loss is largest. **Escalating it would double-count `:179`.** What it *does* legitimately do is strengthen `:179`: W1-2 recorded that in its case the marker's `droppedLines > 0` precondition "was never even met, not merely unlucky timing", i.e. the question was moot there; **`:2657` is the campaign's first live case where the eviction path certainly did fire and the marker still could not**, which converts the `len(p.pending) == 0` gate from a coincidence into the defect. **So the correct action is not a seventh member; it is that `:179` should be re-read with `:2657` beside it when the six are re-read.**
- **The combination question, asked the way W4 asked it, and answered no.** W4's finding was that `:2334` and `:179` are the same defect on both execution backends by two independent mechanisms, so the pair meets the "data loss" disjunct on its face. **Does any W6 entry combine with an earlier one to reach the band?** The candidate pair is `:2630` + `:1521` — reordering and duplication in the same controller loop, both silent, both served by every read surface. **It does not reach it, and the reason is the same property as above**: `:1521`'s surplus rows are *unrecoverable* (nothing anywhere records what the workload emitted, so the corruption is undetectable from inside the system) while `:2630`'s disorder is *fully recoverable* from a column the product already stores. **They are the same loop and not the same kind of damage.** `:2630` is correctly separate from `:1521` and correctly below it.
- **What W6 DOES change, and it is one thing, stated precisely.** Not the set, and not the band — **the shape of the file the band is calibrated against.** For five waves the calibration argument has been "this campaign's `major` band is load-bearing and its `critical` band is empty", where `major` meant *violations*. **W6 puts eight major-severity findings in the observation bucket**, so an operator who triages violations first now skips the wave's most severe material by construction. **That claim is about the bucket and is stated at the strength the branch review left it:** three of the eight (`:2586`, `:2701`, `:2772`) had their band arguments re-argued from `:6-8` — by exclusion in the first, from deliberately-ended windows in the other two — and **all three survive at major with no change of band**, but the set is **not uniform**, and none of this is offered as evidence that the bands themselves moved. **The re-reading recommendation is therefore unchanged in form and extended in scope: the six should be re-read together, once, by the operator, with `:2334`'s "breadth, not kind" as the entry point — and W6's eight major observations should be triaged in the same pass, not after the violations.** **The calibration remains a decision, not a measurement, and W6 does not disturb it.**

### Tooling and asset notes carried forward

- **THE WAVE'S RULE, and it is the third variation on one theme in one wave, which is why it is stated first: an instrument's failure mode and its subject's failure mode must not be the same event, and "the process looks finished" is never evidence that it is** (`:2750`). W6-2a found a capture that would not stop; W6-2b found the same defect in a second tool **and** an arm whose verification consumed it; W6-1 found a sampler that stops when the fault starts and a driver that does not stop when its session does. **The corollary is a merge gate: any capture whose window overlaps another arm's window is void, and the only reliable defence found so far is to run arms in the foreground, one per invocation.**
- **This checkpoint found a SIXTH instance of the stop-class defect, in a tool nobody had suspected, and it was still running at checkpoint time.** `w6-2a/C/mem-during.txt` is a `docker stats` follower, not a `docker compose logs` one, so it is outside the two tools the wave fixed. **The archived copy is the bounded 3,908-line window the entry cites; the scratchpad copy had reached 74,072 lines and was still growing when this checkpoint measured it, hours after the W6-2a session ended, from a live `docker` process started at 14:13:04.** It was killed and the growth confirmed stopped. **Nothing published moves**: the archive is the window, `421.1MiB` occurs **exactly twice in both copies, both before the request**, so `:2600`'s load-bearing "retained, not transient" claim re-derives against the archive unchanged, and the appended lines read `363.1MiB` — a *different, later* stack instance, which is why they cannot contaminate a claim about this one. **`README.md`'s count of stop-class instrument defects moves from five to six, and the rule's scope widens: it is not a `dc`-is-a-shell-function bug, it is any `-f`/`--follow` capture, and `docker stats` was the one nobody wrote a `-window.txt` sidecar for.**
- **Rig facts W7+ needs, each paid for once this wave.** **(i) Run high-rate arms against a controller directly.** `test/ha/nginx.conf` has **no upstream `keepalive`**, so every proxied request opens a fresh TCP connection, and `events {}` leaves `worker_connections` at 512 — **through the LB you measure the rig, not the product**; `compose/ctrlports.override.yaml` exists to publish the three controllers on 18081/18082/18083 for exactly this. **(ii) `docker compose down -v` / `up` re-assigns container IPs**, so per-replica attributions are comparable **only within one stack instance** — `B-B4-maxrate-200w-pg.txt` resolves `172.20.0.7` to controller3 where an earlier capture resolved it to controller2. **Totals are comparable across recreates; splits are not.** **(iii) When `psql` is refused, read `/proc/net/tcp` inside the Postgres container** — it is the only instrument that survives `max_connections`, and it is how `:2523`, `:2705` and `:2732` were taken. **(iv) `pg_stat_activity` includes Postgres's own background workers**, which carry a NULL `datname` and consume no `max_connections` slot: any "at `max_connections`" claim must be checked against the `datname` split first (measured: 96 client backends of 100 against `superuser_reserved_connections = 3`, i.e. one free non-superuser slot rather than none). **(v) `nginx-logfault.conf` fixes `proxy_connect_timeout` inside the bulk location**, so an arm cannot set its own without nginx failing `-t` on a duplicate directive; `compose/nginx-w62b.conf` moves it out to the include for that reason and both files say so. **(vi) An arm that must produce a *hang* rather than a refusal needs a sink with no per-connection state** — `nc -lk -p 8080 -e sleep 3600`, not `nc -l` in a `while` loop.
- **Cost comparison, since W3 established it as a useful number.** W2 needed **~96 MB**; W3 **~4.9 MB**; W4 **729 KB**; **W6 needed 46,651,798 bytes (`du -sb`) / 46 MB block-allocated (`du -sh`) across 365 files** — the second-largest archive in the campaign, and for a reason worth stating rather than apologising for: **W6 is the only wave whose primary instrument is Postgres statement logging**, which W3's checkpoint recommended against arming more than once. W6 armed it for **eleven** windows across three scenarios because nothing else can answer "how many statements did this cost", and the raw logs are gzipped in the archive (~2.1 million raw statement lines in W6-2a alone). **The number a later wave should take from this is not "smaller is better" but "a wave that measures cost pays in evidence, and the payment is statement logs".**
- **Evidence archive — and the naming split is RECONCILED rather than documented, which is the opposite of W4's call, for a reason worth recording.** `edgecase-evidence/w6/` now holds all five directories — `w6-1/`, `w6-1s/`, `w6-2a/`, `w6-2b/`, `w6-3/` — at **46,651,798 bytes (`du -sb`) / 46 MB (`du -sh`) / 365 files**; both figures are stated because they differ and a re-measurer should know which one this is. **`w6-2b/` and `w6-3/` had been archived at the evidence root's top level while the other three went under `w6/`**, which broke the per-wave convention W2, W3 and W4 established. **W4 chose to document its naming trap rather than rename, because renaming would have broken 38 working citations. Here the cost is ONE:** every other W6 citation is a bare relative name (`w6-2a/C/bigbody.txt`) that resolves identically either way, and the only rooted citation into the moved trees was `edgecase-evidence/w6-3/d-run.txt` at `FINDINGS.md:458`. **It is corrected in place, at a preserved line count, and the two directories are moved. The rule W4 stated — decide the directory name at the first capture, from the scenario id — is what would have prevented both; the rule this adds is that a split is cheap to fix only while the citation count is small, so fix it at the checkpoint that finds it.** **W6-1's split across `w6-1/` and `w6-1s/` is deliberate and is NOT reconciled**: `w6-1/` holds Task 1's harness-verification captures (which back `:2517`, an infra entry) and `w6-1s/` holds the W6-1 **scenario**, and eight citations distinguish them.
- **`diff -r` result, stated with its exceptions rather than as a clean claim, because it is not clean and the differences are all deliberate.** All five directories were compared against the session scratchpad. **No capture differs in content.** Four classes of difference exist. **(1) Compression** — every Postgres statement log and every nginx access log is archived `.gz` (the reason `w6-2a` is 4.2 MB archived against 158 MB in scratchpad, and `w6-2b` 17 MB against 113 MB); each `.gz` reproduces its cited uncompressed name and line count under `gunzip -c`. **(2) Drivers, analysers and build artefacts left unarchived** — `analyze.py`, `fixcheck.exe`, `lib.sh`, `conns.sh`, `hb.sh`, `recreate.sh` and the per-arm `*-driver.sh` files; **the two that back a published claim were archived deliberately** — `w6-1s/B-arm.sh` (the foreground one-arm-per-invocation replacement the published B arms come from, carrying the URL and headers that had survived only as a flag string) and `w6-1s/void/void-B-orphan-driver/B-driver.sh` with `B-results.txt` and a `NOTE.txt` enumerating the superseded numbers, exactly as `:2748` records. **(3) Two files differ by one byte-range each, and both differences are the archive being RIGHT.** `w6-2a/C/mem-during.txt` — the archive is the bounded 3,908-line window and the scratchpad copy is the still-growing follower described above. `w6-2b/drv.sh` — the archived copy has the rig admin token replaced by `T=${UNIFIED_TOKEN:?}` with a note naming its source; the scratchpad copy carries the literal. **(4) One rename** — `w6-1/step8-idle-report-SUPERSEDED-28x-undercount.txt` is scratchpad's `w6-idleload-idle-report.txt`, renamed at archival to carry its own warning, which is the correct treatment of a superseded capture and is the pattern W3-3 established with `docs-greps-ORIGINAL-TRUNCATED.txt`. **And one file is deliberately NOT archived and never will be: `w6-3/devpat.secret`, the developer PAT `:2770` was measured with.**
- **Credentials: a fresh regex sweep over the ENTIRE evidence root was run at this checkpoint rather than trusting the per-task sweeps, per the standing rule at `:2124`, and it is clean.** **0** `uc[aer]_` strings of credential length (the regex `uc[aer]_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}` returns zero matches across the whole tree, all waves); every one of the 103 `uc[aer]_` occurrences is **4, 8 or 12 characters** — a bare prefix or an 8-hex credential **id** — with no body anywhere. **0** JWT-shaped strings. **0** files carrying `client-key-data`, `client-certificate-data` or a PEM private key; the single grep hit for those is `README.md`'s own prose describing the sweep. **This is the second consecutive wave that needed no retroactive scrubbing, and as in W4 the reason is structural rather than diligent**: `w6-synth-agent.sh` prints id prefixes by construction and `:2702`'s `loadgen` invocation is archived with `<uca_ redacted>` in the entry itself. **The one credential this wave did handle in the clear was scrubbed at archival, not after** (`w6-2b/drv.sh`, above).
