## W5-1 — **NOT EXECUTED (code-read only)**: `docs/operations.md:191` grounds its rolling-upgrade guarantee on "additive columns/tables — this is the norm for unified-cd's migration history", and **5 of the 17 migrations are backward-incompatible** — 6 column drops, 5 constraint drops, 3 `NOT NULL`-without-default, 3 unqualified data deletions and 3 newly-tightened constraints — so **an N-2 (pre-v0.4.0) controller**, i.e. any controller whose embedded set stops below 015, cannot boot at all against a schema at version >= 15
- **Invariant:** **documented contract**, contradicted. `docs/operations.md:191`, quoted verbatim: *"old and new controller binaries can both be running against the already-migrated schema during a rolling deploy as long as the migration is backward-compatible (additive columns/tables — **this is the norm for unified-cd's migration history**)."* Per `FINDINGS.md:479` a statement in `docs/` is a contract limb. **The conditional is not what is contradicted** — "as long as the migration is backward-compatible" is correct and would be sound advice on its own. **The parenthetical is**: it is a factual claim about this repository's migration history, an operator reads it as licence to skip checking, and it is false for 5 of 17 migrations including three of the last five. On the invariant table nothing is violated: no run is involved (**not I1/I2**), no lock (**not I3**), no log or artifact (**not I4**), nothing is injected (**not I6**), and no product surface states an untruth (**not I7** — the untruth is in a document, which is the contract limb, not the state-display limb). **I5** (bounded recovery) is the one worth naming and declining: recovery from a bad roll is bounded — roll back — and I5's own text is about the system recovering, not about a document being wrong.
- **Severity:** **major**, argued from this file's own bands at `:6-8` and from nothing else. Against **minor** (`:8` — "diagnosability, **docs gap**, cosmetic"): a gap is an absence, and this is an **affirmative statement of fact about the repository that the repository refutes**. The distinction is load-bearing here because the sentence's *function* is to tell an operator they need not check — an absent sentence would have sent them to `internal/store/migrations/`, and this one sends them to a mixed-version deployment. For **major** (`:7` — "incorrect visible behavior, unbounded recovery"): the visible behaviour of an operator who follows the passage is a controller that **fails to boot**, and it fails on **every** attempt with no window — `v0.3.0:cmd/controller/main.go:215` calls `EnsureControllerKey`, whose SQL names `controller_key_hex` (`v0.3.0:internal/store/postgres.go:1876`, `:1879`, `:1881`, `:1883`), and `015_secrets_v2.up.sql:11` drops that column, so the older replica the passage authorises dies with `42703 undefined_column` at startup on any rig and under any configuration. **The oldest binary the passage authorises must be N-2 for this, not N-1** — v0.4.0 embeds 001-016 and 017 is purely additive, so N-1 boots; see the paragraph in Observed below that establishes it. **`:6` (critical) has THREE independent disjuncts — "data loss / silent corruption / security" — and each is declined separately below, because disposing of one and letting the others follow is how a band gets inherited instead of argued.** **Security** is not in play at all: nothing here crosses a privilege boundary, and 015 and 016 both *narrow* exposure (the KEK stops living beside the ciphertext it wraps, `015:3-5`; plaintext refresh tokens become envelope-encrypted, `015:7-10`). **Silent corruption** is declined because nothing is left wrong — the destroyed rows are gone rather than misreported, both migrations announce at the point of change exactly what they destroy and why (`015_secrets_v2.up.sql:1-10`, `016_drop_secret_scope.up.sql:1-12`), and no product surface was found asserting anything false about the removed rows. **The measurement that would flip THAT disjunct, and which was NOT taken:** upgrade a v0.3.0 deployment carrying a live secret past 016 and observe what a running job that references it does — if the run fails obscurely rather than with a "secret not found", or if any surface still lists the secret name after its row is gone, that is silent corruption and this is **critical**. One rig-hour; this entry's highest-value follow-up. **"Data loss" is the third disjunct, it is the one this entry's own evidence establishes, and it is declined here on its own footing rather than inherited from the doc-sentence subject** — this paragraph is that argument, and it is stated at length because the destruction of every secret and every session is the most damaging thing in the enumeration and it must not reach a band by attachment. The destruction is real, unconditional and total: `015_secrets_v2.up.sql:13` `DELETE FROM public.sessions` and `016_drop_secret_scope.up.sql:13` `DELETE FROM public.secrets`, **both with no `WHERE`**, plus the KEK itself by column drop (`015:11`) — and **no document anywhere warns an operator that upgrading destroys their secrets**: a survey of `docs/` (excluding `docs/superpowers/`) for re-set/cleared/deleted-secret and log-in-again phrasings returns **1** hit, `docs/operations.md:16`, which is about losing the *database*, not about upgrading it; `docs/secrets.md` contains no upgrade or migration text at all; and `docs/operations.md`'s own Upgrades section (`:187-198`) says nothing. **Declined at critical on two grounds, both of which are reads of the migration files rather than claims about how operators work.** **(1) The rows had already ceased to be readable before the `DELETE` ran, and no SQL-only migration could have preserved them.** `016:7-9` records that `SecretBinding`'s canonical encoding *is* the AES-GCM additional authenticated data, so dropping `scope`/`scope_ref` from it means "every existing ciphertext (global rows included) can no longer be authenticated"; `015:8-9` says the same of `sessions.refresh_token` ("Existing rows cannot be re-encrypted (their format predates the binding)"). A re-wrap would need the KEK — which `015:3-5` deliberately removes from the database in the same upgrade, because storing it beside the ciphertext it protects is the defect 015 exists to fix. **So `016:13` deletes ciphertext that one migration earlier had already stopped being decryptable: the `DELETE` is the cleanup, not the destruction**, and relocating the cause does not reduce what the operator holds afterwards — which is why this ground alone would not carry the decline. **(2) The migration states its own premise, and the premise is the product's, not this entry's.** `016:9-11` reads verbatim: *"There are no production secrets to preserve, so the rows are deleted and operators re-set their secrets"*. That is the product asserting the deployment fact that makes the destruction tolerable, at the site of the destruction. **The further step — that secret *values* survive in the operator's own source of truth and so what is lost is availability rather than information — is an INFERENCE about operator practice, is labelled as such here, and is deliberately carrying no weight: the tree cannot tell whether `016:10`'s premise holds for any given deployment, and for one where it does not, values are genuinely lost.** **What survives both grounds is silence rather than loss — nothing published warns that the upgrade destroys secrets and sessions — and silence is `:8`'s own word ("docs gap"), which sits below this entry's band, not above it.** **Why this is disposed of here and NOT split into its own entry** (the alternative was weighed): the destruction has no contract or invariant limb of its own — the only published text it contradicts is `docs/operations.md:191`'s "additive columns/tables", which is *this* entry's limb, so a split would file one contract twice, and the campaign has re-banded entries for looser reasoning than that. It is also not an independent subject: the destruction is the single most damaging instance of exactly what the parenthetical denies. **The same test is applied to the sentinel-rule limb in this entry's Notes, and refusing to split there while splitting here would be incoherent.**
- **Repro:** **NONE. This entry was not executed.** No rig was built, no controller was started and no Postgres was touched; every claim below is a read at this branch's HEAD, and the precedent for filing that way is `FINDINGS.md:1864` (W3-6). Runbook: `test/edgecase/scenarios/w5-1-migration-compat-audit.md`. Captures (code surveys, all untruncated): `w5-1/migration-sweep.txt` (the destructive-operation regex over **all 17** `*.up.sql`, 256 lines, regex in the file header), `w5-1/docs-compat-survey.txt`, `w5-1/sentinels-per-tag.txt`, `w5-1/v030-dropped-column-refs.txt`.
- **Observed (code, not measurement — every line below is a read):**
  - **The denominator is 17 and it is enforced by the product's own suite, not only by this sweep.** `internal/store/migrations/` holds 17 `*.up.sql` and 17 `*.down.sql`, numbered contiguously `001_init` .. `017_run_detached`. `internal/store/verify_test.go:30-46` (`TestSchemaSentinelsCoverAllMigrations`) independently counts `.up.sql` entries in the embedded FS and requires `len(schemaSentinels)` to equal it. **All 17 up files were read in full**, not sampled. **The denominator is the POST-SQUASH set and the distinction is stated because `docs/operations.md:191` speaks of "migration history":** `internal/store/migrations/001_init.up.sql:1-4` is itself the squash of a *former* 001-017 (commit `79c1074`, "squash migrations 001-017 into a single consolidated init", 2026-07-04), so "5 of the 17" is 5 of the 17 **currently embedded**, while the pre-squash history the sentence also covers is not in the tree and was not swept. **This does not weaken the finding** — the unswept history can only add backward-incompatible operations, never remove one from this count — but the claim is 5 of 17 embedded, not 5 of every migration this project has ever shipped.
  - **5 of 17 carry at least one backward-incompatible operation: 003, 005, 014, 015, 016.** The other twelve are additive (001 is the baseline, with no earlier binary to be incompatible with). *Backward-incompatible* is used throughout as: a controller binary whose embedded set stops at some version < n can fail or misbehave against a schema on which n has been applied — read failures, write failures and silent data loss all count; a drop the same file compensates before committing does not, and is marked.
  - **Class A — column drop, 6 columns across 4 migrations.** Each turns every older binary's `SELECT`/`INSERT` naming it into `42703 undefined_column`. `app_sources.managed_jobs` (`internal/store/migrations/003_appsource_managed_resources.up.sql:11`); `agent_enrollment_policies.access_token_ttl` (`internal/store/migrations/014_agent_enrollment_policies.up.sql:23`); `controller_settings.controller_key_hex` (`internal/store/migrations/015_secrets_v2.up.sql:11`); `sessions.refresh_token` (`015_secrets_v2.up.sql:15`); `secrets.scope` (`internal/store/migrations/016_drop_secret_scope.up.sql:16`); `secrets.scope_ref` (`016_drop_secret_scope.up.sql:17`).
  - **Class B — constraint drop, 5 statements across 3 migrations, of which 2 are compensated in the same file.** `005_matrix_variant.up.sql:2` and `:6` drop `step_reports_pkey` / `step_outputs_pkey` and **re-add them widened** at `:3` / `:7` — the transient drop is not the incompatibility, the widened key is (Class E). `014:21` and `014:30` are two dynamic `DROP CONSTRAINT` loops driven by `pg_constraint`, so their count is not statically determinable; `013_agent_identity_auth.up.sql:64` created exactly one constraint the first loop can match. `016:15` drops `secrets_name_scope_scope_ref_key` and replaces it with a **narrower** one.
  - **Class C — `NOT NULL` with the default then removed, 3 columns across 2 migrations.** This is the class that breaks an older binary's `INSERT`: the column is mandatory and the database will not supply a value. `agent_enrollment_policies.access_token_ttl_seconds` (`014:35` `SET NOT NULL`, `014:36` `DROP DEFAULT`); `sessions.refresh_token_dek` (`015:16` then `015:18`); `sessions.refresh_token_ct` (`015:17` then `015:19`).
  - **Class D — data deletion, 3 operations across 2 migrations, two of them unqualified.** `015:13` `DELETE FROM public.sessions` (**no `WHERE`**) — every OIDC session; `015:11` `DROP COLUMN ... controller_key_hex` — the **KEK itself**, i.e. the key for every wrapped DEK still in the database; `016:13` `DELETE FROM public.secrets` (**no `WHERE`**) — every secret, deliberately, for the AAD reason quoted in the Severity line.
  - **Class E — newly-tightened constraints, 3 across 3 migrations. This class is not in the wave plan's table and it is the one "additive columns/tables" is least equipped to describe, because all three are `ADD`s.** They reject writes an older binary makes successfully today. `005:3` (and `005:7`) widen the primary keys to `(run_id, step_index, variant)` / `(..., key)`, so an older binary's `ON CONFLICT (run_id, step_index)` would have no matching unique index and would get `42P10` — **this row is INFERRED and is labelled so, because it cannot be checked against any tag: no tag predates 005 (`v0.0.1` already embeds 001-007), and no binary in this repository has ever been shown to write that statement.** The **evidenced** instance of the class is v0.3.0's secret upsert against the *other* changed table — `ON CONFLICT (name, scope, scope_ref)` at `v0.3.0:internal/store/postgres.go:1541`, a real statement in a real released binary, invalidated by `016:15`/`:18`. The class stands on that site plus the two rows below it; the `step_reports` row is retained as the shape-of-the-class illustration, not as evidence. `016:18` adds `secrets_name_key UNIQUE (name)`, rejecting two secrets sharing a name across scopes, which `001_init.up.sql`'s `UNIQUE (name, scope, scope_ref)` permitted. `014:37-38` adds `CHECK (access_token_ttl_seconds >= 300 AND <= 14400)`, rejecting TTLs between 4 h and 24 h that `013:64`'s `CHECK` allowed.
  - **Reachability, stated because it bounds two classes and the entry would overclaim without it.** `git ls-tree v0.0.1 internal/store/migrations/` shows the **earliest tag already embeds 001-007**, so **003 and 005 predate every released tag** and their breakages are not reachable through any tag pair this repository can assemble. They are counted because the enumeration is of the migration *history*, which is exactly what the contradicted sentence makes its claim about. The classes reachable through a real pair (v0.3.0 <-> HEAD) are 014, 015 and 016 — three of the last five migrations.
  - **What an N-2 controller (v0.3.0) actually does, enumerated rather than asserted** (`w5-1/v030-dropped-column-refs.txt`). v0.3.0's `internal/store` references the dropped columns at: `controller_key_hex` — `postgres.go:1876`, `:1879`, `:1881`, `:1883`, reached from the **boot path** at `v0.3.0:cmd/controller/main.go:215`; `sessions.refresh_token` — `postgres.go:1769`, `:1771`, `:1783`, `:1800`, i.e. every OIDC login, lookup and refresh; `secrets.scope`/`.scope_ref` — `postgres.go:1539`, `:1541`, `:1545`, `:1557`, `:1558`, `:1569`, `:1570`, `:1589`, i.e. every secret set/get/list/delete. **So the mixed-version pair `docs/operations.md:191` authorises is not degraded, it is impossible, and it fails at boot rather than under load — for an N-2 binary. It is NOT impossible for N-1:** `git ls-tree v0.4.0 internal/store/migrations/` shows v0.4.0 embeds 001-016 and 017 is purely additive (`017_run_detached.up.sql:1`, `ADD COLUMN detached BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false`, plus one partial index), so **a v0.4.0 controller boots and runs against a HEAD schema**. The breakage needs a binary whose embedded set stops below 015, and the newest such release is v0.3.0 — which is why this entry's title says N-2 and not N-1.
  - **The docs are good at declaring breaks and bad at exactly one summary sentence, which is why this is a localised defect and not a documentation-wide one.** The survey (`w5-1/docs-compat-survey.txt`, `docs/` only, `docs/superpowers/` excluded, untruncated, regex in the file header) returns **27** hits, **13** substantive. Three of them state incompatibilities bluntly and correctly — `docs/operations.md:195` (k8s-agent and sidecar "**must be upgraded in lockstep**"), `docs/agents.md:654` and `docs/jobs.md:638` ("**There is no backward-compatibility shim for this change.**") — and `docs/authorization.md:190-194` correctly describes what a backward-compatible migration in this repository looks like (`002_add_role.up.sql:1-2`, `ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT 'admin'`, so "current single-token workflows keep working"). **The defect is the five-word parenthetical at `:191` that characterises the whole history, and nothing else in `docs/` repeats it.**
- **Expected:** that an operator who reads `docs/operations.md:191` and rolls controller replicas one at a time gets what the sentence describes — both binaries serving against one schema. What they get, if either binary predates v0.4.0, is a replica that exits at startup; and if they cross 015/016 at all, a deployment with no secrets and no sessions, warned about nowhere in `docs/`.
- **Notes:** **The fix is one sentence and one link, not a code change.** Replace the parenthetical at `docs/operations.md:191` with the truth — that unified-cd's migrations are *not* uniformly additive, that 003, 005, 014, 015 and 016 are not, and that crossing 015/016 destroys every secret and every session — and add the destruction to the Upgrades section as a numbered step, next to the `79c1074` squash exception already there, which is the same shape of hazard and is documented properly. `docs/secrets.md` should carry the same warning, since that is where an operator looks when their secrets are gone.
  - **The unenforced-rule limb, filed here rather than as its own entry, with the reasoning stated because it is a judgement.** `internal/store/verify.go:21-27` is one comment block stating two rules. The first (`:21-23`) names its enforcer and the enforcer works: `internal/store/verify_test.go:30-46` counts `.up.sql` entries in the embedded FS, requires `len(schemaSentinels)` to match, and requires versions `1..N` in order with non-empty `migration` and `table`. The second (`:25-27`) — *"A later migration must never drop or rename a sentinel object; if one must, the sentinel entry has to be changed in the same commit, or older binaries verifying a newer database will report false drift"* — **names no enforcer and has none**: `grep -rn "schemaSentinels\|verifySchema" --include=*_test.go internal/` returns **7** lines, all inside `verify_test.go`, and not one compares a sentinel against any later migration's text. **It is filed as a Notes clause and NOT as a second violation or a standalone observation, for three reasons.** (i) **It fails `FINDINGS.md:479`'s INCLUSION limb, which is the clean ground and is used instead of the exclusion limb.** `:479` requires a contract limb to be a *published* promise — *"an exported API field, a schema column, or a statement in `docs/`"* — and a doc comment on an unexported package-level variable is **none of the three**. (The same line's *exclusion* clause names "an unexported helper's own doc comment"; `schemaSentinels` is an unexported **var**, not a helper, so reaching the same verdict through the exclusion would be an analogy where the inclusion is an exact fit. Same outcome, no stretch — and it matters that the enumerated limb is the one applied, because the campaign has re-banded entries for reaching a verdict by analogy.) (ii) Its subject is not independent of this entry's — the rule exists *because* migrations in this repository drop things, so it is corroboration of intent, which is where corroboration belongs. (iii) **The hazard is latent, not live, and that was verified by enumerating every tag rather than sampling**: `schemaSentinels` was extracted from all of them (`w5-1/sentinels-per-tag.txt`) — absent at `v0.0.1`/`v0.0.2` (`internal/store/verify.go` does not exist yet), 1-8 at `v0.0.3` and `v0.1.0`, 1-9 at `v0.2.0`, 1-10 at `v0.2.1`, 1-12 at `v0.3.0`, 1-16 at `v0.4.0`, 1-17 at HEAD — and **every list is a strict prefix of the next**, with no entry ever removed, renumbered or repointed. **"Every ref" means every ref including the non-release one, said rather than silently dropped:** `git tag` returns nine names, and the ninth is `backup/regression-review-pre-rebase`, whose row in the capture is empty for the same reason `v0.0.1`/`v0.0.2` are — `internal/store/verify.go` does not exist at that ref — so the empty row is genuine and the conclusion is unaffected. **The rule has never been violated; it is simply not checked.** The cheap fix is a test that parses `migrations/*.up.sql` for `DROP COLUMN`/`DROP TABLE`/`DROP INDEX`/`RENAME` and fails if any names a sentinel object of an earlier version — a pure-Go test needing no database, unlike the rest of `verify_test.go`.
  - **Cross-reference, not a re-filing.** `FINDINGS.md:1627` already records this campaign being bitten by reading a migration that a later one had superseded: a W3 query written from `001_init.up.sql:247-256`'s `scope`/`scope_ref` errored because `016_drop_secret_scope.up.sql:13-18` had dropped them. **That is the same defect class from the reader's side** — `001_init.up.sql` is still the only place the full `secrets` shape appears, and it has been wrong since 016 — and it is evidence that "the migrations are additive" is a belief this repository actively produces in its readers.

## W5-1 — observation, **NOT EXECUTED (code-read only)**: `verifySchema` runs **after** golang-migrate releases the migration advisory lock, so during a mixed-version boot a replica can read another replica's in-flight `dirty=true` and `os.Exit(1)` with no retry — and the remedy the troubleshooting guide prescribes for exactly this case is "restart the controller", which neither the binary nor the shipped HA compose file performs
- **Invariant:** **none, and the three candidates are named and declined rather than left unexamined**, because the wave plan called this "one real mixed-version-only availability defect" and a violation needs an invariant's own text or a published promise to contradict (`FINDINGS.md:479`). **(a)** `docs/high-availability.md:279` — *"This enables one-at-a-time rolling deploys with no downtime"* — describes the **SIGTERM drain sequence** enumerated immediately above it at `:273-277`, not startup; and with three replicas the loss of one is not service downtime. Its own text does not reach this. **(b)** `docs/troubleshooting.md:1204` **anticipates this exact case** — *"another replica's migration is currently in flight (this can happen transiently during a mixed-version rolling deploy). Restart the controller first"* — so the behaviour is documented, not contradicted; a remedy that requires manual action is not a promise the product breaks. **(c)** No invariant applies: **I1** is run accounting and no run exists yet; **I5** (bounded recovery) is closest and recovery **is** bounded, by the operator restart the docs name. **Filed as an observation on that reasoning.**
- **Severity:** **minor (observation)**, argued from `:8`'s own words — *"diagnosability, docs gap, cosmetic"*. The diagnosability limb is the live one and it is met twice over: the error message the operator sees (`internal/store/verify.go:63-67`) already tells them which of the two causes it might be and what to do, and `docs/troubleshooting.md:1204` repeats it. **Not major** by `:7` ("incorrect visible behavior, unbounded recovery"): the behaviour is a loud, correct, fail-fast exit rather than an incorrect one, and recovery is a single restart, which is the opposite of unbounded. **What keeps it at the top of minor rather than the bottom** is that the prescribed recovery is not automated anywhere the project ships: `cmd/controller/main.go:257-259` exits, and `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml` gives the controllers no `restart:` policy, so in the campaign's own reference deployment the replica stays down until a human notices.
- **Repro:** **NONE. This entry was not executed and no timing of any kind was taken.** Runbook: `test/edgecase/scenarios/w5-1-migration-compat-audit.md` §Step 5. Everything below is a read of this branch's HEAD plus `golang-migrate v4.19.1` from the module cache.
- **Observed (code, not measurement):**
  - **The chain, link by link.** `internal/store/postgres.go:137` calls `m.Up()`. In `golang-migrate v4.19.1`, `func (m *Migrate) Up()` at `migrate.go:265` opens with `m.lock()` at `:266` and every exit returns through `m.unlockErr(...)` at `:283` — **the lock covers `Up()` and nothing after it**. `internal/store/postgres.go:142` then calls `verifySchema(db)`, which is **after `Up()` returned and therefore after `Unlock()` ran**; nothing between `:137` and `:142` re-acquires anything. `internal/store/verify.go:55` reads `SELECT version, dirty FROM schema_migrations`; `:62-68` hard-fails on `dirty` **unconditionally — no retry, no backoff, no re-read anywhere in the function or its caller**. `cmd/controller/main.go:257-259` turns that into `slog.Error("migrate", ...)` and `os.Exit(1)`.
  - **The lock itself is correct, which is why the gap is narrow and specific.** `github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4/database/postgres/postgres.go:233-248`: `Lock()` is `SELECT pg_advisory_lock($1)` at `:241`, with the id from `GenerateAdvisoryLockId(p.config.DatabaseName, p.config.migrationsSchemaName, p.config.migrationsTableName)` at `:235` — **the same three inputs on every replica, so the same id** — and the comment at `:240` records that it blocks indefinitely rather than failing. The lock was scoped to `Up()` because `Up()` is the dangerous part; `verifySchema` was appended after it without the scope being widened.
  - **The precondition is stricter than "a mixed-version boot", and this corrects the wave plan's mechanism.** `dirty=true` is written only from inside `runMigrations`, immediately before executing each migration (`migrate.go:738`, `SetVersion(migr.TargetVersion, true)`, cleared at `:750`), **and `:738` is the only site in the package that ever writes `true`** — `SetVersion` occurs three times in `migrate.go` and the other two are `:374` (`Force`, which passes `false`) and `:750` (the clear). **The corollary is stronger than "the lock is scoped to `Up()`": `Up()` re-reads `dirty` itself at `migrate.go:270-277` — INSIDE the lock, returning `ErrDirty` before anything is applied — so `verifySchema` at `internal/store/postgres.go:142` is the ONLY unlocked `dirty` read in the process.** The library's own read of the same flag is correctly serialised; the product's is the one that is not. **A replica with nothing to apply returns `ErrNoChange` and never writes `dirty` at all.** So three same-version replicas cold-starting a fresh database **cannot** produce this: the first to take the lock applies everything and the other two find nothing. The interleaving requires the replica acquiring the lock **second** to hold a **strictly larger** migration set: replica A (older, set ends at 16) finishes `Up()` and unlocks -> replica B (newer, set ends at 17) acquires and writes `dirty=true` -> A's `verifySchema` at `postgres.go:142` reads `dirty=true` -> `verify.go:62-68` -> `main.go:259` `os.Exit(1)`.
  - **The window width was NOT measured.** Stated plainly because the campaign's rule requires it: no rig was built, no `Up()` was timed, and no interleaving was observed. What is *read* is that the window is bounded below by zero and above by one migration's SQL plus two `SET VERSION` statements — an interval this audit did not time and does not estimate. **Nothing in this entry is a measurement.**
  - **The "no `restart:` policy" claim is verified by enumeration, not asserted.** `grep -rn "restart" test/ha/` returns **2** hits over the whole directory: `docker-compose.ha.yaml:168` and `hardfailure_test.go:115` (a comment). The compose file declares **10** services — `postgres:3`, `garage:25`, `mc:58`, `controller1: &ctrl:78`, `controller2: *ctrl:103`, `controller3: *ctrl:104`, `nginx:106`, `agent-enroll:126`, `agent1:179`, `agent2:216`. The single directive is `restart: "no"` at `:168`, **inside the `agent-enroll` block (`:126-168`), not on a controller**. The three controllers inherit `&ctrl` (`:78-101`), which carries `build:`, `environment:`, `volumes:` and `depends_on:` and no `restart:`. **So the claim is true of the controllers and needs one qualification the plan did not carry: the file is not silent about `restart:` — it names it once, explicitly, on another service, with the value `"no"`.** Compose's default is `no`, so an exited controller stays exited.
- **Expected:** nothing published promises otherwise — see the Invariant line. The gap is between what `docs/troubleshooting.md:1204` tells the operator to do and what anything the project ships actually does.
- **Notes:** **The fix is one line and it is in the product, not the docs**: move `verifySchema(db)` inside the locked region, or — since `Migrate` owns the handle — retry the `dirty` read a bounded number of times before failing, which is what the error message's own "if this error persists across restarts" clause already assumes someone is doing. Either removes the failure mode entirely. **The `restart:` gap is worth closing independently of it**: `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml` is the campaign's reference HA deployment and gives its controllers no restart policy, so *any* transient startup failure — this one, W0-1's `store init` crash-on-first-boot (`FINDINGS.md:43`), or the `garage` `BucketExists` exit the file itself documents at `:96-99` — is permanent there in a way it would not be under a real orchestrator.
  - **How to measure it, if the campaign ever wants to — and it is NOT a compose scenario.** A Postgres-backed unit test in `internal/store`: one test database, two `Migrate` instances over two *different* embedded migration sets (one truncated at 16, one full at 17); run the truncated one to completion, then call `verifySchema` on its handle while the second instance is inside `runMigrations` on a deliberately slow seventeenth migration. `verify_test.go` already stands up and probes throwaway schemas (`:63`, `:69`, `:83`, `:88`, `:102`), so the harness exists. That test answers both "does it fire" and, with timing, "how wide". A compose rig answers neither reliably and costs two cold controller image builds (`test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml:79-81` builds from source; `:103-104` are anchor aliases of the same build, so a second version means a second cold build with no layer sharing).

## W5-1 — observation, **NOT EXECUTED (code-read only)**: the three W5 sub-scenarios that were cut are recorded as **results about the product**, not as omissions — concurrent migration startup is safe by construction, the sentinel drift guard cannot fire for any tag pair this repository can assemble, and a v0.3.0 controller beside HEAD was not built because reading settles what building would have shown
- **Invariant:** none. This entry records three negative results and the enumerations behind them. It is filed because a refuted scenario that leaves no trace becomes a scenario the next wave pays to re-refute, and because two of the three are **positive statements about the product's correctness** that the campaign has otherwise had few occasions to make.
- **Severity:** **minor (observation).** No product defect is claimed in this entry; per `:8` the value is diagnosability — of the campaign's own coverage.
- **Repro:** **NONE.** Runbook: `test/edgecase/scenarios/w5-1-migration-compat-audit.md` §Step 6. Captures: `w5-1/sentinels-per-tag.txt`, `w5-1/v030-dropped-column-refs.txt`.
- **Observed (code, not measurement):**
  - **RESULT 1 — concurrent migration startup is safe by construction, and the construction is nameable.** Three replicas booting simultaneously against one database cannot race inside `Up()`. `github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4@v4.19.1/migrate.go:265-266` takes `m.lock()` as the **first statement** of `Up()` and releases only through `m.unlockErr` at `:283`, so the lock spans the version read, the dirty check, `readUp` and every applied migration. `.../database/postgres/postgres.go:241` implements it as `SELECT pg_advisory_lock($1)` with an id derived at `:235` from `(DatabaseName, migrationsSchemaName, migrationsTableName)` — **identical on every replica, because all three come from the same DSN and the same driver defaults** — and the driver's comment at `:240` records that it blocks indefinitely rather than erroring. Late replicas **queue**; they do not collide and they do not fail. **This is a positive result and it is worth having in writing:** the campaign has repeatedly found that unified-cd's HA safety rests on Postgres primitives rather than application logic, and W0-1 (`FINDINGS.md:22`) is the counter-example where a connection *pooler* broke exactly this assumption for leader election — here the same primitive is used correctly and no pooler sits in the path, because `Migrate` opens its own `stdlib.OpenDB` handle from the raw DSN (`internal/store/postgres.go:118-127`). **The non-trivial corollary: this is also why the entry above exists** — the lock is scoped to `Up()` precisely because `Up()` is the dangerous part, and `verifySchema` was appended after it without the scope being widened.
  - **RESULT 2 — the sentinel drift guard cannot fire for ANY tag pair this repository can assemble, established by enumerating every tag rather than the two the plan sampled.** `schemaSentinels` was extracted from all of them (`w5-1/sentinels-per-tag.txt`): **absent** at `v0.0.1` and `v0.0.2` (`internal/store/verify.go` does not exist yet — there was no guard to fire); **1-8** at `v0.0.3` and `v0.1.0`; **1-9** at `v0.2.0`; **1-10** at `v0.2.1`; **1-12** at `v0.3.0`; **1-16** at `v0.4.0`; **1-17** at HEAD; and **absent** at the ninth ref `git tag` returns, `backup/regression-review-pre-rebase`, for the same reason as `v0.0.1`/`v0.0.2` — **that row is named rather than omitted, because "every tag" is the load-bearing word in this result and a silently skipped ref would make it unverifiable.** **Every list is a strict prefix of the next** — no entry is ever removed, renumbered or repointed at a different object — and the objects themselves survive: of the twelve a `v0.3.0` binary would probe (`runs`, `pats.role`, `app_sources.managed_resources`, `audit_logs`, `step_reports.variant`, `app_sources.sync_status`, `step_reports.child_run_id`, `runs_job_name_created_idx`, `agents.capabilities`, `sidecar_status`, `runs_terminal_updated_idx`, `run_log_archives.line_count`), **none is touched by any of migrations 013-017**. So that binary reads `version=17`, probes all twelve — the skip guard at `internal/store/verify.go:70` is `if s.version > version { continue }`, which exists to skip migrations **not yet applied** and therefore skips nothing when the database is *ahead* of the binary — finds all twelve, and **`verifySchema` returns nil**. **The result is the part that matters: `verifySchema` passing is not the same as the binary working.** It passes, and the binary then dies on its first query against a dropped column. The false-drift hazard `verify.go:25-27` warns about is **latent**, and a scenario built around it would have measured nothing.
  - **RESULT 3 — a v0.3.0 controller beside HEAD was deliberately not built, and reading settles what building would have shown.** The wave plan's reason is a rig property: v0.3.0 predates `UNIFIED_CONTROLLER_KEY_FILE` and reads only `UNIFIED_CONTROLLER_KEY`, while `test/ha/docker-compose.ha.yaml:84` supplies the former. **The stronger reason is rig-independent**: `v0.3.0:cmd/controller/main.go:215` calls `EnsureControllerKey` on the **boot path**, and its SQL names `controller_key_hex` four times (`v0.3.0:internal/store/postgres.go:1876`, `:1879`, `:1881`, `:1883`) — the column `internal/store/migrations/015_secrets_v2.up.sql:11` drops. **Boot-time `42703 undefined_column`, guaranteed, zero window, on any rig and under any environment.** And it is not the only site: the same capture enumerates `sessions.refresh_token` at `v0.3.0:internal/store/postgres.go:1769`, `:1771`, `:1783`, `:1800` (every OIDC login, lookup and refresh) and `secrets.scope`/`.scope_ref` at `:1539`, `:1541`, `:1545`, `:1557`, `:1558`, `:1569`, `:1570`, `:1589` (every secret operation, including an `ON CONFLICT (name, scope, scope_ref)` at `:1541` that is Class E as well as Class A). **Two cold controller images — npm ci + vite + Go, no layer sharing — were not spent to observe a `42703` that four `git grep`s establish.** This is recorded as a decision with its cost, not as an omission.
- **Expected:** n/a — these are results, and two of the three are the product behaving correctly.
- **Notes:** **The transferable rule this task adds, since it is the one that produced its three corrections: when a plan states a count, recount it; when a plan states a mechanism, re-derive it.** The wave plan's `file:line` claims all resolved — an eighth consecutive wave for that half of the pattern — and its **counts** did not: "four of the last five migrations" is **three** (013 is purely additive and belongs with 017 in the clean column; the headline appears to have counted table rows rather than migrations in the window), and the docs survey is **27 hits / 13 substantive** against a recorded 20 / 8. Nor did one mechanism: the `dirty` race needs the second locker to hold the *newer* set, not merely a *different* one. **Full corrections list, with the reasoning, in `test/edgecase/scenarios/w5-1-migration-compat-audit.md` §"Corrections to the wave plan's reconnaissance".**
